chapters.chapter_name: Reflection of Light at Curved Surfaces

pages.text: 1.1 Reflection of light by spherical mirrors The first law of reflection tells us A light ray incident at an angle with the normal at the point of incidence will get reflected making equal angle with the normal. This law is true for all surfaces, be it a plane surface or a curved one. The important words here are ‘the angle made with normal at the point of A incidence’. If for any surface one can decide the normal and find the incident N angle, it is possible to deduce the angle made by the reflected ray. It is very easy to find a normal at any point on the plane surface but for aA curved or uneven surface it is not straight forward. G Activity 1 N Finding the normal to a curved surface A L E T fig-1(a) fig-1(b) fig-1(c) , Take a small piTece of thin foam or rubber (like the sole of a slipper). Put some pins along a straight line on the foam as shown in the fig.-1(a). R All these pins are perpendicular to the plane of foam. If the foam is consideEred as a mirror, each pin would represent the normal at that point. Any ray incident at the point where the pin makes contact with the surface C will reflect with the same angle as the incident ray made with the pin- S normal. Now bend the foam piece inwards as shown in fig.-1(b), what differences will you observe to the pins? They still represent the normal at various points, but you will notice that all the pins tend to converge at a point (or intersect at a point). If we bend the foam piece outwards, we will see that the pins seem to move away from each other or in other words they diverge as shown in fig.-1(c). 2 Reflection of light at curved surfaces

This gives us an idea of what is likely to happen with a spherical mirror. A concave mirror will be like the rubber sole bent inwards (fig-1(b)) and the convex mirror will be like the rubber sole bent out wards (fig-1(c)). For a concave mirror, like these pins in fig.-1(b), all normals will converge towards a point. This point is called centre of curvature(C) of A the mirror. N Recall a little bit of geometry: while learning about circleAs and tangents, you have learnt that a radius is always perpendicular G to the tangent to the circle drawn at the point. N This gives us a clue about how we can find normal at a point on a A spherical mirror. All that we have to do is to draw a line from the point on the mirror to cenLtre of the Normal sphere. principal axis E P(pole) C It is much easier to imagine this in a two T fig-2(a) dimensional fig. as shown in fig.-2(a). The concave r mirror is actually a part of a big sphere. In order to , find this centre poinTt (centre of curvature) we have to C R think of the centre of the sphere to which the concave i R r mirror belongs. The line drawn from C to any point on E P C the mirror gives the normal at that point. CFor the ray R, the incident angle is the angle it fig-2(b) makes with the normal shown as i and the reflected S angle is shown as r in fig.-2(b). We know by first law of reflection i = r. The mid point (Geometrical centre) of the mirror is called pole (P) of the mirror. The horizontal line shown in the fig.s which passes through the centre of curvature and pole is called principal axis of the mirror. The distance from P to C is radius of curvature (R) of the mirror. Try to construct different reflected rays for any array of rays that are parallel to the principal axis as shown in fig. 2(b). What is your observation? 3 Reflection of light at curved surfaces

1.1.1 Verifying your drawing with experiment: To verify this we must first find out some way of obtaining a beam of parallel rays. How do we do that? A First we need to know the situation fig-3 N in which one gets parallel rays of light. In the fig.-3 we have stuck two pins on a thermocole block. TAhe pins are parallel to each other. As we see in the fig., when a source of light is G kept very near, we see the shadows diverging (from the base of the pins). N As we move the source away from the pins, the angle of divergence gets reduced. If we move the source far away we willA get parallel shadows. But as we move the candle away, the light intensity becomes low. That means L to get a beam of parallel rays the source should be at a long distance and it E must be of sufficient intensity. Where do we find one such source? T Yes, we have one easily available source, you probably have guessed it: The Sun. Let us do an experiment with sun rays and a concave mirror. , T Activity 2 R Hold a concave mirror such that sunlight falls on it. Take a small paper E and slowly move it in front of the mirror and find out the point where you C get the smallest and brightest spot, which will be the image of the sun. (See to it that your paper is small so that it does not obstruct the incoming S sun rays.) The rays coming from the sun parallel to the principal axis of concave mirror converge to a point (see fig.-4). P F C This point is called Focus or focal point (F) of the concave mirror. fig-4 4 Reflection of light at curved surfaces

Measure the distance of this spot from the pole of the mirror. This distance is the focal length (f) of the mirror. The radius of curvature will be twice this distance (R=2f). Does the reflected rays converge to a point in the picture you draw with different rays based on fig. 2(b)? A · What happens if you hold the paper at a distance shorter than the focal N length from the mirror and move it away? · Does the image of the sun become smaller or bigger? A You will notice that the image of the sun first keeps on becoming small, G beyond the focal point it keeps on becoming enlarged. Note: while drawing a ray diagram N sometimes it is not clear which is the A reflecting side of the mirror. Hence we follow L a convention of showing lines on the non- E reflecting side(coated side). C F P Can you draw the same diagramT for a convex mirror? , fig-5 See fig.-5. The pTarallel rays appear to diverge after reflection. If we extend the reflected rays backwards they R meet at ‘F’ i.e. focus of the convex mirror. E Think and discuss C · See fig.-5. A set of parallel rays are falling on a convex mirror. S What conclusions can you draw from this? · Will you get a point image if you place a paper at the focal point? When parallel rays are incident on a concave mirror, on reflection they meet at the focus. · Do we get an image with a concave mirror at the focus every time? Let us find out. 5 Reflection of light at curved surfaces

Lab Activity Aim: Observing the types of images and measuring the object distance and image distance from the mirror. Material required: A candle, paper, concave mirror (known focal length), V-stand, measuring tape or meter scale. A Procedure: Place the concave mirror on V-stand, arrange a candle N and meter scale as shown in fig.-6. A Keep the candle at different distances from the mirror (10cm to 80cm) along the axis and by moving the paper (screen) find thGe position where you get the sharp image on paper. (Take care that flame is above the axis of N mirror, paper is below the axis). Note down your observations in table-1. It is possible you may not get any image at some positions, note down that too! Since we know the focal point and centre of curvature, we can reclassify our above observations as shown in table-2. What do you infer from this table?. 6 Reflection of light at curved surfaces

At this point we suggest that you make one more observation. You have been trying to get the image on a paper when the object is at different positions. At the same time also look into the mirror and note your observations about how the image appears. · Is it inverted or erect? enlarged or diminished? A Table - 2 N Position of the Position of Enlarged/ Inverted or Real or candle (object) the image diminished erect virtual A Between mirror & F G At focal point N Between F and C At centre of curvature A Beyond C L What do you infer from the table-2? E Let us try to draw ray diagrams with concave mirrors and compare T them with your inferences. 1.2 Ray diagrams (Im,age formation by concave mirror) T In activity-2 we saw the ray diagram of sunrays parallel to the concave R mirror and the image of the sun was very small at the focal point (See fig.E-4). Now we shall develop a technique to draw ray diagrams when an object is placed anywhere on the axis of the mirror and validate the C above observations. S Here we will take at least two rays originating from the same point on the object but with different direction, see how they get reflected from the mirror and find out the point where they meet to form the image. Let us take an example. B As shown in the fig.-7, assume a concave mirror A and a candle placed at some distance along the axis of the mirror. fig-7 7 Reflection of light at curved surfaces

The diagram shows two rays coming from the tip of the flame (object). The reflected rays are constructed based on the laws of reflection.They meet at point A. The tip of the flame of the reflected image will be at the point of intersection, A. · Why only at point A? If we hold the screen at any point before or beyond point A (for example A at point B), we see that the rays will meet the screen at different points. N Therefore, the image of the tip of the flame will be formed at different points due to these rays. If we draw more rays emanating from the sAame tip we will see that at point A they will meet but at point B they won’t. So, the G image of the tip of the flame will be sharp if we hold the screen at point A and will become blurred (due to overlaping of multiple images) when we N move the paper slightly in any direction (forward or backward). A Is this not something that you observed during the previous experiment with sun rays? L However, it is not going to be easy to evaluate the angle of reflection E for any arbitrary ray, every time we will have to find the normal, measure T the incident angle and construct a ray with equal angle on the other side. This would be a tedious task, can R 1 , we find any other simpler method? T Yes, there are a few. Based on our discussion so R far, we can identify some appropriate rays which we P F C can take as E representative rays to find the point ‘A’. fig- f 8 ig-8 We have seen that all rays that are parallel to the C axis get reflected such that they pass through the focal Spoint of the mirror. So, for drawing any diagram the most suitable ray to draw will be the one that comes from the object and goes parallel to the axis of the mirror. The reflected ray will be the line drawn from the point of incidence on the mirror and passes through the focal point of the mirror. To make it more convenient we will always take rays that come from the tip of the object. See the ray R in fig.-8. 1 The converse situation of previous one is also true; that is, a ray that passes through the focal point of the mirror will travel parallel to the axis after reflection. 8 Reflection of light at curved surfaces

This gives us our second ray. This will be the ray coming from the tip of the flame and going through the focal point and falling on the mirror. After reflection, this ray travels parallel to the axis. So we draw the R 2 reflected ray as a line parallel to the axis coming P F C from the point where the incident ray meets the A mirror. See R in fig.-9. 2 Nfig-9 Using the rays R , R and finding the point 1 2 where they intersect we know the point where the A image of the tip is formed. The second ray that we chose for earlier ray diagrams is the ray coming from the tip of the object and going through the focal point but it is not possible as such a ray will not meet the mirror. So we must use the third ray, a ray coming from the tip of the object and going through the centre of curvature. But that to does not seem to be possible. So we make a small change. They appear to be coming from one point. We can get this point by extending the rays backwards as shown in fig.-14. The image does not really exist the way we see in other cases, but it is visible to us. As seen in the fig.-14, the image will be erect and enlarged. Does this match with your observations? This image that we get by extending the rays backwards is called a virtual image. We cannot get this on a screen like a real image. 11 Reflection of light at curved surfaces

They enlarge the image when the E object is held close to the mirror (less than the focal length). Also, the T image is erect. This property is used at many places and most commonly in shaving mirrors and mirr,ors used by dentists. Another property is the T way that it can converge the rays to its focal point. This is extensively used R in many places. Look at the shape of TV dish antennas. If you Elook around you will see many curved surfaces but all surfaces are not concave, many of C these are convex. summary: 1.1 Reflection of light by spherical mirrors The first law of reflection tells us A light ray incident at an angle with the normal at the point of incidence will get reflected making equal angle with the normal. This law is true for all surfaces, be it a plane surface or a curved one. The important words here are ‘the angle made with normal at the point of A incidence’.

If for any surface one can decide the normal and find the incident N angle, it is possible to deduce the angle made by the reflected ray. It is very easy to find a normal at any point on the plane surface but for aA curved or uneven surface it is not straight forward. This law is true for all surfaces, be it a plane surface or a curved one. The important words here are ‘the angle made with normal at the point of A incidence’. If for any surface one can decide the normal and find the incident N angle, it is possible to deduce the angle made by the reflected ray. It is very easy to find a normal at any point on the plane surface but for aA curved or uneven surface it is not straight forward. pages.text: A CHAPTER N 2 A Chemical Equations G N A We had discussed in the previous classes on different changes that L occur around us and we have classified those changes into Physical and Chemical changes. E Now, just think about the changes involved in the following processes T in our daily life. · The process of dige,stion. T · Burning of the crackers. R · The process of Respiration. · PoEwdered lime added to water. · Ripening of the Mango. C · Exposing iron nails to moisture in air for longer period. S What changes do you notice? Are they physical changes or chemical changes ? Are they temporary changes or permanent changes? In all the above processes, the nature of original substance would be changed. If new substances are formed with properties completely unlike to those of the original substances, we say that a chemical change has taken place. · How do we know that a chemical reaction has taken place? Let us perform some activities to know this. 22 Chemical Equations

Activity 1 Take about 1 g of quick lime (calcium oxide) in a beaker. Add 10 ml of water to this. Touch the beaker with your finger. · What do you notice? You notice that the beaker is hot. The reason is that the calcium oxide (quick lime) reacts with water with the liberation of heat energy. Calcium A oxide dissolves in water producing colourless solution. Test the nature of solution with litmus papers. N · What is the nature of the solution? A A red litmus paper turns blue when dipped in the above solution. A blue litmus does not change its colour. Hence, the solution is a basic G solution. Activity 2 N Take about 100 ml of water in a beaker and dissolve a A small quantity of sodium sulphate (Na SO ). 2 4 Take about 100ml of water in anothLer beaker and dissolve a small quantity of barium chloride (BaCl ). E 2 Observe the colours of the solutions obtained. NaSO 2 4 T · What are the colours of the above solutions? · Can you name the solution s obtained? BaCl 2 , Add Na SO solution to BaCl solution and observe. T 2 4 2 fig-1:Formation of barium · Do you observe any change on mixing these solutions? sulphate precipitate R Activity 3 Take soEme zinc granules in a conical flask. Add about 20 ml of dilute hydrochloric acid to C the zinc granules in the conical flask. Observe the changes in the conical flask. S · What changes do you notice? Now keep a burning match stick near the H gas 2 mouth of the conical flask. Conical plask · What happens to burning match stick? · Touch the bottom of the conical flask with Dil. HCl your fingers. What do you notice? Zinc granules · Is it hot? fig-2:Formation of hydrogen gas by the action of dilute HCl From the above activities you can on zinc and testing of H gas conclude that during a chemical change: 2 23 Chemical Equations

1. The original substances lose their characteristic properties. Hence these may be products with different physical states and colours. 2. Chemical changes may be exothermic or endothermic i.e, heat may be liberated or absorbed. 3. They may form an insoluble substance known as precipitate. A 4. Gas may be evolved In our daily life we observe variety of changes taking place around uNs. In this chapter we study various types of chemical reactions and their A symbolic representation. G 2.1 Chemical Equations In activity 1, when calcium oxide reacts with wateNr a new substance is formed which is unlike to either calcium oxide or water. The description A of chemical reactions in a sentence in activity-1 is quite long. It can be written in shorter form as a word equation.L The word equation of the above rEeaction is, calcium oxide + water g calcium hydroxide ......................... (1) T (Reactants) (Product) The substances which undergo chemical change in the reaction are , T called reactants and the new substances formed are called products. A chemical Rreaction written in the form of word equation shows the change of reactants to products by an arrow placed between them. The E reactants, are written on the left side of the arrow and the final substances, or prCoducts are written on the right side of the arrow. The arrow head point faces the products showing the direction of the reaction. S If there is more than one reactant or product involved in the reaction, they are indicated with a plus (+) sign between them. 2.1.1 Writing a Chemical Equation · Can you write a chemical reaction in any other shorter way other than the way we discussed above? Chemical equations can be made more precise and useful if we use chemical formulae instead of words. 24 Chemical Equations

Generally, a compound is written by giving its chemical formula, which lists the symbols of the constituent elements and uses the subscript to indicate the number of atoms of each element present in the compound. If no subscript is written the number 1 is understood. Thus we can write calcium oxide as CaO, water as H O and the compound formed by the 2 reaction of these two compounds is calcium hydroxide Ca (OH) . 2 A Now the reaction of calcium oxide with water can be written as: CaO + H O g Ca (OH) ............................ (2)N 2 2 In the above chemical equation, count the number of atoms of each A element on left side and right side of arrow. · Is the number of atoms of each element are equal on both sides? G Observe the following reactions and their chemical equations. Zinc metal reacts with dilute HCl to yield ZnCl and libNerates Hydrogen gas. 2 Zn+ HCl g ZnCl + H ............................ (3) 2 A2 Sodium sulphate reacts with barium chloride to give white precipitate, barium sulphate and sodium chloride. L Na SO + BaCl g BaSOE + NaCl ............................. (4) 2 4 2 4 · Do the atoms of each element on left side equal to the atoms of the T element on the right side of the equation? · Do the atoms of all ,the elements of the reactants also there on the T product side? R THINK AND WRITE You have brushed the wall with an aqueous suspension of Ca(OH). After two E 2 days the wall turned to white colour. ·CWrite the balanced chemical reactions for the above changes using the appropriate symbols and formulae?. S 2.1.2 Balancing Chemical Equations According to the law of conservation of mass, the total mass of the products formed in chemical reaction must be equal to the total mass of reactants consumed. You know that an atom is the smallest particle of an element that takes part in a chemical reaction. It is the atom which accounts for the mass of any substance. As per the law of conservatioin of mass the number of atoms of each element before and after reaction must be the same. 25 Chemical Equations

All the chemical equations must be balanced, because atoms are neither created nor destroyed in chemical reactions. A chemical equation in which the number of atoms of different elements on the reactant side (left side) are same as those on product side (right side) is called a balanced reaction. Formula units: Balancing a chemical equation involves finding out how many A formula units of each substance take part in the reaction.as the name N implies, is one unit – whether atom, ion or molecule – corresponding to a given formula. One formula unit of NaCl for example is one NaA+ (Sodium ion) and one Cl– (Chlorine ion); one formula unit of MgBr is one Mg2+ G2 ion and two Br– ions and one formula unit of water is one H O molecule. 2 Now let us balance the chemical equation using a systematic method. N For this take the example of hydrogen reacting with oxygen to form water. A Step 1: Write the equation with the correct chemical formulae for each reactant and product. L For example, in the reaction of hydrogen with oxygen to yield water, E you can write chemical equations as follow: T H + O g H O ……(5) NNoo ooff aattoommss 2 2 2 EElleemmeenntt Step 2: After writing th e molecular formulae LLHHSS RRHHSS , of the substances the equation is to be balanced. HH 22 22 T For this we should not touch the ratio of atoms in OO 22 11 the moleculesR of the susbtances but we may assign suitable numbers as the coefficients before the formulae. E In the above equation write ‘2’ before the molecular formula of hyCdrogen and also ‘2’ before the molecular formula of water. Observe whether atoms of both the elements hydrogen and oxyen are same (or) S different on both the sides. They are in the same number on both sides. Therefore, the equation is balanced. 2H + O g 2H O …………..(6) 2 2 2 Step 3: Sometimes there is a possibility that the coefficients of all the substances getting divided with a suitable number. Since we require the lowest ratio of coefficient for reactants and products the above operation is to be done. If no common factor is there, there is no need to divide the equation. The above equation needs no division of the coefficients of the substances. 26 Chemical Equations

Step 4: Verify the equation for the balancing of atoms on both sides of the equations. The above equation (6) is a balanced equation. Let us work out some more examples to see how equations are balanced. Eg-1: Combustion of propane (C H ) in presence of oxygen 3 8 Propane, C H is a colourless, odourless gas often used as a heating A 3 8 and cooking fuel. Write the chemical equation for the combustion reaction N of propane. The reactants are propane and oxygen and the products are carbon dioxide and water. Write the reaction in terms of symAbols and formulae of the substances involved and follow the four steps described G in previous discussion. Step 1: Write the unbalanced equation using correct chemical formulae N for all substances. A C H + O g CO + H O ............(7), (Skeleton equation) 3 8 2 2 2 Note: Unbalanced chemical equatioLn containing molecular formulae of the substances is known as skeleton equation. E Step 2: Compare number of atoms T of each element on both sides. Find the No of atoms Element coefficients to balance the e quation. It LHS RHS , is better to start with the most complex C 3(in C H ) 1 (in CO ) T 3 8 2 substance – in this case C H .Look at H 8 (in C H ) 2(in H O) R 3 8 3 8 2 the skeleton equation, (7) and note that O 2 (in O ) 3 (in CO , H O) 2 2 2 there are 3 carbon atoms on the left E side of the equation but only 1 on the right side. If we add a coefficient of C 3 to CO on the right side the carbon atoms get balanced. 2 C H + O g 3CO + H O ................... (8) S3 8 2 2 2 Now, look at the number of hydrogen atoms. There are 8 hydrogens on the left but only 2 on the right side. By adding a coefficient of 4 to the H O on the right, the hydrogen atoms get balanced. 2 C H + O g 3CO + 4H O .................(9) 3 8 2 2 2 Finally, look at the number of oxygen atoms. There are 2 on the left side but 10 on the right side, by adding a coefficient of 5 to the O on the 2 left, the oxygen atoms get balanced. C H + 5O g 3CO + 4H O .....................(10) 3 8 2 2 2 27 Chemical Equations

Step 3: Make sure the coefficients are reduced to their smallest whole- number values. In fact, the equation (10) is already with the coefficients in smallest whole number. There is no need to reduce its coefficients, but this might not be achieved in each chemical reaction. Let us assume that you have got chemical equation as shown below: 2C H + 10O g 6CO + 8H O ................... (11) 3 8 2 2 2 · Is it a balanced equation as per rules? A · How do you say? Though the equation (11) is balanced, the coefficients are noNt the smallest whole numbers. It would be necessary to divide all coefficients of equation (11) by 2 to reach the final equation. There are m any natural materials like litmus, extract of red cabbage, , turmeric solution and extracts of coloured petals of some flowers contain T dye molecules which are weak acids or bases. In adition to the above natural acid-base indicators, there are some synthetic E indicators such as methyl orange and phenolphthalein that can be used to C test for acids and bases. In this chapter you study the reactions of acids and bases. How do S acids neutralize bases? Many more interesting activities that we use and see in our day-to-day life are also studied. Do you know? Litmus solution is a dye extracted from lichen, a plant belonging to the division of Thallophyta and is used as indicator. In neutral solution litmus colour is purple. pages.text: What we have learnt · Acid – base indicators are dyes or mixtures of dyes which are used to detect the presence of acids and bases. · Acidic nature of a substance is due to the formation of H+ (aq) ions in solution. Formation of OH- (aq) ions in solution is responsible for the basic nature of a substance. A · When a base reacts with a metal with the evolution of hydrogen gas, a salt is formed. N · When an acid reacts with a metal carbonate or metal hydrogen carbonate gives the corresponding salt, carbon dioxide gas and water. A · Acidic and basic solutions in water conduct electricity because they produce hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions respectively. G · The strength of an acid or an alkali can be tested by using a scale called the pH scale (0-14) which gives the measure of hydrogen ion concentratiNon in a solution. · A neutral solution has a pH of 7, while an acidic solution has a pH less than 7 and a basic A solution has a pH more than 7. · Living beings carry out their metabolic activities within an optimal pH range. L · Mixing concentrated acids or bases with water is a highly exothermic process. E · Acids and bases neutralize each other to form corresponding salts and water. · Water of crystallization is the fixed number of water molecules chemically attached to each T formula unit of a salt in its crystalline form. · Salts have various uses in everyday life and in industries. , T Improve your learning R I. CHAPTER A Refraction of Light at N 4 Curved Surfaces A G It is a common observation that some people use spectacles for N reading. The watch repairer uses a small magnifying glass to see tiny parts of a watch. A · Have you ever touched a magnifyingL glass with your hand? · Have you touched the glass inE the spectacles used for reading with your hand? T · Is it a plane surface or curved surface? · Is it thicker in the midd le or at the edge? , We have learnt aboTut refraction of light at a plane surface in the previous class. Now let us understand refraction of light at curved surfaces. R Let us do an activity to understand refraction of light at curved surfaces. E 4.1 Refraction of light at a curved surface C Activity 1 S Draw an arrow of length 4 cm using a black sketch pen on a thick sheet of paper. Take an empty cylindrical-shaped transparent vessel such as glass tumbler. Keep it on the table. Ask your friend to bring that sheet of paper on which arrow was drawn behind the vessel while you looking at it from the other side (The arrow mark should be in horizontal position). · What do you see? You will see a diminished (small-sized) image of the arrow · Why do you see a diminished image? 62 Refraction of Light at Curved Surfaces

· Is the image real or virtual? · Can you draw a ray diagram showing how it is formed? Ask your friend to fill the vessel with water. Look at the mark of arrow from the same position as before. · What do you see now? · Do you get an inverted image? A · How could this happen? In the first case, when the vessel is empty, light from the arrow mark N refracts at the curved interface, travels through the glass and enters into air then it again undergoes refraction on the opposite A curved surface of the vessel (at the other end from where G Air Water we are looking) and comes out into the air. In this way light travels through two media and comes out of the N vessel and forms a diminished image. In the second case, light enters through thAe curved Curved surface, travels through water, comes out of the glass and surface L forms an inverted image. fig-1 E When the vessel is filled with water, there is a curved interface between two different media (air and water). Assume that the T refractive indices of both water and glass are the same (infact they are not equal). This setup of air and water separated by a curved surface is shown , in fig.- 1. T · What happens to a ray that is incident on a curved R surface separating the two media? · Are the E laws of refraction still valid? Light Normal rays Let us find out. C C Consider a curved surface separating two different P Principal axis media as shown in fig.- 2. The centre of the sphere, of S which curved surface is a part, is called as the centre of curvature. It is denoted by letter ‘C’. fig-2 Any line drawn from the centre of curvature to a point on the curved surface becomes normal to the curved surface at that point. The direction of the normal changes from one point to another point on the curved surface. The centre of the curved surface is called the pole (P) of the curved surface. The line that joins the centre of curvature and the pole is called ‘principal axis’. · How do rays bend when they are incident on a curved surface? 63 Refraction of Light at Curved Surfaces

As in the case of plane surfaces, a ray will bend towards the normal if it travels from a rarer to denser medium and it bends away from the normal if it travels from a denser to a rarer medium . Let us see how we can draw ray diagrams for certain useful cases. · What happens to a ray that travels along the principal axis? Similarly, a ray that travels through the centre of curvature? A According to Snell’s law the ray which travels NRay passing along the normal drawn to the surface does not thorugh C deviate from its path. Hence both rays mentioned C A P Ray passing above will travel along the normal (see fig.-3), so along they do not deviate. Gpri a n x c i i s pal · What happens to a ray travelling parallel to the N fig-3 principal axis? Observe the following figures 4(a), 4(bA), 4(c), and 4(d). In all the cases as represented by the L diagrams, the incident ray is parallel to the principal axis. (see fig.-4(a)) , Case2: A ray travelTling parallel to the principal axis fig-4(a) strikes a convex surface and passes from a denser R medium to rarer medium. (see fig.-4(b)) E Normal Case3: A ray travelling parallel to the principal axis strikes a concave surface and passes from a denser C C medium to rarer medium. (see fig-4(c)) Denser Rarer SCase4: A ray travelling parallel to the principal axis fig-4(b) strikes a concave surface and passes from a rarer Normal medium to denser medium. Normal (see fig. 4(d)) · What difference do C C you notice in the Rarer Denser Denser Rarer refracted rays in fig-4(d) figures 4(a) and 4(b)? fig-4(c) 64 Refraction of Light at Curved Surfaces

· What could be the reason for that difference? · What difference do you notice in refracted rays in fig.- 4c and 4d? · What could be the reasons for that difference? You might have noticed that in figures 4(a) and 4(c) the refracted ray reaches a particular point on the principal axis.In figures 4(b) and 4(d) the refracted ray moves away from the principal axis. When you extend the refracted ray backwards along the A ray as shown in 4(b) and 4(d), the extended ray intersects the principal axis at some point. The point where refracted ray intersects the axis in all the above Ncases is called the focal point. (F) A You might have observed that a lemon in a glass of water appears bigger than its actual size, when viewed from the sides of tumbler. G · How can you explain this change in the size of lemon? · Is the lemon that appears bigger in size an image of lemon or is it the real lemon? N · Can you draw a ray diagram to explain this phenomenon? Let us find out. A 4.1.1 Image formation L Consider a curved surface separating two media of refractive indices n and n 1 2 E (fig.- 5). A point object is placed on the principal axis at point O. The ray, which travels along the principal axis passes through the pole undeviated. The second ray, which forms T an angle a with principal axis, meets the interface (surface) at A. The angle of incidence is q . The ray bends and passes through the second medium along the line AI. The angle 1 , of refraction is q . Water, Navaratan oil) and now it will acts like a lens with two different materials .Put a light source (object) in front of this lens and note the observations and write a report on it. 85 Refraction of Light at Curved Surfaces CHAPTER A Human Eye and N 5 Colourful world A G N You have studied refraction of light through lenses in the previous A chapter. You have learnt about nature, position and relative size of image formed by lenses for various distances of objects. In class IX, chapter VI L on sense organs in Biological science text book, explained the structure of the human eye. The human eye funEctions on the principle of sensation of vision. We see objects because the light scattered from them falls on T the eye. The eye has a lens in its structure. In the previous chapter, y ou learned that the focal length of lens and , object distance determine the nature, position and size of image. T · What is the function of lens in human eye? R · How does it help to see objects at long distances and short distances? · How is it possible to get the image at the same distance on the retina? E · Are we able to see all objects in front of our eye clearly? · HCow do the lenses used in spectacles correct defects of vision? To answer these questions, you need to understand the structure and S functioning of the human eye. Let us do the following activities to know about some interesting facts about our vision. 5.1 Least distance of distinct vision Activity 1 Take a text book and hold it with your hands in front of you at a certain distance. Now try to read the contents on the page. Slowly move the book towards your eye till it is very close to your eyes. 86 Human Eye and Colourful World · What changes do you notice? You may see that printed letters on the page of the text book appear blurred or you feel strain in the eye. Now slowly move the book backwards to a position where you can see clear printed letters without straining your eye. Ask your friend to measure the distance between your eye and text book at this position. Note down its value. Repeat the activity with other friends and note down the distances A for distinct vision in each case. Find the average of all these distances of clear vision. N · What value do you get for average distance? From this activity you will come to know that to see Aan object comfortably and distinctly, you must hold it at a distance about 25 cm G from your eyes. This distance is called least distance of distinct vision. This varies from person to person and with age. At a young age (say below 10 years) the muscles around the eye are strong anNd flexible and can bear more strain. Therefore the least distance of distinct vision at this age is as A close as 7 to 8 cm. Generally for a healthy person the least distance of distinct vision is around 25 cm. In old age the muscles cannot sustain L more strain hence the least distance of distinct vision shifts to a larger value, say, about 1 to 2 m or even Emore. · Are you able to see the top and bottom of an object placed at a distance T of about 25 cm from your eye irrespective of its shape? Let us find out. , ActivityT 2 Collect aR few wooden sticks used in cloth roller in clothes store (or) collect waste PVC pipes that are used for electric wiring. If this angle is below BI B E 600, we can see the whole object. If this angle is above D fig-2 600, then we can see only the part of the object. C This maximum angle, at which we are able to see the whole object is Scalled angle of vision. The angle of vision for a healthy human being is about 600. It varies from person to person with the age. You have learnt that the value of least distance of distinct vision is about 25 cm and the value of angle of vision of human beings is about 600. You also learnt that these values change from person to person and with age of person. · Why do the values of least distance of distinct vision and angle of vision change with person and age? To answer the above question, we need to understand the structure of eye and its functioning. 88 Human Eye and Colourful World 5.2 Structure of human eye ciliary muscles The human eye is one of the most important sense organs. It enables us to see the object and iris colours around us. retina pupil lens Fig.-3 shows schematically the basic components of human eye. The eye ball is nearly aqueous humour A spherical in shape. The front portion is more cornea sharply curved and is covered by a transparent Nfig-3 optic nerve protective membrane called the ‘cornea’. It is this portion which is visible from outside. Behind the cornea, theAre is place filled with a liquid called aqueous humour and behind this a crystalline G lens which is responsible for the image formation. Between the aqueous humour and the lens, we have a muscular diaphragm called ‘iris’ which has a N small hole in it called pupil. Iris is the coloured part that we see in an eye. The pupil appears black because any light falling on it goes into the A eye and there is almost no chance of light coming back to the outside. Iris helps in controlling the amount of lightL entering the eye through ‘pupil’. In low light condition, the iris makes the pupil to expand so that more light E is allowed to go in and in the case of bright (or) excess light condition, it makes the pupil contract andT there by prevent the excess light not to go into eye. Thus ‘iris’ enables pupil to act as a “variable aperture” for entry of light into the eye. , The lens is hardT in the middle and gradually becomes soft towards the outer edge. The light that enters the eye forms an image on the retina. (It R covers the rear part of eyeball). The distance between the lens and retina is about 2.5 cm i.e., for any position of object in front of the eye the E image distance is fixed and about 2.5 cm. C · How can we get this same image distance for various positions of objects? S · Can you answer this question using concepts of refraction through lenses? In the previous chapter, you have learnt that for different positions of object, the image distance remains constant only when there is a change in focal length of lens. Further, the focal length of a lens depends on the material by which it has been made and radii of curvature of lens. We need to change focal length of eye lens to get same image distance for various positions of object in front of the eye. This is only possible when the eye lens is able to change its shape. 89 Human Eye and Colourful World · How does eye lens change its focal length? · How does this change take place in the eye ball? Let us know The ciliary muscle to which eye lens is attached (see fig-3) helps the eye lens to change its focal length by changing the radii of curvature of the eye lens. A When the eye is focussed on a distant object, the ciliary muscles are N relaxed so that the focal length of eye lens has its maximum value which is equal to its distance from the retina. The parallel rays coming into the eye A are then focussed on to the retina and we see the object clearly. When the eye is focussed on a closer object, the cilGiary muscles are strained and focal length of eye-lens decreases. The ciliary muscles adjust the focal length in such a way that the image is foNrmed on retina and we see the object clearly. This process of adjusting focal length is called A “accommodation”. However these muscles cannot strain beyond a limit and hence if the object is brought too close to eyes, the focal length cannot L be adjusted to form an image on the retina. Thus there is a minimum distance for distinct vision of an object whicEh is roughly equal to 25 cm as we have learned in activity-1. T · Does eye lens form a real image or virtual image? · How does the image formed on retina help us to perceive the object , without change Tin its shape, size and colour? Let us know R The eye-lens forms a real and inverted image of an object on the retina. The retiEna is a delicate membrane, which contains about 125 million receptors called ‘rods’ and ‘cones’ which receive the light signal (cones- C identify the colour: rods-identify the intensity of light). These signals are transmitted to the brain through about 1 million optic-nerve fibres. The S brain interprets these signals and finally processes the information so that we perceive the object in terms of its shape, size and colour. In our previous discussion, you have learnt that eye-lens itself changes its focal length in accordance with distance of the object with the help of ciliary muscles. · Is there any limit to the change of focal length of the eye-lens? · What are the maximum and minimum focal lengths of the eye lens? How can we find them? The ability of eye-lens to change its focal length is called “accommodation of lens”. · What happens if the eye lens is not able to adjust its focal length? · What happens if the focal length of eye lens is beyond the range of 2.5 cm to 2.27 cm? Let us find out. 5.3 Defects of Vision Sometimes the eye may gradually lose its ability for accommodation. 91 Human Eye and Colourful World In such conditions the person cannot see an object clearly and comfortably. The vision becomes blurred due to accommodation defects of the eye lens. There are mainly three common defects of vision. They are: i. Myopia ii. Hypermetropia A iii. Presbyopia. N 5.3.1 Myopia A Some people cannot see objects at long distances but can see nearby objects clearly. This type of defect in vision is called ‘MyoGpia’. It is also called ‘near sightedness’. For these people the maximum focal length is less than 2.5 cm. In such cases the rays coming from Ndistant objects, after refraction through the eye lens, form an image before the retina as shown A in figures-5(a) and (b). A healthy person can see objects at aLll distances more than 25 cm clearly but a person with myopia E can see objects clearly up to a certain distance. If the object is at M or in M L E fig-5(b) between M and point of least distance of distinct vision C (L),the eye lens can form an L Simage on the retina (see fig.- M fig-5(c) 5(c) and 5(d)). This point M is called ‘far point’. The point of maximum O L distance at which the eye lens M fig-5(d) can form an image on the retina is called ‘far point’. The defect, in which people cannot see objects beyond far point is called ‘Myopia’. 92 Human Eye and Colourful World · What can we do to correct myopia? T · Is it a plane surface or curved surface? · Is it thicker in the midd le or at the edge? , We have learnt aboTut refraction of light at a plane surface in the previous class. Now let us understand refraction of light at curved surfaces. R Let us do an activity to understand refraction of light at curved surfaces. E 4.1 Refraction of light at a curved surface C Activity 1 S Draw an arrow of length 4 cm using a black sketch pen on a thick sheet of paper. Take an empty cylindrical-shaped transparent vessel such as glass tumbler. Keep it on the table. Ask your friend to bring that sheet of paper on which arrow was drawn behind the vessel while you looking at it from the other side (The arrow mark should be in horizontal position). · What do you see? You will see a diminished (small-sized) image of the arrow · Why do you see a diminished image? 62 Refraction of Light at Curved Surfaces · Is the image real or virtual? · Can you draw a ray diagram showing how it is formed? Ask your friend to fill the vessel with water. Look at the mark of arrow from the same position as before. · What do you see now? · Do you get an inverted image? A · How could this happen? In the first case, when the vessel is empty, light from the arrow mark N refracts at the curved interface, travels through the glass and enters into air then it again undergoes refraction on the opposite A curved surface of the vessel (at the other end from where G Air Water we are looking) and comes out into the air. In this way light travels through two media and comes out of the N vessel and forms a diminished image. In the second case, light enters through thAe curved Curved surface, travels through water, comes out of the glass and surface L forms an inverted image. fig-1 E When the vessel is filled with water, there is a curved interface between two different media (air and water). Assume that the T refractive indices of both water and glass are the same (infact they are not equal). This setup of air and water separated by a curved surface is shown , in fig.- 1. T · What happens to a ray that is incident on a curved R surface separating the two media? · Are the E laws of refraction still valid? Light Normal rays Let us find out. C C Consider a curved surface separating two different P Principal axis media as shown in fig.- 2. The centre of the sphere, of S which curved surface is a part, is called as the centre of curvature. It is denoted by letter ‘C’. fig-2 Any line drawn from the centre of curvature to a point on the curved surface becomes normal to the curved surface at that point. The direction of the normal changes from one point to another point on the curved surface. The centre of the curved surface is called the pole (P) of the curved surface. The line that joins the centre of curvature and the pole is called ‘principal axis’. · How do rays bend when they are incident on a curved surface? 63 Refraction of Light at Curved Surfaces As in the case of plane surfaces, a ray will bend towards the normal if it travels from a rarer to denser medium and it bends away from the normal if it travels from a denser to a rarer medium . lessonSections.fullText: CHAPTER A Human Eye and N 5 Colourful world A G N You have studied refraction of light through lenses in the previous A chapter. You have learnt about nature, position and relative size of image formed by lenses for various distances of objects. In class IX, chapter VI L on sense organs in Biological science text book, explained the structure of the human eye. The human eye funEctions on the principle of sensation of vision. We see objects because the light scattered from them falls on T the eye. The eye has a lens in its structure. In the previous chapter, y ou learned that the focal length of lens and , object distance determine the nature, position and size of image. T · What is the function of lens in human eye? R · How does it help to see objects at long distances and short distances? · How is it possible to get the image at the same distance on the retina? E · Are we able to see all objects in front of our eye clearly? · HCow do the lenses used in spectacles correct defects of vision? To answer these questions, you need to understand the structure and S functioning of the human eye. Let us do the following activities to know about some interesting facts about our vision. 5.1 Least distance of distinct vision Activity 1 Take a text book and hold it with your hands in front of you at a certain distance. Now try to read the contents on the page. Slowly move the book towards your eye till it is very close to your eyes. 86 Human Eye and Colourful World · What changes do you notice? You may see that printed letters on the page of the text book appear blurred or you feel strain in the eye. Now slowly move the book backwards to a position where you can see clear printed letters without straining your eye. Ask your friend to measure the distance between your eye and text book at this position. Note down its value. Repeat the activity with other friends and note down the distances A for distinct vision in each case. Find the average of all these distances of clear vision. N · What value do you get for average distance? From this activity you will come to know that to see Aan object comfortably and distinctly, you must hold it at a distance about 25 cm G from your eyes. This distance is called least distance of distinct vision. This varies from person to person and with age. At a young age (say below 10 years) the muscles around the eye are strong anNd flexible and can bear more strain. Therefore the least distance of distinct vision at this age is as A close as 7 to 8 cm. Generally for a healthy person the least distance of distinct vision is around 25 cm. In old age the muscles cannot sustain L more strain hence the least distance of distinct vision shifts to a larger value, say, about 1 to 2 m or even Emore. · Are you able to see the top and bottom of an object placed at a distance T of about 25 cm from your eye irrespective of its shape? Let us find out. , ActivityT 2 Collect aR few wooden sticks used in cloth roller in clothes store (or) collect waste PVC pipes that are used for electric wiring. Prepare sticks E or pipes of 20 cm, 30 cm, 35 cm, 40 cm, 50 cm from them. Place a retort stand on a table and stand near the table such that your C head is beside the vertical rod (see fig 1). Adjust the clamp Son the horizontal rod and fix it at a distance of 25 cm from your eyes. Ask one of your friends to fix a wooden stick of 30 cm height to the clamp in a vertical position as shown in fig1. Now keeping your vision parallel to horizontal rod of the stand, try to see the top and bottom of wooden stick kept fig-1 in vertical position. · Are you able to see both ends of the stick simultaneously without any movement (shaking) in your eyes? 87 Human Eye and Colourful World In activity-1, you learned that least distance for distinct vision is about 25 cm. It varies from person to person. If you are not able to see both end of the stick at this distance (25 cm), adjust the vertical stick on the horizontal rod till you are able to see both ends of the stick at the smallest possible distance from your eye. Fix the vertical stick at this position with the help of the clamp. Without changing the position of the clamp on the horizontal rod, A replace this stick of 30 cm length with other sticks of various lengths one N by one and try to see the top and bottom of the stick simultaneously without any change in the position of eye either upwards downwards or side ways. A · Are you able to see both ends of the sticks in all these cases? If not why? G Let us know. Observe the following fig.-2. You can see the wNhole object AB which is at a distance of 25 cm (least distance of distinct vision) because the A rays coming from the ends A and B of the object AB will enter the eye. Similarly you can also see whole object CD with eye as explained above. L Let us assume that AB moves closer to the eye to a position AI BI as shown E in fig.2. · Will you be able to see the whole object now? T From the fig.-2, you notice that you will be able C to see only the part (EF) of the object AI BI because AI A , the rays coming from E and F enter your eye. The T E rays coming from AI and BI cannot enter your eye. The rays R coming from the extreme ends of an F object form an angle at the eye. If this angle is below BI B E 600, we can see the whole object. If this angle is above D fig-2 600, then we can see only the part of the object. C This maximum angle, at which we are able to see the whole object is Scalled angle of vision. The angle of vision for a healthy human being is about 600. It varies from person to person with the age. You have learnt that the value of least distance of distinct vision is about 25 cm and the value of angle of vision of human beings is about 600. You also learnt that these values change from person to person and with age of person. · Why do the values of least distance of distinct vision and angle of vision change with person and age? To answer the above question, we need to understand the structure of eye and its functioning. 88 Human Eye and Colourful World 5.2 Structure of human eye ciliary muscles The human eye is one of the most important sense organs. It enables us to see the object and iris colours around us. retina pupil lens Fig.-3 shows schematically the basic components of human eye. The eye ball is nearly aqueous humour A spherical in shape. The front portion is more cornea sharply curved and is covered by a transparent Nfig-3 optic nerve protective membrane called the ‘cornea’. It is this portion which is visible from outside. Behind the cornea, theAre is place filled with a liquid called aqueous humour and behind this a crystalline G lens which is responsible for the image formation. Between the aqueous humour and the lens, we have a muscular diaphragm called ‘iris’ which has a N small hole in it called pupil. Iris is the coloured part that we see in an eye. The pupil appears black because any light falling on it goes into the A eye and there is almost no chance of light coming back to the outside. Iris helps in controlling the amount of lightL entering the eye through ‘pupil’. In low light condition, the iris makes the pupil to expand so that more light E is allowed to go in and in the case of bright (or) excess light condition, it makes the pupil contract andT there by prevent the excess light not to go into eye. Thus ‘iris’ enables pupil to act as a “variable aperture” for entry of light into the eye. , The lens is hardT in the middle and gradually becomes soft towards the outer edge. The light that enters the eye forms an image on the retina. (It R covers the rear part of eyeball). The distance between the lens and retina is about 2.5 cm i.e., for any position of object in front of the eye the E image distance is fixed and about 2.5 cm. C · How can we get this same image distance for various positions of objects? S · Can you answer this question using concepts of refraction through lenses? In the previous chapter, you have learnt that for different positions of object, the image distance remains constant only when there is a change in focal length of lens. Further, the focal length of a lens depends on the material by which it has been made and radii of curvature of lens. We need to change focal length of eye lens to get same image distance for various positions of object in front of the eye. This is only possible when the eye lens is able to change its shape. 89 Human Eye and Colourful World · How does eye lens change its focal length? · How does this change take place in the eye ball? Let us know The ciliary muscle to which eye lens is attached (see fig-3) helps the eye lens to change its focal length by changing the radii of curvature of the eye lens. A When the eye is focussed on a distant object, the ciliary muscles are N relaxed so that the focal length of eye lens has its maximum value which is equal to its distance from the retina. The parallel rays coming into the eye A are then focussed on to the retina and we see the object clearly. When the eye is focussed on a closer object, the cilGiary muscles are strained and focal length of eye-lens decreases. The ciliary muscles adjust the focal length in such a way that the image is foNrmed on retina and we see the object clearly. This process of adjusting focal length is called A “accommodation”. However these muscles cannot strain beyond a limit and hence if the object is brought too close to eyes, the focal length cannot L be adjusted to form an image on the retina. Thus there is a minimum distance for distinct vision of an object whicEh is roughly equal to 25 cm as we have learned in activity-1. T · Does eye lens form a real image or virtual image? · How does the image formed on retina help us to perceive the object , without change Tin its shape, size and colour? Let us know R The eye-lens forms a real and inverted image of an object on the retina. The retiEna is a delicate membrane, which contains about 125 million receptors called ‘rods’ and ‘cones’ which receive the light signal (cones- C identify the colour: rods-identify the intensity of light). These signals are transmitted to the brain through about 1 million optic-nerve fibres. The S brain interprets these signals and finally processes the information so that we perceive the object in terms of its shape, size and colour. In our previous discussion, you have learnt that eye-lens itself changes its focal length in accordance with distance of the object with the help of ciliary muscles. · Is there any limit to the change of focal length of the eye-lens? · What are the maximum and minimum focal lengths of the eye lens? How can we find them? Let us find 90 Human Eye and Colourful World When the object is at infinity, the parallel rays from the object falling on the eye lens are refracted and they form a point sized image on retina (see fig- 4(a)). In this situation, eye-lens has a maximum focal length. fig-4(a) When the object is at infinity, A u= - ¥; v = 2.5 cm (image distance which is equal to distance between eye-lens and retina) N 1 1 1 using the formula = - A f v u 1 1 1 G = + f 2.5 ¥ max N 1 1 = + 0 f 2.5 max A f = 2.5 cm max we get, f = 2.5 cLm max consider that an object is placed at distance of 25 cm from our eye. In this E situation eye has minimum focal length. Here u = - 25 cm; v = 2.5T cm 1 1 1 Using the formula = - ,f v u T1 1 1 L = + f 2.5 25 R min 1 11 fig-4(b) = Ef 25 min 25 C f = = 2.27 cm min 11 If the position of an object is between infinity and the point of least S distance of distinct vision, then the eye lens adjusts it’s focal length in between 2.5 cm to 2.27 cm to form a clear image on the retina. The ability of eye-lens to change its focal length is called “accommodation of lens”. · What happens if the eye lens is not able to adjust its focal length? · What happens if the focal length of eye lens is beyond the range of 2.5 cm to 2.27 cm? Let us try to understand E the idea of scattering. C · Do you know what happens to the free atom or molecule when it is exposed to certain frequency of light? S Atoms or molecules which are exposed to light absorb light energy and emit some part of the light energy in different directions. This is the basic process happens in scattering of light. The effect of light on a molecule or an atom depends on the size of atom or molecule. If the size of the particle (atom or molecule) is small, it will be affected by higher frequency (lower wave length) light and vice versa. 105 Human Eye and Colourful World Let us consider that a certain frequency of light is incident on an atom. Due to fig-16 N these vibrations, the atom re-emits a certain fraction fig-16 of absorbed energy in all directions withA different intensities. The re-emitted light is called scattered light and the process L of re-emission of light in all directions with different intensity is called E scattering of light. Let us take the angle ‘q’ between the incident light and a direction in which T the intensity of scattered light is observed, we call this angle as angle of scattering. In morning and evening times, during sunrise and sunset, except red light all colours scatter more and vanish before A they reach you. Since scattering of redlight is very small, it reaches you. N As a result sun appears red in colour during sunrise and sunset. · Can you guess the reason why sun does not appear red duriAng noon hours? G During noon hours, the distance to be travelled by the sun rays in the atmosphere is less than that compared to morninNg and evening hours. Therefore all colours reach your eye without much scattering. Hence the A sun appears white during noon hours. L Do you Know? E Our beloved scientist and Noble prize winner, Sir T C.V. Raman explained the phenomenon of light scattering in gases a nd liquids. He found , experimentally that the frequency of scattered light T by the liquids is greater than the frequency of incident R light. This is called Raman Effect. By using this effect Sir CV Raman scientists determine the shapes of the molecules. E CSo far, we have learned some ideas of the light such as refraction, dispersion and scattering. These are wonderful phenomena occuring in our S surroundings. When you observe any phenomena, try to resolve the problem and appreciate the wonderful world based on the behaviour of light. Key words Least distance of distinct vision, Angle of vision, Accommodation of eye lens, Myopia, Hypermetropia, Presbyopia, Power of lens, Prism, Angle of prism or refracting angle of prism, Angle of minimum deviation, Dispersion, Scattering. 108 Human Eye and Colourful World What we have learnt · The least distance of distinct vision is about 25cm and the angle of vision is about 600. · The ability of eye lens to change its focal length is called accommodation of lens. · The defect in which people cannot see objects beyond far point is called Myopia. S 111 Human Eye and Colourful World CHAPTER A N 6 Structure of Atom A G N You have studied in the previous class about sub-atomic particles like negatively charged electrons, positively charged protons and electrically A neutral neutrons. L · How do these sub-atomic particles coexist in an electrically neutral atom? E You have acquired some fundamental ideas about atomic models T suggested by J J Thomson, Ernest Rutherford and Niels Bohr which have been presented in Class 9. , ActivityT 1 On the baRsis of your previous knowledge you prepare a model of an atom. Present it in your classroom. E · Can you arrange the sub-atomic particles in any other way in an atom? C (Take the help of your friends, your teacher and the Internet). SObserve your atomic model and the models prepared by your friends carefully and try to answer the questions. · Do all atoms have the same sub-atomic particles? · Why is an atom of one element different from the atoms of other elements? · How are the electrons distributed in an atom? To answer the above questions, we need to understand the nature of light, coloured flames and their characteristics. 112 Structure of Atom 6.1 Spectrum You must have observed the formation of a rainbow. · How many colours are there in a rainbow? There are seven colours namely violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange and red (VIBGYOR) in a rainbow. You can find the colours spreading continuously and the intensity of A each colour varies from one point to the other. N Wave nature of light A When you throw a stone into a still pond, you observe ripples, which are transmitting the disturbance in the form of waves on the surface G of water in all directions. You know that sound waves are produced whenN something vibrates; like a drum. A In the same way electromagnetic waves are produced when an electric charge vibrates (moves back and forth). L A vibrating electric charge creates a change in the electric field. The change in electric field creates a cEhange in magnetic field. This process continuoTus, with both the created fields being perpendicular to each other and at right angles to the direction of propagation of the wave. , T Visible light is an electromagnetic wave and the speed of light (c) is 3 × 108 m s–1. R 6.1.1 Characteristics of electromagnetic wave E Wave length C S Electric field Direction of wave fig-1: An electromagnetic wave Magnetic field Electromagnetic energy travelling through a vaccum behaves in same way like ocean waves travelling through water. Like ocean waves, electromagnetic energy is characterized by wavelength (l), and frequency (u). 113 Structure of Atom The wavelength (l) of the wave is the distance from one crest/trough to the next. The frequency (u) of a wave is simply the number of crests/troughs (waves) that pass by a given point per unit time, expressed in units of reciprocal seconds (1/s or s–1). The relation between these quantities is given by lµ 1/u or c = ul It is a universal relationship and applies to all waves. As the frequencyA increases, the wavelength becomes smaller. N Electromagnetic waves can have a wide variety of frequencies. The entire range of electromagnetic wave frequencies is known as the A electromagnetic spectrum. G The familiar example of the visible spectrum in nature is the formation of a rainbow. N Each colour in a rainbow is characterized by a specified wavelength from red (higher wavelength) to violet (shorter wavelength). These colours A (wavelengths), that the human naked eye is sensitive to, are called visible L light. The range of wavelengths covering red colour to violet colour is called the visible spectrum. E 6.1.2 Electromagnetic spectrum T Electromagnetic waves can have a wide range of wavelengths. The entire range of wavelengths is kn own as the electromagnetic spectrum. , The electromaTgnetic spectrum consists of a continuous range of wavelengths from gamma rays at the shorter wavelength to radio waves at R 10-9 m 10 -6 m 10-3 m 100 m 103 m 10-12 m E1 nm 1000 nm 1 mm 1 m 1 km Cosmic x-rays Micro Radio Broadcast Crays waves band g-rays UV IR Radar S Short wavelength Long wavelength Ultraviolet (UV) Infrared (IR) rays rays Visible light 400 nm 500 nm 600 nm 700 nm fig-2: Electromagnetic Spectrum the longer wavelength. But our eyes are sensitive only to visible light. · What happens when you heat an iron rod on a flame? · Do you find any change in colour on heating an iron rod? 114 Structure of Atom When you heat an iron rod, some of the heat energy is emitted as light. First it turns red (lower energy corresponding to higher wavelength) and as the temperature rises it glows with orange, yellow, blue(higher energy and of lower wavelength) or even white (all visible wavelengths) if the temperature is high enough. · Do you observe any other colour at the same time when one colour is A emitted? When the temperature is high enough, other colours will also be N emitted, but due to higher intensity of one particular emitted colour (e.g., red), others cannot be observed. A Max Planck broke with the ‘continuous energy’ tradition of electromagnetic energy by assuming that the energy is alwGays absorbed or emitted in multiples of hu; For example: hu, 2 hu, 3 hu... nhu N That is, the energy for a certain frequency E can be represented by the A equation E = hu, where ‘h’ is Planck’s constant which has the value 6.626 X 10-34Js and ‘u’ is the frequency of the radiation absorbed or L emitted. The energy (E) for the red Ecolour (higher wavelength or lower frequency) is lower compared to the energy of blue colour (lower T wavelength or higher frequency). The energy emitted from a material body increases with increase in temperature. The significance of P,lanck’s proposal is that, electromagnetic energy T can be gained or lost in discrete values and not in a continuous manner. Hence, emRission or absorption spectrum of light is a collection of a group of wavelengths. E · Do you enjoy Deepavali fireworks? CVariety of colours is seen from fireworks. · How do these colours come from fireworks? S Activity 2 Take a pinch of cupric chloride in a watch glass and make a paste with concentrated hydrochloric acid. Take this paste on a platinum loop and introduce it into a non-luminous flame. · What colour do you observe? Carry out similar activity with strontium chloride. Cupric chloride produces a green colour flame while strontium chloride produces a crimson red flame. · Do you observe yellow light in street lamps? 115 Structure of Atom Sodium vapours produce yellow light in street lamps. · Why do different elements emit different flame colours when heated by the same non-luminous flame? Scientists found that each element emits its own characteristic colour. These colours correspond to certain discrete wavelengths of light and are A called line spectra. The lines in atomic spectra can be used to identify unknown atoNms, just like fingerprints are used to identify people. A G Niels Henrik David Bohr was a Danish physicist who made foundationaNl contributions to understanding atomic structure and quantum theory, for which he A received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1922. Bohr was L also a philosopher and a promoter. E T 6.2 Bohr’s model of hydrogen atom and its limitations Niels Bhor proposed an atomic model based on hydrogen atomic , spectrum. T · What does a line spectrum of R hydrogen atom tell us about the structure of an atom? E Postulates of Niels Bohr EClectrons in an atom occupy ‘stationary’ orbits (states) of fixed S energy at different distances from the nucleus. fig-3: Hydrogen Spectrum When an electron ‘jumps’ from a lower energy state (ground state) to higher energy state (excited state) it absorbs energy or emits energy when such a jump occurs from a higher energy state to a lower energy state. The energies of an electron in an atom can have only certain values E , E , E ……; that is, the energy is quantized. The states corresponding 1 2 3 to these energies are called stationary states and the possible values of the energy are called energy levels. 116 Structure of Atom

It is not possible to explain the splitting of white light into different E colours using ray theory. · Why is this so? C Let us see 5.4.3 Dispersion of Light S In activity 3, we observe that the angle of deviation is minimum for red Red Orange as compared to the angles of deviation Yellow of other colours and maximum for Green Blue violet. Indigo Violet The splitting of white light into fig-12 different colours (VIBGYOR) is called dispersion. In our previous discussion, we learnt that for a particular refractive index of prism there must be only one angle of minimum deviation and 101 Human Eye and Colourful World according to Fermat’s principle, light ray always chooses the path of least time. But in activity-3,we noticed that light has choosen different paths. · Does this mean that the refractive index of the prism varies from colour to colour? · Is the speed of light of each colour different? The situation we witnessed in activities (3) and (4) rule out ray theory A of light. We can consider that white light is a collection of waves with different wavelengths. Violet colour is known to have the shoNrtest wavelength while red is of the longest wavelength. A According to wave theory, light can be thought of a wave propagating in all directions. Light is an electromagnetic wave. Here no particle physically G oscillates back and forth. Instead, the magnitude of electric and magnetic fields, associated with the electromagnetic wave, vary periodically at every N point. These oscillating electric and magnetic fields propagate in all directions with the speed of light. A · Can you guess now, why light splits into different colours when it L passes through a prism? The reason lies in the fact thatE, while the speed of light is constant in vacuum for all colours, it depends on the wavelength of light when it passes T through a medium. We know that refractive index is the ratio of speeds in vacuum and in the medium. Consequently, the refractive index of a medium depends on wavelength of, light. When white light passes through a medium, T each colour selects its least time path and we have refraction of different colours to different extents. This results in separation of colours, producing R a spectrum on the wall and in the mirror as we saw in activities (3) and (4). It has beEen experimentally found that refractive index decreases with an increase in wavelength. If we compare the wave lengths of seven colours C in VIBGYOR, red colour has longest wavelength and violet colour has shortest wavelength. The refractive index of red is low hence it suffers S low deviation. We noticed that when white light passes through a prism, it splits into seven colours. Let us assume that you have sent a single colour ray through the prism. · Does it split into more colours? Why? We know that the frequency of light is the property of the source and it is equal to number of waves leaving the source per second. This cannot be changed by any medium. Hence frequency doesn’t change due to refraction. Thus coloured light passing through any transparent medium retains its colour. 102 Human Eye and Colourful World When refraction occurs at the interface, the number of waves that are incident on the interface in a second must be equal to the number of waves passing through any point taken in another medium. This means that the frequency of the light wave remains unaltered while its wavelength changes depending on the medium through which it passes. We know that the relation among the speed of wave (v), wavelength ( l) and frequency (u) is. A v = u l (frequency denoted by u) For refraction at any interface, v is proportional to l. Speed oNf the wave increases with increase in wavelength of light and vice versa. A · Can you give an example in nature, where you observe colours as seen in activity 3? G Your answer certainly is a rainbow. That is a good example of dispersion of light. N · When do you see a rainbow in the sky? · Can we create a rainbow artificially? A Let us see how. At this first refraction, Violet the white light is dispersed into Red its spectrum of colours, fig-13 103 Human Eye and Colourful World violet being deviated the most and red the least. Reaching the opposite side of the drop, each colour is reflected back into the drop because of total internal reflection. Arriving at the surface of the drop, each colour is again refracted into air. At the second refraction the angle between red and violet rays further increases when compared to the angle between those at first refraction. A The angle between the incoming and outgoing rays can be anything N between 00 and about 420. We observe bright rainbow when the angle between incoming and outgoing rays is near the maximum angle of 420. A Diagrammatically it is shown in fig.- 13.Although each drop disperses a G full spectrum of colours, an observer is in a position to see only a single colour from any one drop depending upon its position. N If violet light from a single drop reaches the eye of an observer, red light from the same drop can’t reach his eye. ItA goes elsewhere possibly downwards of the eye of the L observer (see in fig.- 14). To see red light, one must look at E Sun light Water 40o the drop higher in the sky. The T drops colour red will be seen when the 42o angle between a beam, of T Violet sunlight and light sent back by a Violet drop is 420. TheR colour violet Red is seen when the angle between Red E fig-14 a sunbeam and light sent back by a Cdrop is 400. If you look at an angle between 400 and 420, you will observe the remaining colours of VIBGYOR S · Why does the light dispersed by the raindrops appear as a bow? To find answer this question, we need a little geometric reasoning. First of all, a rainbow is not the Sun light flat two dimensional arc as it appears to us. The rainbow Sun 40o you see is actually a three 42o dimensional cone with the tip at your eye as shown in fig.- 15. fig-15 104 Human Eye and Colourful World All the drops that disperse the light towards you lie in the shape of the cone – a cone of different layers. The drops that disperse red colour to your eye are on the outer most layer of the cone, similarly the drops that disperse orange colour to your eye are on the layer of the cone beneath the red colour cone. In this way the cone responsible for yellow lies beneath orange and so on it till the violet colour cone becomes the innermost A cone.(see in fig.- 15). N Think and discuss A · Can you imagine the shape of rainbow when observeGd during travel in an airplane? Discuss with your friends and collect information. The effect of light on a molecule or an atom depends on the size of atom or molecule.
