R This is the reason for the appearance of clear blue colour when look at the sky Ein a direction perpendicular to the direction of the sun rays. If our angle of view is changed, the intensity of blue colour also changes. C Now you might have got a doubt why scattering of light gives blue Scolour only. Why can’t it give other colours? Let us find out whether the scattering centres are responsible for the blue colour of the sky? We know that our atmosphere contains different types of molecules and atoms. The reason for blue sky is due to the molecules N and O . The 2 2 sizes of these molecules are comparable to the wavelength of blue light. These molecules act as scattering centres for scattering of blue light. · Why is that the sky appears white sometimes when you view it in certain direction on hot days? 106 Human Eye and Colourful World Our atmosphere contains atoms and molecules of different sizes. According to their sizes, they are able to scatter different wavelengths of light. For example, the size of the water molecule is greater than the size of the N or O . It acts as a scattering centre for other frequencies which 2 2 are lower than the frequency of blue light. A On a hot day, due to rise in the temperature water vapour enters into atmosphere which leads to abundant presence of water molecules iNn the atmosphere. These water molecules scatter the colours of other A frequencies (other than blue). All such colours of other frequencies reach your eye and the sky appears white. G · Can we demonstrate scattering of light by an experiment? N Let us try A Activity 6 Take a solution of sodium-thio-sulphLate (hypo) and sulphuric acid in a glass beaker. Place the beaker in an open place where abundant sun light is E available. Watch the formation of grains of sulphur and observe changes T in the beaker. You will notice that sulphur precipitates as the reaction is in progress. , At the beginning, thTe grains of sulphur are smaller in size and as the reaction progresses, their size increases due to precipitation. R Sulphur grains appear blue in colour at the beginning and slowly their E colour becomes white as their size increases. The reason for this is scCattering of light. At the beginning, the size of grains is small and almost comparable to the wave length of blue light. Hence they appear blue in the S beginning. As the size of grains increases, their size becomes comparable to wave lengths of other colours. As a result of this, they act as scattering centres for other colours. The combination of all these colours appears as white. · Do you know the reasons for appearance the red colour of sun during sunrise and at sunset? The atmosphere contains free molecules and atoms with different sizes. These molecules and atoms scatter light of different wavelengths which 107 Human Eye and Colourful World are comparable to their size. Molecules having a size that is comparable to the wavelength of red light are less in the atmosphere. Hence scattering of red light is less when compared to the other colours of light. The light from the sun needs to travel more distance in atmosphere during sunrise and sunset to reach your eye. In morning and evening times, during sunrise and sunset, except red light all colours scatter more and vanish before A they reach you. Since scattering of redlight is very small, it reaches you. N As a result sun appears red in colour during sunrise and sunset. · Can you guess the reason why sun does not appear red duriAng noon hours? G During noon hours, the distance to be travelled by the sun rays in the atmosphere is less than that compared to morninNg and evening hours. Therefore all colours reach your eye without much scattering. Hence the A sun appears white during noon hours. L Do you Know? E Our beloved scientist and Noble prize winner, Sir T C.V. Raman explained the phenomenon of light scattering in gases a nd liquids. He found , experimentally that the frequency of scattered light T by the liquids is greater than the frequency of incident R light. This is called Raman Effect. By using this effect Sir CV Raman scientists determine the shapes of the molecules. E CSo far, we have learned some ideas of the light such as refraction, dispersion and scattering. These are wonderful phenomena occuring in our S surroundings. When you observe any phenomena, try to resolve the problem and appreciate the wonderful world based on the behaviour of light. N Wave nature of light A When you throw a stone into a still pond, you observe ripples, which are transmitting the disturbance in the form of waves on the surface G of water in all directions. You know that sound waves are produced whenN something vibrates; like a drum. A In the same way electromagnetic waves are produced when an electric charge vibrates (moves back and forth). L A vibrating electric charge creates a change in the electric field. The change in electric field creates a cEhange in magnetic field. This process continuoTus, with both the created fields being perpendicular to each other and at right angles to the direction of propagation of the wave. , T Visible light is an electromagnetic wave and the speed of light (c) is 3 × 108 m s–1. R 6.1.1 Characteristics of electromagnetic wave E Wave length C S Electric field Direction of wave fig-1: An electromagnetic wave Magnetic field Electromagnetic energy travelling through a vaccum behaves in same way like ocean waves travelling through water. Like ocean waves, electromagnetic energy is characterized by wavelength (l), and frequency (u). 113 Structure of Atom The wavelength (l) of the wave is the distance from one crest/trough to the next. The frequency (u) of a wave is simply the number of crests/troughs (waves) that pass by a given point per unit time, expressed in units of reciprocal seconds (1/s or s–1). The relation between these quantities is given by lµ 1/u or c = ul It is a universal relationship and applies to all waves. As the frequencyA increases, the wavelength becomes smaller. N Electromagnetic waves can have a wide variety of frequencies. The entire range of electromagnetic wave frequencies is known as the A electromagnetic spectrum. G The familiar example of the visible spectrum in nature is the formation of a rainbow. N Each colour in a rainbow is characterized by a specified wavelength from red (higher wavelength) to violet (shorter wavelength). These colours A (wavelengths), that the human naked eye is sensitive to, are called visible L light. The range of wavelengths covering red colour to violet colour is called the visible spectrum. E 6.1.2 Electromagnetic spectrum T Electromagnetic waves can have a wide range of wavelengths. The entire range of wavelengths is kn own as the electromagnetic spectrum. , The electromaTgnetic spectrum consists of a continuous range of wavelengths from gamma rays at the shorter wavelength to radio waves at R 10-9 m 10 -6 m 10-3 m 100 m 103 m 10-12 m E1 nm 1000 nm 1 mm 1 m 1 km Cosmic x-rays Micro Radio Broadcast Crays waves band g-rays UV IR Radar S Short wavelength Long wavelength Ultraviolet (UV) Infrared (IR) rays rays Visible light 400 nm 500 nm 600 nm 700 nm fig-2: Electromagnetic Spectrum the longer wavelength. But our eyes are sensitive only to visible light. · What happens when you heat an iron rod on a flame? · Do you find any change in colour on heating an iron rod? 114 Structure of Atom When you heat an iron rod, some of the heat energy is emitted as light. First it turns red (lower energy corresponding to higher wavelength) and as the temperature rises it glows with orange, yellow, blue(higher energy and of lower wavelength) or even white (all visible wavelengths) if the temperature is high enough. · Do you observe any other colour at the same time when one colour is A emitted? When the temperature is high enough, other colours will also be N emitted, but due to higher intensity of one particular emitted colour (e.g., red), others cannot be observed. A Max Planck broke with the ‘continuous energy’ tradition of electromagnetic energy by assuming that the energy is alwGays absorbed or emitted in multiples of hu; For example: hu, 2 hu, 3 hu... nhu N That is, the energy for a certain frequency E can be represented by the A equation E = hu, where ‘h’ is Planck’s constant which has the value 6.626 X 10-34Js and ‘u’ is the frequency of the radiation absorbed or L emitted. The energy (E) for the red Ecolour (higher wavelength or lower frequency) is lower compared to the energy of blue colour (lower T wavelength or higher frequency). The energy emitted from a material body increases with increase in temperature. The significance of P,lanck’s proposal is that, electromagnetic energy T can be gained or lost in discrete values and not in a continuous manner. Hence, emRission or absorption spectrum of light is a collection of a group of wavelengths. E · Do you enjoy Deepavali fireworks? CVariety of colours is seen from fireworks. · How do these colours come from fireworks? Take this paste on a platinum loop and introduce it into a non-luminous flame. · What colour do you observe? Carry out similar activity with strontium chloride. Cupric chloride produces a green colour flame while strontium chloride produces a crimson red flame. · Do you observe yellow light in street lamps? 115 Structure of Atom Sodium vapours produce yellow light in street lamps. · Why do different elements emit different flame colours when heated by the same non-luminous flame? Scientists found that each element emits its own characteristic colour. These colours correspond to certain discrete wavelengths of light and are A called line spectra. The lines in atomic spectra can be used to identify unknown atoNms, just like fingerprints are used to identify people. A G Niels Henrik David Bohr was a Danish physicist who made foundationaNl contributions to understanding atomic structure and quantum theory, for which he A received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1922. Bohr was L also a philosopher and a promoter. E T 6.2 Bohr’s model of hydrogen atom and its limitations Niels Bhor proposed an atomic model based on hydrogen atomic , spectrum. T · What does a line spectrum of R hydrogen atom tell us about the structure of an atom? E Postulates of Niels Bohr EClectrons in an atom occupy ‘stationary’ orbits (states) of fixed S energy at different distances from the nucleus. fig-3: Hydrogen Spectrum When an electron ‘jumps’ from a lower energy state (ground state) to higher energy state (excited state) it absorbs energy or emits energy when such a jump occurs from a higher energy state to a lower energy state. The energies of an electron in an atom can have only certain values E , E , E ……; that is, the energy is quantized. The states corresponding 1 2 3 to these energies are called stationary states and the possible values of the energy are called energy levels. 116 Structure of Atom

pages.text: The lowest energy state of the electron is known as ground state. The electron moves to a higher energy level i.e. to the excited state by gaining energy. · Does the electron retain the absorved energy forever? The electron does not stay in the excited level for long. The electron loses the energy and comes back to its ground state. The A energy emitted by the electron is seen in the form of electromagnetic N energy of specific warelength and when the wavelength is in the visible region it is visible as an emission line. A Bohr’s model explains all the line spectra observed in the case of hydrogen atom. It is a successful model as far as line speGctra of hydrogen atom is concerned. N But the line spectrum of hydrogen atom when observed through a high resolution spectroscope appears as groups of finer lines. A · Did Bohr’s model account for the splitting of line spectra of a hydrogen atom into finer lines? L Bohr’s model failed to accounEt for splitting of line spectra. 6.3 Bohr-Sommerfeld model of an atom T , l=0 l=0 T l=0 R l=0 l=1 l=1 l=1 l=2 E l=2 l=3 nC=1 n=2 n=3 n=4 fig-4: The allowed electronic orbits for the main Quantum numbers by Bohr - Sommerfeld model S In an attempt to account for the structure (splitting) of line spectra known as fine spectra, Sommerfeld modified Bohr’s atomic model by adding elliptical orbits. While retaining the first of Bohr’s circular orbit as such, he added one elliptical orbit to Bohr’s second orbit, two elliptical orbits to Bohr’s third orbit, etc., such that the nucleus of the atom lies at one of the principal foci of these elliptical orbits. He was guided by the fact that, in general, periodic motion under the influence of a central force will lead to elliptical orbits with the nucleus situated at one of the foci. 117 Structure of Atom

Bohr-Sommerfeld model, though successful in accounting for the fine line structure of hydrogen atomic spectra, does not provide a satisfactory picture of the structure of atom in general. This model failed to account for the atomic spectra of atoms of more than one electron. · Why is the electron in an atom restricted to revolve around the nucleus A in stationary orbits located at certain fixed distances? N Max Karl Ernst Ludwig Planck was a German theoretical physicist who originated quAantum theory, which won him the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1918. Planck made G many contributions to theoretical physics, but his fame rests primarily on his role as originator of the quantum theory. N This theory revolutionized human understanding of atomic and subatomic processes. A 6.4 Quantum mechanical model of an atom L · Do the electrons follow defined paths around the nucleus? E If the electron revolves around the nucleus in defined paths or orbits, T the exact position of the electron at various times will be known. For that we have to answer two que stions: , · What is the velocity of the electron? T · Is it possible to find the exact position of the electron? R Electrons are invisible to naked eye. Then, how do you find the position and veloEcity of an electron? To find articles during dark nights we take the help of torchlight. C Similarly, we can take the help of suitable light to find the position and Svelocity of electron. As the electrons are very small, light of very short wavelength is required for this task. This short wavelength light interacts with the electron and disturbs the motion of the electron. Hence, simultaneously the position and velocity of electron cannot be measured accurately. From the above discussion, it is clear that electrons do not follow definite paths in an atom. Do atoms have a definite boundary, as suggested by Bohr’s model? If the electrons are not distributed in orbits around the nucleus this 118 Structure of Atom

means that an atom does not have a definite boundary.) As a result, it is not possible to pinpoint an electron in an atom. Under these circumstances in order to understand the properties of electrons in an atom, a quantum mechanical model of atom was developed by Erwin Schrodinger. According to this model of an atom, instead of orbits of Bohr’s model, the electrons are thought to exist in a particular region of space around A the nucleus at a given instant of time · What do we call the region of space where the electron might be N , at a given time? The region of space around the nucleus where the probabilityA of finding the electron is maximum is called an orbital. In a given space around the nucleus, only certain oGrbitals can exist. Each orbital of a stable energy state for the electron is described by a particular set of quantum numbers. N 6.5 Quantum numbers A Each electron in an atom is described by a set of three numbers n, l, and m .These numbers are called quaLntum numbers. These numbers l indicate the probability of finding the electron in the space around the E nucleus. · What information do the qTuantum numbers provide? The quantum numbers describe the space around the nucleus where the electrons are found a,nd also their energies. T · What does each quantum number signify? 6.5.1 PrincipRal Quantum Number (n) The principal quantum number is related to the size and energy of the main shEell. ‘n’ has positive integer values of 1, 2, 3,… C As ‘n’ increases, the shells become larger and the electrons in those shells are farther from the nucleus. S An increase in ‘n’ also means higher energy. n = 1, 2, 3, ... are often represented by the letters K, L, M… For each ‘n’ value there is one main shell. Shell K L M N n 1 2 3 4 6.5.2 The angular - momentum quantum number (l) This quantum number is represented by a letter ‘l’. ‘l’ has integer values from 0 to n-1 for each value of ‘n’. Each ‘l’ value represents one sub-shell. 119 Structure of Atom

Each value of ‘l’ is related to the shape of a particular sub-shell in the space around the nucleus. The value of ‘l’ for a particular sub-shell is generally designated by the letters s, p, d . . . as follows: l 0 1 2 3 Name of the sub-shell s p d f A When n = 1, there is only one sub-shell with l = 0. This is designated N as ‘1s’ orbital. A When n = 2, there are two sub-shells, with l = 0, the ‘2s’ sub-shell and with l = 1, the ‘2p’ sub-shell. G · What is the maximum value of ‘l’ for n=3? N · How many values can ‘l’ have for n = 4? and what are sub shells. 6.5.3 The magnetic quantum number A(m) l The magnetic quantum number (m) has integer values between -l and L l l, including zero. Thus for a certain value of l, there are (2l +1) integer E values of m as follows: l T -l, (-l+1) . . ., –1, 0, 1, . . . (+l - 1), +l These values describe the spatial orientation of the orbital in space , relative to the otherT orbitals in the atom. When l = 0, (2l+ 1) = 1 and there is only one Table-1 R value of m, thus we have only one orbital i.e., 1s. l Sub- Number of l E When l= 1, (2l+ 1) = 3, that means m has shell degenerated l three values, namely, -1, 0, and 1 or three p orbitals C orbitals, with different orientations along x, y, z 0 s S 1 p axes. These are labelled as p , p , and p. x y z 2 d · Do these three p-orbitals have the same 3 f energy? The number of ‘m’ values indicates the number of orbitals in a sub- l shell with a particular l value. Orbitals in the sub-shell belonging to the same shell possess same energy. These are called degenerated orbitals. Fill the table-1 with the number of degenerated orbitals per sub-shell using (2l+1) rule. 120 Structure of Atom

s-orbital is spherical in shape, p-orbitals are dumbell-shaped and d-orbitals are double dumbell-shaped as shown below. A N A G fig-5: Shapes of orbitals in s, p, d subshells N The following table-2 represents the shells, sub-shells and the number of orbitals in the sub-shells. A Table-2 n l m sub-shell notation No of orbitals L l in the subshell E 1 0 0 1s 1 0 0T 2s 1 2 1 -1 ,0,+1 2p 3 , 0 0 3s 1 T 3 1 -1,0,+1 3p 3 R 2 -2,-1,0,+1,+2 3d 5 E 0 0 4s 1 C1 -1,0,+1 4p 3 4 2 -2,-1,0,+1,+2 4d 5 S 3 -3,-2,-1,0,+1,+2,+3 4f 7 Table-3 Each sub-shell holds a Sub shells Number of Maximum maximum of twice as many orbitals (2l+1) number of electrons as the number of electrons orbitals in the sub-shell. s (1=0) 1 2 The maximum number of p (1=1) 3 6 electrons that can occupy various d (1=2) 5 10 sub-shells is given in the f (l=3) 7 14 following table 3. 121 Structure of Atom

6.5.4 Spin Quantum Number (m ) s The three quantum numbers n, l, and m describe the size (energy), l shape, and orientation, respectively, of an atomic orbital in space. As you have observed in the case of street lights (sodium vapour lamp), yellow light is emitted. This yellow light is comprised of a very closely spaced doublet when analyzed using high resolution spectroscope. A Alkali and alkaline earth metals show such type of lines. N To account for such a behavior of electron an additional quantum number is introduced. This is spin quantum number. This reprAesents the property of the electron. It is denoted by ‘m’. s G This quantum number refers to the two possible orientations of the spin of an electron, one clockwise and the other antNiclockwise spin. These are represented by + ½ and -½. If both are positive/negative values, then A the spins are parallel otherwise the spins are anti-parallel. The importance of the spin quantumL number is seen when electrons occupy specific orbitals in multi-electron atoms. E · How do electrons in an atom occupy shells, sub-shells and orbitals? T The distribution of electrons in shells, sub-shells and orbital in an atom is known as electroni c configuration. , T 6.6 Electronic Configuration Let us fiRrst consider the hydrogen atom for understanding the arrangement of electrons, as it contains only one electron. E The shorthand notation consists of the principal energy level (n value), thCe letter representing sub-level (l value), and the number of electrons (x) in the sub-shell is written as a superscript as shown below: S nl x For the hydrogen (H) atom having atomic number (Z) = 1, the number of electrons is one, then the electronic configuration is 1s1. Denotes the number of electrons in orbital 1s1 Denotes the principle quantum number Denotes the angular momentum quantum number 122 Structure of Atom

The electron configuration can also be represented by showing the spin of the electron. For the electron in H, as you have seen, the set of quantum numbers is: n = 1, l = 0, m = 0, m = ½ or – ½. l s # A For many-electron atoms, we must know the electron configuration of the atom. The distribution of electrons in various atomic orbitals N provides an understanding of the electronic behavior of the atom and, in turn, its reactivity. Let us consider the helium (He) atom. A · Helium (Z=2) atom has two electrons. How are they arranged? G To describe the electronic configuration for more than one electron N in the atom, we need to know three principles: Those are the Pauli Exclusion Principle, Aufbau principle and Hund’s Rule. A Let us discuss them briefly. L 6.6.1 The Pauli Exclusion Principle E Helium atom has two electrons. The first electron occupies ‘1s’ orbital. The second electron joins the first in the 1s-orbital, so the electron T configuration of the ground state of ‘He’ is 1s2. Then the question is: · What are the spins o,f these two electrons? T According to Pauli Exclusion Principle no two electrons of the same atom can haveR all four quantum numbers the same. If n, l, and m are same for two electrons then m must be different. In El s the helium atom the spins must be paired. CElectrons with paired spins are denoted by ‘#$’. One electron has 1 S1 m= + , the other has m= - . They have anti-parallel spins. s 2 s 2 · How many electrons can occupy an orbital? The major consequence of the exclusion principle involves orbital occupancy. Since only two values of m are allowed, an orbital can hold s only two electrons and they must have opposite spins. Hence, the electronic configuration of helium atom is: 1s2 ## 123 Structure of Atom

6.6.2 Aufbau Principle As we pass from one element to another one of next higher atomic number, one electron is added every time to the atom. The maximum number of electrons in any shell is ‘2n2’, where ‘n’ is the principal quantum number. The maximum number of electrons in a sub-shell (s, p, d or f) is equal to 2(2l+1) A where l = 0, 1, 2, 3… Thus these sub-shells can have a maximum of 2, 6, 10, and 14 N electrons respectively. In the ground state the electronic configuration can be built up by placing electrons A in the lowest available orbitals until the total number of electrons added is equal to the atomic number. This is called the Aufbau principle (ThGe German word “Aufbau” means “building up.”).Thus orbitals are filled in the order of increasing energy. N Two general rules help us to predict electronic configurations. A 1. Electrons are assigned to orbitals in order of increasing value of (n+l). 2. For sub-shells with the same valueL of (n+l), electrons are assigned first to the sub-shell with lower ‘n’. E The following diagram (fig-6) shows the increasing value of (n+l). T Ascending order of energies of various atomic orbitals is given below. , 1s < 2s < 2p < 3s < 3p < 4s < 3d < 4p < 5s < 4d < T 5p < 6s < 4f < 5d < 6p < 7s < 5f < 6d < 7p < 8s … R The electronic configurations of some elements in the increasing atomic number (Z) value are given below. E H(Z=C1) 1s1 # S He(Z=2) 1s2 ## Li(Z=3) 1s22s1 ## # Be(Z=4) 1s22s2 ## ## B(Z=5) 1s22s22p1 ## ## # fig-6: The filling order of atomic orbitals (Moeller Chart) 124 Structure of Atom

· For carbon (C) atom (Z=6), where does the 6th electron go? · Whether the electron pairs up in the same p-orbital or will it go to the next p-orbital? 6.6.3 Hund’s Rule According to this rule electron pairing in orbitals starts only when all available empty orbitals of the same energy (degenerate orbitals) are singly occupied. The configuration of Carbon (C) atom (Z=6) is 1s22s22p2. The first four electrons A go into the 1s and 2s orbitals. The next two electrons go into separate 2p orbitals, with both electrons having the same spin N # # # # # # A Note that the unpaired electrons in the 2p orbitals arGe shown with parallel spins. What we have learnt · Ligth can be characterized by its wavelength (l), frequency (J) and these quantities are related to speed of light as C=Jl. · Spectrum is a group of wavelengths. · Electromagnetic energy (Light) can have only certain discrete energy values which is given by A the equation E=hu · Electrons in an atom can gain energy by absorbing a particular frequencyN of light and can lose energy by emitting a particular frequency. · Bohr’s model of atom: Electrons are present in stationary states. TAhe electron moves to higher energy level if it absorbs energy in the form of electromagnetic energy or moves to a lower G energy state by emitting energy in the form of electromagnetic energy of appropriate frequency. · Atomic line spectra arise because of absorption /emission of certain frequencies of light energy. N · It is not possible to measure accurately the position and velocity of an electron simultaneously. · The space around the nucleus where the probability of finding the electron is maximum is called A orbital. · The three quantum numbers n, l, mdescLribe the energy, shape and orientation respectively, of l an atomic orbital. Spin is an intrinsic property of an atom. E · Spin is an intrinsic property of an electron. · The arrangement of electronTs in shells, sub-shells and orbitals in an atom is called the electron configuration. · According to Pauli Exclusion Principle no two electrons of the same atom can have all the four , quantum numbersT same. · Aufbau principle: The lowest-energy orbitals are filled first. R · Hund’s rule: The orbitals of equal energy (degenerate) are occupied with one electron each before pairing of electrons starts. E Improve your learning C I. Reflections of concepts S 1. While retaining the first of Bohr’s circular orbit as such, he added one elliptical orbit to Bohr’s second orbit, two elliptical orbits to Bohr’s third orbit, etc., such that the nucleus of the atom lies at one of the principal foci of these elliptical orbits. He was guided by the fact that, in general, periodic motion under the influence of a central force will lead to elliptical orbits with the nucleus situated at one of the foci. 117 Structure of Atom Bohr-Sommerfeld model, though successful in accounting for the fine line structure of hydrogen atomic spectra, does not provide a satisfactory picture of the structure of atom in general. This model failed to account for the atomic spectra of atoms of more than one electron. · Why is the electron in an atom restricted to revolve around the nucleus A in stationary orbits located at certain fixed distances? N Max Karl Ernst Ludwig Planck was a German theoretical physicist who originated quAantum theory, which won him the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1918. Planck made G many contributions to theoretical physics, but his fame rests primarily on his role as originator of the quantum theory. N This theory revolutionized human understanding of atomic and subatomic processes. A 6.4 Quantum mechanical model of an atom L · Do the electrons follow defined paths around the nucleus? E If the electron revolves around the nucleus in defined paths or orbits, T the exact position of the electron at various times will be known. For that we have to answer two que stions: , · What is the velocity of the electron? T · Is it possible to find the exact position of the electron? R Electrons are invisible to naked eye. Then, how do you find the position and veloEcity of an electron? To find articles during dark nights we take the help of torchlight. C Similarly, we can take the help of suitable light to find the position and Svelocity of electron. As the electrons are very small, light of very short wavelength is required for this task. This short wavelength light interacts with the electron and disturbs the motion of the electron. Hence, simultaneously the position and velocity of electron cannot be measured accurately. From the above discussion, it is clear that electrons do not follow definite paths in an atom. Do atoms have a definite boundary, as suggested by Bohr’s model? If the electrons are not distributed in orbits around the nucleus this 118 Structure of Atom means that an atom does not have a definite boundary.) As a result, it is not possible to pinpoint an electron in an atom. Under these circumstances in order to understand the properties of electrons in an atom, a quantum mechanical model of atom was developed by Erwin Schrodinger. According to this model of an atom, instead of orbits of Bohr’s model, the electrons are thought to exist in a particular region of space around A the nucleus at a given instant of time · What do we call the region of space where the electron might be N , at a given time? The region of space around the nucleus where the probabilityA of finding the electron is maximum is called an orbital. In a given space around the nucleus, only certain oGrbitals can exist. Each orbital of a stable energy state for the electron is described by a particular set of quantum numbers. N 6.5 Quantum numbers A Each electron in an atom is described by a set of three numbers n, l, and m .These numbers are called quaLntum numbers. These numbers l indicate the probability of finding the electron in the space around the E nucleus. · What information do the qTuantum numbers provide? The quantum numbers describe the space around the nucleus where the electrons are found a,nd also their energies. T · What does each quantum number signify? 6.5.1 PrincipRal Quantum Number (n) The principal quantum number is related to the size and energy of the main shEell. ‘n’ has positive integer values of 1, 2, 3,… C As ‘n’ increases, the shells become larger and the electrons in those shells are farther from the nucleus. Atomic number of an element (Z) indicates not only the positive charges i.e., the protons in the nucleus of the atom of the element but also the number of electrons in the neutral atom of that element. So The physical and chemical properties of atoms of the elements depend not on the number of protons A but on the number of electrons and their arrangements (electronic configurations) in atoms. N Therefore, the modern periodic law may be stated as “The physical and chemical properties of elements are thAe periodic functions of the electronic configurations of their atoms.” 7.5.1 Positions of elements in the Modern PeriodicG Table The modern periodic table has eighteen vertical columns known as groups and seven horizontal rows known as perioNds. A We can explain the classification of the elements in the modern periodic table in terms of certain eleLctron arrangements which are periodically repeated. This model failed to account for the atomic spectra of atoms of more than one electron. · Why is the electron in an atom restricted to revolve around the nucleus A in stationary orbits located at certain fixed distances? N Max Karl Ernst Ludwig Planck was a German theoretical physicist who originated quAantum theory, which won him the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1918. Planck made G many contributions to theoretical physics, but his fame rests primarily on his role as originator of the quantum theory. N This theory revolutionized human understanding of atomic and subatomic processes. A 6.4 Quantum mechanical model of an atom L · Do the electrons follow defined paths around the nucleus? E If the electron revolves around the nucleus in defined paths or orbits, T the exact position of the electron at various times will be known. For that we have to answer two que stions: , · What is the velocity of the electron? T · Is it possible to find the exact position of the electron? R Electrons are invisible to naked eye. Then, how do you find the position and veloEcity of an electron? To find articles during dark nights we take the help of torchlight. C Similarly, we can take the help of suitable light to find the position and Svelocity of electron. As the electrons are very small, light of very short wavelength is required for this task. This short wavelength light interacts with the electron and disturbs the motion of the electron. Hence, simultaneously the position and velocity of electron cannot be measured accurately. From the above discussion, it is clear that electrons do not follow definite paths in an atom. Do atoms have a definite boundary, as suggested by Bohr’s model? As a result, it is not possible to pinpoint an electron in an atom. Under these circumstances in order to understand the properties of electrons in an atom, a quantum mechanical model of atom was developed by Erwin Schrodinger. According to this model of an atom, instead of orbits of Bohr’s model, the electrons are thought to exist in a particular region of space around A the nucleus at a given instant of time · What do we call the region of space where the electron might be N , at a given time? The region of space around the nucleus where the probabilityA of finding the electron is maximum is called an orbital. In a given space around the nucleus, only certain oGrbitals can exist. Each orbital of a stable energy state for the electron is described by a particular set of quantum numbers. These numbers l indicate the probability of finding the electron in the space around the E nucleus. · What information do the qTuantum numbers provide? Even in chRemistry, from the earliest times, scientists have been trying to classify the available elements in to a limited number of groups on the E basis of their properties. 7.C1 What is the Need for the arrangement of elements in an organised manner? S Robert Boyle (1661) defined an element as any substance that cannot be decomposed into a further simple substance by a physical or chemical change. At his time, about thirteen elements were known. Towards the end of the eighteenth century, by the time of Lavoisier another eleven elements were discovered. By 1865 about sixty three elements were known and by 1940, a total of ninety one elements from natural sources and another seventeen elements were synthetically prepared. 129 Classification of Elements - The Periodic Table By now, including synthetic elements, there are more than 118 elements. As the number of elements increased, it became difficult to keep in memory the chemistries of individual elements and their compounds. Newlands (1865) found that when elements were arranged in the ascending order of their atomic weights they appeared to fall into 7 groups. Each group contained elements with similar chemical properties. Based on these observations, Newlands proposed the law of octaves. The law of octaves states that when elements are arranged in the ascending order of their atomic weights they fall into a pattern in which their properties repeat at regular intervals. He divided the chart into 8 vertical columns k,nown as groups. Each group is T divided into A, B sub groups. Each column contained the R elements of similar chemical properties. S This atomic number concept forced the periodic law to be changed. The periodic law is changed from atomic weight concept to atomic number concept and now it is called the modern periodic law. We know that Mendeleeff’s periodic law is stated as “The properties of elements are the periodic functions of their atomic weights”. Now, let us try to understand modern periodic law. The modern periodic law may be stated as “the properties of the elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.” 138 Classification of Elements - The Periodic Table Based on the modern periodic law, the modern periodic table which is given here (page 23) is proposed. It is the extension of the original Mendeleeff’s periodic table known as short form of the table and this modern table is called the long form of the periodic table. Atomic number of an element (Z) indicates not only the positive charges i.e., the protons in the nucleus of the atom of the element but also the number of electrons in the neutral atom of that element. So The physical and chemical properties of atoms of the elements depend not on the number of protons A but on the number of electrons and their arrangements (electronic configurations) in atoms. N Therefore, the modern periodic law may be stated as “The physical and chemical properties of elements are thAe periodic functions of the electronic configurations of their atoms.” 7.5.1 Positions of elements in the Modern PeriodicG Table The modern periodic table has eighteen vertical columns known as groups and seven horizontal rows known as perioNds. Let us see what decides the position of an element in modern periodic table. A We can explain the classification of the elements in the modern periodic table in terms of certain eleLctron arrangements which are periodically repeated. The elements with similar outer shell (valence shell) E electronic configurations in their atoms are in the same column called group. Elements listed in a group down to it are in the order of their T increasing principal quantum numbers. In the chapter ‘Structure of atom’ you have learnt that ‘s’ sub-shell with one orbital contains, a maximum of two electrons. Each ‘p’ sub-shell contains 3 orbitals aTnd accommodates a maximum of six electrons. The‘d’ sub-shell contains 5 orbitals and accommodates a maximum of 10 electrons R and ‘f’ sub-shell contains 7 orbitals with 14 electrons maximum. Depending upon to which sub-shell the differentiating electron. i.e., the last coming electronE enters in the atom of the given element, the elements are classified as ‘s’ ‘p’, ‘d’ and ‘f’ block elements. C For example, sodium (Na) gets its new coming electron (differentiating electron) into 3s level. Therefore ‘Na’ is an s-block element. SAluminium (Al) gets its differentiating electron into ‘p’ subshell and it is a p-block element. Scandium (Sc) gets its differentiating electron into ‘d’ subshell. Therefore it is a d-block element. Cerium (Ce) gets its new coming electron into ‘f’ subshell, hence,it is an f-block element. Let us observe the electronic configurations of the following elements. Hence the second period contains 8 elements Li, Be, B, C, N O, F and Ne in the order given. Thus, the 2nd period consists two s-block elements (Li, Be) and six p- block elements (B to Ne). 142 Classification of Elements - The Periodic Table

pages.text: 4. Third period starts with third main shell (M). This shell (M) has 3 sub- shells, namely, 3s, 3p and 3d, but while electrons are being filled into the shells, ‘3d’ gets electrons only after ‘4s’ is filled. Therefore, the 3rd period contains again 8 elements, which includes two s-block elements (Na, Mg) and six p-block elements (Al to Ar). 5. Fourth Period starts with Fourth main shell (N). This shell (N) has four sub-shells namely 4s, 4p, 4d and 4f, but while electrons are being A filled into the shell, electrons enter the atoms in the order 4s, 3d and N 4p. Due to this, the fourth period contains 18 elements which includes two s-block (K, Ca), 10 elements from d block (Sc to Zn) and six A elements from p-block ( Ga to Kr). There are altogether eighteen 31 36 elements in the fourth period. G 6. On the same lines, we can explain why there are 18 elements in the fifth period ( Rb to Xe). N 37 54 7. There are thirty two elements in the Sixth period from Cs to Rn 55 86 which includes 2 elements from s-bloAck (6s) 14 elements from f-block (4f) 10 elements from d-block (5d) and 6 elements from L p-block (6p). ‘4f’ elements are called LanthEanoids or lanthanides. Elements from Ce to Lu possess almost the same properties as La. So, the name 58 71 T 57 lanthanoids is the most appropriate one for these elements. 7th period is incomplet e and contains 2 elements from s-block (7s) , 14 elements from f-block (5f), 10 elements from d-block (6d) and some T elements from p-block (7p). The 5f elements are called Actinoids or as Actinides. ThRey are from Th to Lr . 90 103 The f-block elements known as lanthanoids and actinoids are shown E separately at the bottom of the periodic table. C Do you know? S ‘Ide’ means ‘heir’ and it is used generally for a change like Cl to Cl-. ‘Cl’ is chlorine atom and Cl- is chloride ion. ‘Oid’ means ‘the same’. Some scientists suggest lanthanoids as La to Yb, some suggest them as 57 70 Ce to Lu and some take La to Lu (15 elements). There is another argument 58 71 57 71 that even Sc and Y should be included in lanthanoids. All these suggestions have 21 39 substance because Sc, Y and La to Lu all have the similar outer shells 21 39 57 71 configurations. Also in the case of actinoids. There are different arguments like actinoids are from Th to Lr or Ac to No or Ac to Lr. 90 103 89 102 89 103 143 Classification of Elements - The Periodic Table

Think and discuss · Why lanthanoids and actinoids are placed separately at the bottom of the periodic table? · If they are inserted within the table imagine and draw how the table would be? A 7.5.4 Metals and Non metals N You have learnt about the properties of metals in the chapter Metals A and Non Metals in class VIII. Let us study the metallic properties of elements in periodic table. G The elements with three or less electrons in the outer shell are considered to be metals and those with five or morNe electrons in the outer shell are considered to be non metals. We may find some exceptions to A this. ‘d’ block elements (3rd group to 12th group) are metals and they are also known as transition metals and thLe metallic character of d-block elements decreases gradually fErom left to right in periodic table. Lanthanoids and actinoids actually belong to 3rd group (III B) which is within T the transition elements: hence they are called the inner transition elements. Metalloids or semi-me tals are elements which have properties that , are intermediate beTtween the properties of metals and non metals. They possess properties like metals but are brittle like non metals. They are R generally semi conductors. Eg: B, Si, As, Ge. All Eelements in s-block are metals, whereas in p-block (except 18th group) there are metals, non metals and metalloids. In periodic table you C will notice a staircase like demarcation. (zig zag line) The elements to the Sleft of this demarcation are metals and to the right are non-metals. The elements on staircase (or) very near to it like B, Si, As, Ge etc., are metalloids. 7.5.5 Periodic properties of the elements in the modern table The modern periodic table is organized on the basis of the electronic configuration of the atoms of elements. Physical and chemical properties of elements are related to their electronic configurations particularly the outer shell configurations (valence shell). The atoms of the elements in a group possess similar electronic configurations. Therefore, we expect all the elements 144 Classification of Elements - The Periodic Table

in a group should have similar chemical properties and there should be a regular gradation in their physical properties from top to bottom. Similarly, across the table, i.e., from left to right in any period elements get an increase in the atomic number by one unit between any two successive elements. Therefore, the electronic configuration of valence shell of any two elements in a given period is not same. Due to this reason elements along a period possess different chemical properties A with regular gradation in their physical properties from left to right. To understand this we will take some properties of elements and discuss N how they vary in groups and in periods. 7.6 Properties of elements and their trends in Groups and in Periods A 7.6.1 Valence: Valence (or) valency of an element was defined as the combining power of an element with respect to hydroGgen, oxygen or indirectly any other element through hydrogen and oxygen. Valence of an element with respect to hydrogen is the number of N hydrogen atoms with which one atom of that element chemically combines. Valence of an element with respect to oxygen is twice the number of A oxygen atoms with which one atom of that element combines. Note that the group number of an element gives the maximum valence of that element L as per old notation that is I to VIII groups but it is 18-group number as per IUPAC numbering. E For example one atom of ‘Na’ chemically combines with one atom of ‘H’ to give NaH. Therefore,T the valence of Na is 1. One atom of ‘Ca’ combines with one atom of ‘O’ to give CaO. So the valency of Ca is 2. In general, the valence of an element with respect to hydrogen is its , traditional group number. If the element is in the group V or above, its T valence is 8– group number. For example, valence of chlorine which is a 7th gorup element is 8-7 = 1. R In general, each period starts with valency 1 for 1st group elements, increases upto 4 with respect to the group number and then decreases E from 4 to 3 to 2 to 1 to zero in the following groups (this is applicable only for main group elements i.e., ‘s’ and ‘p’ block elements with respect C to hydrogen. Now a days valence of an elment is generally taken as the number of valence S shell (outer most shell) electrons in its atom. Oxidation number concept almost is the latest subsititute to the valence concept in the modern literature. Activity 3 · Find out the valencies of first 20 elements. · How does the valency vary in a period on going from left to right? · How does the valency vary on going down a group? 7.6.2 Atomic radius Atomic radius of an element may be defined as the distance from the centre of the nucleus of the atom to its outermost shell. 145 Classification of Elements - The Periodic Table

Atomic radius of an element is not possible to measure in its isolated state. This is because it is not possible to determine the location of the electron that surrounds the nucleus. However, we can measure the distance between the nuclei of adjacent atoms in a solid. From this we can estimate the size of the atom by assigning half of this distance to the radius of each atom. This method is best suited to elements such as the metals that exist in the solid state. More than 75 percent of the elements are metals and A atomic radii of metals are called metallic radii. Another way of estimating the size of an atom is to measure the distNance between the two atoms in covalent molecules. A The size of a chlorine atom is estimated by measuring the length of the covalent bond between two chlorine atoms in a Cl molecule. Half of 2 G this distance is taken as atomic radius which is called as the covalent radius of chlorine atom. N Atomic radius is measured in ‘pm’ (pico meter) units. 1 pm = 10-12m A Variation of atomic radii in groupL Atomic radii increase from top to bottom in a group (column) of the E periodic table. As we go down in a group, the atomic number of the element T increases. Therefore to accommodate more number of electrons, more shells are required. As a result the number of shells in a group from top to bottom increases. The d,istance between the nucleus and the outer most T shell of the atom increases. Hence the atomic size increases with atomic number whenR we go down the group. Table-6 E Group Element (atomic radius in pm) C Group1: Li (152), Na (186), K (231), Rb (244) and Cs (262) SGroup 17: F (64), Cl (99), Br (114), I (133) and At (140) Variation of atomic radii in period Atomic radii of elements decrease across a period from left to right. As we go to right, electrons enter into the same main shell or even inner shell in case of ‘d’ block and ‘f’ block elements. Therefore, there should be no change in distance between nucleus and outer shell but nuclear charge increases because of the increase in the atomic number of elements in period. Hence, the nuclear attraction on the outer shell electrons increases. As a result the size of the atom decreases. 146 Classification of Elements - The Periodic Table

Table-7 Period Elements (atomic radius in pm) 2nd period Li (152), Be (111), B (88), C (77), N (74), O (66), F (64) 3rd period Na (186), Mg (160), Al (143), Si (117), P(110), S(104), Cl(99) · Do atom of an element and its ion have same size? A Let us consider the following situation. N Assume that sodium (Na) atom has lost an electron and formed a cation of sodium (Na+). A Which one between Na and Na+ would have more size? Why? Atomic number of sodium (Na) is 11. Therefore soGdium (Na) atom contains 11 protons and 11 electrons with outer electron as 3s1. On the other hand Na+ ion has 11 protons but only 10 eleNctrons. The 3s shell of Na+ level has no electron in it. Hence its outer shell configuration is 2s2 2p6. As proton number is more than electArons in it, the nucleus of Na+ ion attracts outer shell electrons with strong nuclear force. As a result the L Na+ ion shrinks in size. Therefore, the size of Na+ ion is less than ‘Na’ atom. In general the positive ion (cation) of an element has less size than E its neutral atom Example. Na (157pm) NaT+ (98pm); K (203pm) K+(133pm); Mg (136pm) Mg2+(6,5pm); T Al (125pm) Al3+(50pm) for neutral atoms covalent radiai are given. ConsiderR another example: Assume that chlorine (Cl) atom has gained an electron to form anion of chlorEine (Cl–) i.e. chloride ion. · Which one, between Cl and Cl– would have more size? Why? C Electronic configuration of chlorine (Cl) atom is 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p5 and the electronic configuration of chloride (Cl–) ion is 1s2 2s2 2p6 S 3s2 3p6. Both chlorine and chloride ion have 17 protons each but there are 17 electrons in chlorine atom, where as 18 electrons in chloride ion. Therefore, the nuclear attraction is less in Cl– ion when compared with chlorine atom. Therefore the size of the chlorine (Cl) atom is less than size of Cl- ion. In general negative ion (anion) of an element has bigger size than its neutral atom. Example. Chloride ion of Cl (99pm) Cl– (181pm); F (64pm), F– (133pm); O (73pm), O2- (140pm); N (75pm), N3- (171pm); 147 Classification of Elements - The Periodic Table

· Which one in each of the following pairs is larger in size or radius? (a)Na, Al (b) Na, Mg+2 (c) S2-, Cl– (d) Fe2+, Fe3+ (e) C4-, F– 7.6.3 Ionization Energy or Ionization Potential Ionization energy is one of the important properties of elements. The minimum energy required to remove an electron from the outer most orbit or shell of a neutral gaseous atom is called ionization energy. The energy required to remove the first electron from the outer most orbit or shell of a A neutral gaseous atom of the element is called its first ionization energy. The energy required to remove an electron from uni- positive ion of the eleNment is called the 2nd ionization energy of that element and so on. M + IE g M+ + e- (M = neutral atom), A (g) 1 (g) (IE = first ionization energy) G 1 M+ + IE g M+2 + e- (M+ = uni-positive ion) (g) 2 (g) N (IE = second ionization energy) 2 Think and discuss A · Second ionization energy of an element is higher than its first L ionization energy. why? E Ionization energy of an element depends on its 1. Nuclear charge: MorTe the nuclear charge, more is the ionization energy. eg:Between Na and, Cl, Chlorine atom has more ionization energy. 11 T17 2. Screening effect or sheilding effect: more the shells with electrons betwReen the nucleus and the valence shell, they act as screens and decrease nuclear attraction over valence electrons. This is called the E screening effect. More the screening effect, less is the ionization energy. BeCtween Li and Cs, the element Cs has more inner shells and so has 3 55 55 less ionization energy. S 3. Penetration power of the orbitals: Orbitals belonging to the same main shell have different piercing power towards the nucleus, for examle 4s>4p>4d>4f in the penetration. It is easier to remove 4f electron than 4s. Between Be 1s2 2s2 and B 1s2 2s2 2p1, the element B has less ionization 4 5 energy due to less penetration power of ‘2p’ compared to ‘2s’ Therefore it is easy to remove electron from Boron than Berylium. 4. Stable configuration: If the orbitals in any attom are fully or half filled, then their electronic configuration is called stable electronic configuration. It is easier to remove one electron from O 8 148 Classification of Elements - The Periodic Table

(1s22s22p4) than N (1s22s22p3). This is because, N has stable half 7 7 filled configuration. Comparitively with oxygen, nitrogen has stable in filled orbitals. Tehrefore Ionization energy of Nitrogen is high. 5. Atomic radius: More the atomic radius, less is the ionization energy. Therefore, ionization energy of ‘F’ is greater than that of ‘I’ and the ionization energy of ‘Na’ is more than that of ‘Cs’. A Ionization energy of elements decreases as we go down in a group and generally increases from left to right in a period, but does not follow a N regular order or trend. Ionization energy is expressed in kJ mol-1 Ionization energy is also called the ionization potential but when we use A the term the ionization potential, it is better to write the unit eV atom–1. 7.6.4 Electron affinity - Electron gain enthalpy Atoms of some elements gain electrons while forming ionic compounds. An atom is able to gain an electron only when the electron outside the atom is attracted by its nucleus. Attraction involves the liberation of energy. The electron affinity of an element is defined as the energy liberated A when an electron is added to its neutral gaseous atom. Electron affinity of N an element is also called electron gain enthalpy of that element. M + e- g M- + E (M = Element, E = First electronA affinity) (g) (g) 1 1 M- + e- g M-2 + E (E = Second electron affini G ty). (g) (g) 2 2 The energy liberated when an electron is added to a uni-negative ion of the element is called the 2nd electron affinity of tNhat element. However, practically no element shows liberation of energy when the 2nd electron is A added to its uni-negative ion. It does not mean that di-negative or tri- negative ions do not form. They do form,L but for adding 2nd electron, energy in another way like bond formatioEn must be given. Table-10 T Groups Electron affinity value (in kJ mol-1) VIIA (halogen,s) F(-328); Cl(-349); Br (-325); I(-295); At(-270) T VIA (chalcogens) O(-141); S(-200); Ge(-195); Te(-190); PO (-174) R Electron gain enthalpy values decrease as we go down in a group, but increaseE along a period from left to right. Metals have very low electron gain enthalpy values and alkaline earth C metals have even positive values. Note that the negative sign for energy value Sin table indicates that energy is liberated or lost, and the positive sign tells that the energy is gained or absorbed. All the factors which influence the ionization energy would also influence the electron gain enthalpy. Think and discuss · The calculated electron gain enthalpy values for alkaline earth metals and noble gases are positive. How can you explain this? · The second period element for example ‘F’ has less electron gain enthalpy than the third period element of the same group for example 150 Classification of Elements - The Periodic Table

7.6.5 Electronegativity The ionization energy and the electron gain enthalpy are properties of isolated atoms of elements. There has been a need to have a comparative scale relating to the abilities of elements to attract electrons when their atoms are combined. For this purpose, the concept of electronegativity is introduced. A The electronegativity of an element is defined as the relative tendency N of its atom to attract electrons towards it self when it is bonded to the atom of another element. A All the factors that influence the ionization energy and the electron affinity of elements influence the electronegativity Gvalues of those elements. Because of this, Mulliken proposed that the electronegativity N of an element is the average value of its ionization energy and electron affinity. A ionization energy + electron affinity Electronegativity = L 2 Linus Pauling assigned the eleEctronegativity values for elements on the basis of their bond energies. He assumed that the electronegativity of T hydrogen is 2.20 and calculated the values of other elements with respect to hydrogen. Observe the v alues in the following example , T Table-11 Period/group R Element (electronegativity with respect to hydrogen) VIIA (Halogens): F(4.0), Cl(3.0), Br(2.8), I(2.5) E 2nd period: Li(1.0), Be(1.47), B(2.0), C(2.5), N(3.0), O(3.5), F(4.0), Ne(0) C Electronegativity values of elements decrease as we go down in a group S and increase along a period from left to right. The most electronegative element is ‘F’ and the least electronegative stable element is ‘Cs’. 7.6.6 Metallic and Non-Metallic Properties Metals generally show less electronegative character. In compounds, they generally show a tendency to remain as positive ions. This property is often termed as electropositive character. Metals are electropositive elements. 151 Classification of Elements - The Periodic Table

Non metals are generally more electronegative due to their smaller atomic radii. Let us examine the elements of 3rd period. 3rd period: Na Mg Al Si P S Cl We know that Na and Mg are metals, Al and Si are semi metals (metalloids), P, S and Cl are non metals. So we find metals on left side and non metals on right side of the periodic table. This means metallic character A decreases while non metallic character increases as we move along a period N (from left to right). Let us take group 14 (IVA) elements. A IVA group: C Si Ge Sn Pb Here also we know that carbon is a non-metal. Si and GGe are metalloids. Sn and Pb are metals. So we find nonmetals particularly at the top rigNht hand side and metals at the bottom left and right hand side of the periodic table. This means A metallic character increases while non metallic character decreases in a group as we move from top to bottom. More than 75 percent of the elements are metals and A atomic radii of metals are called metallic radii.

A 7.5.4 Metals and Non metals N You have learnt about the properties of metals in the chapter Metals A and Non Metals in class VIII. Let us study the metallic properties of elements in periodic table. G The elements with three or less electrons in the outer shell are considered to be metals and those with five or morNe electrons in the outer shell are considered to be non metals. We may find some exceptions to A this. ‘d’ block elements (3rd group to 12th group) are metals and they are also known as transition metals and thLe metallic character of d-block elements decreases gradually fErom left to right in periodic table. Lanthanoids and actinoids actually belong to 3rd group (III B) which is within T the transition elements: hence they are called the inner transition elements. Metalloids or semi-me tals are elements which have properties that , are intermediate beTtween the properties of metals and non metals. They possess properties like metals but are brittle like non metals. They are R generally semi conductors. Eg: B, Si, As, Ge. All Eelements in s-block are metals, whereas in p-block (except 18th group) there are metals, non metals and metalloids. In periodic table you C will notice a staircase like demarcation. (zig zag line) The elements to the Sleft of this demarcation are metals and to the right are non-metals. The elements on staircase (or) very near to it like B, Si, As, Ge etc., are metalloids. 7.5.5 Periodic properties of the elements in the modern table The modern periodic table is organized on the basis of the electronic configuration of the atoms of elements. Physical and chemical properties of elements are related to their electronic configurations particularly the outer shell configurations (valence shell). The atoms of the elements in a group possess similar electronic configurations. Therefore, we expect all the elements 144 Classification of Elements - The Periodic Table in a group should have similar chemical properties and there should be a regular gradation in their physical properties from top to bottom. Similarly, across the table, i.e., from left to right in any period elements get an increase in the atomic number by one unit between any two successive elements. Therefore, the electronic configuration of valence shell of any two elements in a given period is not same. Due to this reason elements along a period possess different chemical properties A with regular gradation in their physical properties from left to right. To understand this we will take some properties of elements and discuss N how they vary in groups and in periods. 7.6 Properties of elements and their trends in Groups and in Periods A 7.6.1 Valence: Valence (or) valency of an element was defined as the combining power of an element with respect to hydroGgen, oxygen or indirectly any other element through hydrogen and oxygen. Valence of an element with respect to hydrogen is the number of N hydrogen atoms with which one atom of that element chemically combines. Valence of an element with respect to oxygen is twice the number of A oxygen atoms with which one atom of that element combines. Note that the group number of an element gives the maximum valence of that element L as per old notation that is I to VIII groups but it is 18-group number as per IUPAC numbering. E For example one atom of ‘Na’ chemically combines with one atom of ‘H’ to give NaH. Therefore,T the valence of Na is 1. One atom of ‘Ca’ combines with one atom of ‘O’ to give CaO. So the valency of Ca is 2. In general, the valence of an element with respect to hydrogen is its , traditional group number. If the element is in the group V or above, its T valence is 8– group number. For example, valence of chlorine which is a 7th gorup element is 8-7 = 1. R In general, each period starts with valency 1 for 1st group elements, increases upto 4 with respect to the group number and then decreases E from 4 to 3 to 2 to 1 to zero in the following groups (this is applicable only for main group elements i.e., ‘s’ and ‘p’ block elements with respect C to hydrogen. Now a days valence of an elment is generally taken as the number of valence S shell (outer most shell) electrons in its atom. Oxidation number concept almost is the latest subsititute to the valence concept in the modern literature. Activity 3 · Find out the valencies of first 20 elements. · How does the valency vary in a period on going from left to right? · How does the valency vary on going down a group? 7.6.2 Atomic radius Atomic radius of an element may be defined as the distance from the centre of the nucleus of the atom to its outermost shell. 145 Classification of Elements - The Periodic Table Atomic radius of an element is not possible to measure in its isolated state. This is because it is not possible to determine the location of the electron that surrounds the nucleus. However, we can measure the distance between the nuclei of adjacent atoms in a solid. From this we can estimate the size of the atom by assigning half of this distance to the radius of each atom. This method is best suited to elements such as the metals that exist in the solid state. More than 75 percent of the elements are metals and A atomic radii of metals are called metallic radii. Another way of estimating the size of an atom is to measure the distNance between the two atoms in covalent molecules. A The size of a chlorine atom is estimated by measuring the length of the covalent bond between two chlorine atoms in a Cl molecule. Half of 2 G this distance is taken as atomic radius which is called as the covalent radius of chlorine atom. N Atomic radius is measured in ‘pm’ (pico meter) units. 1 pm = 10-12m A Variation of atomic radii in groupL Atomic radii increase from top to bottom in a group (column) of the E periodic table. As we go down in a group, the atomic number of the element T increases. Therefore to accommodate more number of electrons, more shells are required. As a result the number of shells in a group from top to bottom increases. The d,istance between the nucleus and the outer most T shell of the atom increases. Hence the atomic size increases with atomic number whenR we go down the group. Table-6 E Group Element (atomic radius in pm) C Group1: Li (152), Na (186), K (231), Rb (244) and Cs (262) SGroup 17: F (64), Cl (99), Br (114), I (133) and At (140) Variation of atomic radii in period Atomic radii of elements decrease across a period from left to right. As we go to right, electrons enter into the same main shell or even inner shell in case of ‘d’ block and ‘f’ block elements. Therefore, there should be no change in distance between nucleus and outer shell but nuclear charge increases because of the increase in the atomic number of elements in period. Hence, the nuclear attraction on the outer shell electrons increases. As a result the size of the atom decreases. 146 Classification of Elements - The Periodic Table Table-7 Period Elements (atomic radius in pm) 2nd period Li (152), Be (111), B (88), C (77), N (74), O (66), F (64) 3rd period Na (186), Mg (160), Al (143), Si (117), P(110), S(104), Cl(99) · Do atom of an element and its ion have same size? A Let us consider the following situation. N Assume that sodium (Na) atom has lost an electron and formed a cation of sodium (Na+). A Which one between Na and Na+ would have more size? Why? Atomic number of sodium (Na) is 11. Therefore soGdium (Na) atom contains 11 protons and 11 electrons with outer electron as 3s1. On the other hand Na+ ion has 11 protons but only 10 eleNctrons. The 3s shell of Na+ level has no electron in it. Hence its outer shell configuration is 2s2 2p6. As proton number is more than electArons in it, the nucleus of Na+ ion attracts outer shell electrons with strong nuclear force. As a result the L Na+ ion shrinks in size. Therefore, the size of Na+ ion is less than ‘Na’ atom. In general the positive ion (cation) of an element has less size than E its neutral atom Example. Na (157pm) NaT+ (98pm); K (203pm) K+(133pm); Mg (136pm) Mg2+(6,5pm); T Al (125pm) Al3+(50pm) for neutral atoms covalent radiai are given. ConsiderR another example: Assume that chlorine (Cl) atom has gained an electron to form anion of chlorEine (Cl–) i.e. chloride ion. · Which one, between Cl and Cl– would have more size? Why? C Electronic configuration of chlorine (Cl) atom is 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p5 and the electronic configuration of chloride (Cl–) ion is 1s2 2s2 2p6 S 3s2 3p6. Both chlorine and chloride ion have 17 protons each but there are 17 electrons in chlorine atom, where as 18 electrons in chloride ion. Therefore, the nuclear attraction is less in Cl– ion when compared with chlorine atom. Therefore the size of the chlorine (Cl) atom is less than size of Cl- ion. In general negative ion (anion) of an element has bigger size than its neutral atom. Example. Chloride ion of Cl (99pm) Cl– (181pm); F (64pm), F– (133pm); O (73pm), O2- (140pm); N (75pm), N3- (171pm); 147 Classification of Elements - The Periodic Table · Which one in each of the following pairs is larger in size or radius? The minimum energy required to remove an electron from the outer most orbit or shell of a neutral gaseous atom is called ionization ene

There has been a need to have a comparative scale relating to the abilities of elements to attract electrons when their atoms are combined. For this purpose, the concept of electronegativity is introduced. A The electronegativity of an element is defined as the relative tendency N of its atom to attract electrons towards it self when it is bonded to the atom of another element. A All the factors that influence the ionization energy and the electron affinity of elements influence the electronegativity Gvalues of those elements. Because of this, Mulliken proposed that the electronegativity N of an element is the average value of its ionization energy and electron affinity. It was learnt that there are over 118 elements. · How do they usually exist? L · Do they exist as a single atomE or as a group of atoms? In Class IX, we saw that several elements like oxygen, nitrogen and T hydrogen exist as diatomic molecules. What is the force that is holding these constituent atoms ,together in molecules? Since the formation of chemical compounds takes place as a result of combination of atoms of various elements in different S ways, it raises many questions. · Why do some elements and compounds react vigorously while others are inert? · Why the chemical formula for water is H O and for sodium chloride 2 NaCl, why not HO and NaCl ? 2 2 · Why do some atoms combine while others do not? We will try to answer such questions in this chapter. 157 Chemical Bonding · Are elements and compounds simply made up of separate atoms individually arranged? · Is there any attraction between atoms? Let us take the example of common salt, NaCl. When you shake salt from a shaker (Shaking mechine) does it separate into sodium and chlorine? A No! This shows that the sodium and chlorine atoms are being held together. N · What is that holding them together? By the late 19th century and early 20th century, scientists knew about A three types of forces i.e gravitational, magnetic and electrostatic. G Do you know? N Davy’s experiment – A Humphry Davy (1778-1819), a Lprofessor of chemistry at the Royal Institution in London, constructed a E battery of over 250 metallic plates. T In 1807, using electricity from this battery, he was able to extract highly , T reactive metals like potassium and A Votaic pile sodium from their salt solutions. R It was seen that the metal part of the comEpound (Salt solutions) migrated towards the negative electrode and the C non-metal part towards the positive electrode. So it was proposed that metals S are responsible for positively charged particles and non-metals are responsible for negatively charged particles. The oppositely charged particles are held together by electrostatic forces in a Experimental set up by Davy compound. Do you agree with this explanation? Why? While this explanation could explain bonding in NaCl, KCl etc. it could not explain bonding in carbon compounds or diatomic molecules of elements. 158 Chemical Bonding They also knew about the existence of electrons and protons. So it was believed that electrostatic forces were the cause of attraction between atoms in a molecule. When two atoms come sufficiently close together, the electrons of each atom experience the attractive force of the nucleus of the other atom. But the electrons which are negatively charged and repel each other, and the positively charged nuclei also repel each other. The strength of attraction or repulsion will decide bond formation. If attraction is more than the repulsion then atoms combine. If repulsion is more than A attraction then the atoms do not combine. The nucleus and the electrons in the inner shell remain unaffected when atoms come close togetherN. But the electrons in the outermost shell (valence shell) of atoms get affected. Electrons in valence shell (valence electrons) are responsibAle for the formation of bonds between atoms. In previous lessons you studied about exothermic Gand endothermic reactions. The discovery of nob,le gases and the understanding of their electronic T configurations helped us in explaining the formation of chemical bonds among the atoms of the elements. Noble gases which belong to zero group R (18th group or VIII A) are typical gases with almost negligible chemical activity when compared to other elements. They undergo few or no chemical E changes. They are more stable and do not form molecules by allowing their atoms to combine among themselves or with the atoms of other C elements. · What could be the reason for this? S Let us investigate. We represent the nucleus and inner shell N electrons of the atom by the symbol of the element and electrons in the A outer shell by dots (.) or cross marks (x). Let us see how? Noble gases of VIII A possess eight electrons in the valence shells of their atoms. Helium is an exception. Its atom has only two electrons, but its only shell is completely filled. Noble gases with eight electrons in the A valence shell in their atoms are highly stable and rarely participate in N chemical changes. Therefore it is concluded that any species (atom or ion) with eight electrons in the valence shell is stable. Based on the above observations a statement known as “ The Octet Rule” is framed. L 8.3 Octet rule: E It may be stated as “The atoms of elements tend to undergo chemical changes that help to leave theTir atoms with eight outer-shell electrons.” Lewis depicted the atom in terms of a positively charged kernel (Kernel is the nucleus and all ot,her electrons in the atom except the outer most T shell electrons) and the outershell that could accommodate a maximum of eight electRrons. There are many types of chemical bonds, but here we discuss only about ionic bond and covalent bond. 8.4 Ionic and Covalent bonds 8.4.1 Ionic bond Kossel proposed the ionic bond (electrostatic bond) based on the following facts. 163 Chemical Bonding (i) Ionic bond is formed between atoms of two dissimilar elements due to transfer of electrons from the atom of one element to the other. (ii) There are highly reactive metals like alkali metals (IA) and highly reactive non-metals like halogens (VIIA) on the left side and right side of the periodic table respectively. (iii) Noble gases except helium have eight electrons in the valence shells of their atoms. They are chemically inactive and stable. Factors affecting the formation of cation and anion: In previous lesson you have learnt about variation of metallic and non metallic character of elements in a group or period of the periodic table. Recall the facts about metallic and non metallic character of elements. Generally elements of metals have tendency of losing electron to attain the octet in their valence shell. This property is called as the metallic A character or electropositivity. Elements with more electropositive character form cations. Similarly non metals like oxygen ( O), fluorine 8 N ( F) and chlorine ( Cl) acquire electron configuration of elements of inert 9 17 gases by gaining electrons this property is called the nonA-metallic character or electronegativity of the element. Elements with more G electronegative character form anions. · Can you explain the reasons for all these? Lewis (1916) proposed that atoms of some elements could achieve an octet in their valence shells without transfer of electrons between them. They can attain octet configuration in their valence shells by sharing the valence electrons with one or more atoms. The electrons shared between two atoms belong to both the atoms and the sharing of electrons between them leads to the formation of a chemical bond known as covalent bond. 168 Chemical Bonding

For example, take two fluorine atoms which form a stable molecule. Each fluorine atom contributes one electron for bonding and the electron pair that is formed in this way is mutually shared by both the fluorine atoms. Each atom in the F molecule has an octet of valence electrons. 2 A N A G The dots around fluorine atom shows theN valence electrons of respective atoms. What we have learnt · Location of elements in the periodic table helps in predicting the type of bonding that will take place between atoms of the elements. · Ions are positively or negatively charged particles formed by the loss or gain of electrons respectively. · The force between any two atoms or a group of atoms that results in the formation of a stable A entity is called chemical bond. · The outer most shell of an atom is called valence shell and electrons in this shell are called N valence electrons. · The gases belonging to ‘O’ group are called noble gases because they are reluctant to combine A with other atoms. Except helium all other noble gases have an octet of electron configuration in their valence shells. G · Chemically active elements have an incomplete octet in the valence shells of their atoms. · The number of valence electrons available in the atoms of elements decides the type of bond N formed by the atom of the element. · Elements which have a tendency to gain electrons for attaining octet in their valence shell are A called with more electro negative character. They form anions. · In the formation of ionic bond the atoms of electro positive elements lose their valence electrons L to atoms of electro negative elements so that both of them can attain octet in their valence E shells. · The electrostatic attractive force that keeps cation and anion together to form a new electrically T neutral entity is called an ionic bond. · Ionic compounds are often crystalline solids with high melting points. · A chemical bond that f,ormed by sharing of valence-shell electrons between the atoms so that T both of them can attain octet or duplet in their valence shells is called covalent bond. · A single covalent bond is formed when two atoms share a pair of electrons R · Each shared pair of electrons is equivalent to one covalent bond. · Electrons are not always shared equally between the atoms in a covalent bond. The free electrons in the conductor are accelerated towards the postive 187 Electric Current terminal of the battery and when these electrons – Potential difference + are in motion under the influence of the field, they A B collide with positive ions, lose energy and may even come to a halt at every collision. They are Direction of electric field again accelerated by the electric field and make fig-3: Motion of electron collisions with other positive ions. In this way they A continue to move along the conductor. The motion of electron is shown in fig.-3. N Hence, we assume that electrons in the conductor move with a constant average speed. We call this speed as drift speed or drift velocity. A Let us calculate the drift speed of free charges quantitatively. D Consider a conductor with cross sectional area A. Let v be the drift speed of the charges fig-4: Drift of positive charges d A as shown in fig.- 4 and n be the number of charges present in the conductor in a unit volume (charge density). The average L distance covered by one charge in one second is v . Then the volume of E d the conductor for this distance is equal to Av (see fig.- 4). The number of d charges contained in that volume is equal to nAv . Let q be the charge of T d each carrier.
