When we switch on any electric circuit, irrespective of length of the connecting wire (conductor) an electric field is set up throughout the conductor instantaneously due to the potential difference of the source 188 Electric Current (battery) connected to the circuit. This electric field makes all the electrons to move in a specified direction simultaneously. The equation I = nqAv indicates that the values of n and A are positive. The d direction of electric current is determined by the signs of the charge q and drift speed v . For electrons (negative charges), q is negative and v is d d positive. Then the product of q and v is negative. This negative sign shows d that the direction of electric current is opposite to the flow of negative A charge. For positive charges the product of q and v is positive. Hence, the d N direction of electric current can be taken as the direction of flow of positive charges. When the ends of a conducting wire are connected to the terminals of a battery, an electric field is setup throughout the condNuctor. This field exerts a force on the charge (electron). Let F be the force exerted by the electric e field on a free charge q. The free charges accAelerate in the direction of the electric field (If the free charges are electrons, then the direction of electric force on them is opposite to the directioLn of electric field). It means the electric field does some work to move free charges in a specified direction. E · Can you find the work done by the electric force? Potential difference is denoted by a symbol V. The potential difference between two points separated by a distance l in a conducting wire is given by, W F l V = = e q q This potential difference is also called voltage. The SI unit of potential difference is “Volt” and it is denoted by V. 1 Volt = 1 Joule/1 Coulomb 1V = 1J/C 189 Electric Current · What is the direction of electric current in terms of potential difference? · Do positive charges move in a conductor? Can you give an example of this? Let us recall your experience of electrolysis and electroplating and conductivity of fluids that you had learned in earlier classes. When electric current is allowed to pass through fluids, the positive ions (cations) and A negative ions (anions) move in opposite directions. The direction of the motion of positive charges in an electrolyte is always in the directioNn of the electric field while negative charges move in a direction opposite to that of positive charges. Thus for conduction in fluids there exiAsts motion of both positive and negative charges. Whereas in case of metal conductors there will be only motion of electrons. (The positive chaGrges are fixed in the lattice) If positive charges move from point A to B in a cNonductor, the electric field does positive work so W/q is positive for free positive charges. You can say that the direction of the electric fieldA is from A to B and the point A is at high potential and point B is at low potential. As negative charges L always move in a direction opposite to the electric field we consider that electrons move from low potential to high potential. E We know that in a battery or cell a constant potential difference is maintained till the battery is cTompletely discharged. · How does a battery maintain a constant potential difference between its terminals? , · Why does the battery discharge when its positive and negative terminals T are connected through a conductor? To answeRr this, we need to know about how a battery or a cell works. A battery consists of two metal plates (electrodes) and a chemical (electroElyte). The electrolyte (chemical) between the two metal plates consists of positive and negative ions which move in opposite directions C (see fig.- 6). The electrolyte exerts a certain force on these ions and makes them move in a specified direction. Let us call this force as a chemical S force (F ). Depending upon the nature of the chemical, positive ions move c towards one of the plates and accumulate on that plate. As a result of this accumulation of charges on this plate it becomes positively charged (called anode). Negative ions move in a direction opposite to the motion of positive ions and accumulate on the other plate. As a result of this the plate becomes negatively charged (called cathode). This accumulation of different charges on respective plates continues fig-6 till both plates are sufficiently charged. 190 Electric Current But the ions in motion experience another force when sufficient number of charges are accumulated on the plates. Let us call this force as electric force (F ). The direction of this force is opposite to the direction of e chemical force F and the magnitude of this force depends on the amount c of charge accumulated on the plates. The motion of ions continue towards their respective plates if the chemical force F c F A e F is stronger than electric force F . See fig.- F FN c e e c 7. The accumulation of charges on plates is continuous till the electric force F becomes Afig-7 e equal to chemical force F . At this situation c G there will not be any motion in ions due to F F c e balance of forces F and F . It is shown in fig.- e c NF F 8. The new battery that we buy from the shop e c is at a stage where the ions in the electrolyte A fig-8 are under the influence of balanced forces. See fig.- 9. This is the reason for the consLtant potential difference between the terminals of E a battery. The amount of charge accumTulated on the fig-9 plates depends on nature of the chemical used in the battery. , · What happeTns when the battery is connected in a circuit? When a conducting wire is connected to the terminals of the battery, a R potential difference is created between the ends of the conductor. This potentiaEl difference sets up an electric field throughout the conductor (the direction of electric field is from positive terminal to negative C terminal in the conductor). We know that the conductor contains large number of electrons. The S electrons near the positive terminal of the battery are attracted by it and start to move towards positive terminal. As a result, the amount of positive charge on this plate decreases. So the electric force F becomes weaker e than chemical force F and chemical force pulls negative ions from the c positive plate (anode) and makes them move towards the negative plate (cathode). The negative terminal pushes one electron into the conductor because of stronger repulsion between negative terminal and negative ion. Hence, the total number of electrons in the conductor remains constant during the current flow. The above said process continuous till equilibrium is attained between the forces F and F . e c 191 Electric Current

pages.text: 9.3 Electromotive force (emf) When the ends of the conductor are connected to the terminals of a battery, the electrons in the conductor move with a drift speed from negative terminal to positive terminal because of the electric force acting on them. At the same time negative ions of equal amount of charge move from positive terminal to negative terminal against the electric force (F ) because e of the chemical force acting on them within battery. Thus, some chemical A energy is spent to move ions in the battery. It means that an amount of N work is done by the chemical force (F ). c Let us assume that work done by the chemical force to move a negative A charge q from positive terminal to negative terminal against the electric force F be ‘W’ and also assume that the magnitude of chemical force F is e Gc equal to magnitude of electric force (F ). e The work done on negative charge q by the chemical force, W = Fd where N c ‘d’ is the distance between the terminals. Then work done by the chemical force to move 1 Coulomb charge from positiveA terminal to negative terminal is given by, W/q = F d/q . We know that F = F, then we get = W/q = F d/q. e c e e L W This is the work done by the chemical force on unit negative charge to q E move it from positive terminal to negative terminal. This is called emf (e). T e = W/q = Fd/q e Generally, emf is defined as the work done by the chemical force to move unit positive charge fro,m negative terminal to positive terminal of the T battery. · How canR we measure potential difference or emf? Generally a volt meter is used to measure potential difference or emf across aEn electric device like battery. It must be connected in parallel to the electric device to measure the potential difference across the ends of C the electric device. When a battery in a torch is used for several weeks, the light from its bulb S becomes dim. We say that the battery or cell in the torch is discharged. This fact was established by German Physicist, V George Simon Ohm and it is popularly known as Ohm’s law. (in volt) fig-12 We can define Ohm’s law as follow. The potential difference between the ends of a conductor is directly proportional to the electric current passing through it at constant temperature. Let V be the potential difference between the ends of the conductor and I be the current passing through it. V µ I (temperature is constant) V = Constant I This constant is called resistance of the conductor. It is denoted by ‘R’. V Then we get = R. I V = IR The SI unit of resistance is Ohm. The symbol of ohm is W. 1 Ohm = 1 Volt/1 Ampere 1 W = 1V/A · Can you guess the reason why the ratio of V and I in case of LED is not constant? · Do all materials obey Ohm’s law? · Can we classify the materials based on Ohm’s law? Based on Ohm’s law materials are classified into two categories. Those which obey Ohm’s law are called ohmic materials. For example, metals are ohmic materials. Those which do not obey Ohm’s law are called non ohmic materials. For example, LEDs are non ohmic materials. 9.4.1 Limitations of Ohm’s Law Ohm’s law is valid for metal conductors provided the temperature and other physical conditions remain constant. The resistance of the material changes with temperature. Hence for changing temperature the V-I graph for a conductor will be non-linear. Ohm’s law is not applicable to gaseous conductors. It is also not applicable to semiconductors such as germanium and silicon. 194 Electric Current I )erepma ni(

· What is resistance? · Is the value of resistance the same for all materials? When a conductor is connected to a battery the free electrons start moving with a drift speed in a specified direction. During the motion, the electrons collide with positive ions (fixed) of the lattice and come to halt. This means that they lose mechanical energy in the form of heat. Due to the electric field that was set up by the battery throughout the conductor, these electrons A regain the energy from the field and proceed to move. The motion of electrons is obstructed by the lattice ions. The obstruction offered tNo the flow of electrons in a conductor by lattice ions depends upon the nature of the material. A Therefore, the resistance of a conductor is defined as the obstruction to G the motion of the electrons in a conductor. The material which offers resistance to the motion of electrons is called resistor. · Is there any application of Ohm’s law in daily Nlife? · What causes electric shock in the human body – current or voltage? A Let us see. 9.5 Electric shock L Let us assume that human body is a resistor. The resistance of the human body generally varies from 100 EW (if body is wet with salt water) to 5,00,000 W (if the skin is very dry). Let us calculate the amount of current that flows through the humanT body. Let us assume you have touched the two electrodes of a battery of 24V with dry fingers in such a way that the circuit is complete. Let, your body resistance be 1,00,000W. Then the current flowing throTugh your body is given by I = 24/100000 = 0.00024A. This current is very small. When such small current passes through the R human body, it does not affect the functioning of various organs inside the body. E · Do you know the voltage of mains that we use in our household circuits? C · What happens to our body if we touch live wire of 240V? SThe current passing through our body when we touch a live wire of 240V is given by I = 240/100000 = 0.0024A. When this quantities of current flows through the body the functioning of organs inside the body gets disturbed. This disturbance inside the body is felt as electric shock. If the current flow continues further, it damages the tissues of the body which leads to decrease in resistance of the body. When this current flows for a longer time, damage to the tissues increases and thereby the resistance of human body decreases further. Hence, the current through the human body will further increase. If this current reaches 0.07A, it effects the functioning of the heart and if this much current passes through the heart for more than one second it could be fatal. If this current flows for a longer time, 195 Electric Current

the person in electric shock is being killed. See the table 2 that describes the effects of electric current on human body. Table-2 Current in Effect on human body ampere 0.001 Can be felt 0.005 Is painful A 0.010 Causes involuntary muscle contractions (spasms) N 0.015 Causes loss of muscle control 0.070 If through the heart, causes serious disruption ; probably fatal if current A lasts for more than one second G From the above discussions, we can conclude that an electric shock can be experienced when there is a potential difference exists between one N part of the body and another part. When current flows through human body, it chooses the path which offers low resistance. The resistance of a body A is not uniform throughout it. For example, skin offers more resistance than the organs inside the body. As longL as current flow continues inside the body the current and resistance of human body goes on changing E inversely. Hence, the electric shock is a combined effect of potential difference, electric current and resistance of the human body. T Do you know? , A multi meteTr is an electronic measuring instrument that combines several measurement functions in one unit. R Digital multi meter displays the measured value in numerals. EA multi meter has three parts Display: The display usually has four digits and the ability to C display a negative sign. S Selection knob: The selection knob allows the user to set the multi meter to read different functions such as milliamps (mA) of current, voltage (V) and resistance (W). Ports: Multi meters generally have two ports. One is usually labelled as ‘COM’ (common or ground port). This is where black test lead is connected. The other is labelled as mAVW port where the red lead is conventionally plugged in. WARNING: Most multi meters can measure AC quantities also, but AC circuits can be dangerous. So measure DC quantities only. 196 Electric Current

· Why doesn’t a bird get a shock when it stands on a high voltage wire? There are two parallel transmission lines on electric poles. The potential difference between these two lines is 240V throughout their lengths. If you connect any conducting device across these two wires, it causes current to flow between the wires. When the bird sits on a high voltage wire, there is no potential difference between the legs of the bird because it stands on A a single wire. So no current passes through the bird. Hence, it doesn’t feel any electric shock. Circuits may have more than one device (called as component) that receives electric energy from the source. These devices are commonly connected in the circuit either in series or in parallel. When the components of the circuit are connected in series, there will be a single path for flow of electrons between the terminals of the battery, generator or wall socket (which is simply and extension of these terminals). When these components are connected in parallel, they form branches and each branch provides a separate path for the flow of electrons. 200 Electric Current

N 5 3 I 4 We have seen that the current divides at P. The current A drawn from the battery is equal to the sum of the currents through fig-23 the resistors. P is called junction. The junction is a point where L three or more conducting wires meet. E At any junction point in a circuit where the current can divide, the sum of the currents into the Tjunction must equal the sum of the currents leaving the junction. This means that there is no accumulation of electric charges at any junction in a circuit. , T From fig.- 23, we have I + I R+ I = I + I + I 1 4 6 5 2 3 This law is based on the conservation of charge. E 9.8.2 Loop Law C The algebraic sum of the increases and decreases in potential difference across various components of the circuit in a closed circuit S loop must be zero. This law is based on the conservation of energy. Let us imagine in a circuit loop the potential difference between the two points at the beginning of the loop has a certain value. As we move around the circuit loop and measure the potential difference across each component in the loop, the potential difference may decrease or increase depending upon the nature of the element like a resistor or a battery. But when we have completely traversed the circuit loop and arrive back at our starting point, the net change in the potential difference must be zero. Thus, the algebraic sum of changes in potential differences is equal to zero. 205 Electric Current

If the current flow continues further, it damages the tissues of the body which leads to decrease in resistance of the body. When this current flows for a longer time, damage to the tissues increases and thereby the resistance of human body decreases further. Hence, the current through the human body will further increase. If this current reaches 0.07A, it effects the functioning of the heart and if this much current passes through the heart for more than one second it could be fatal. When current flows through human body, it chooses the path which offers low resistance. The resistance of a body A is not uniform throughout it. This fact was established by German Physicist, V George Simon Ohm and it is popularly known as Ohm’s law. (in volt) fig-12 We can define Ohm’s law as follow. The potential difference between the ends of a conductor is directly proportional to the electric current passing through it at constant temperature. Let V be the potential difference between the ends of the conductor and I be the current passing through it. V µ I (temperature is constant) V = Constant I This constant is called resistance of the conductor. It is denoted by ‘R’. V Then we get = R. I V = IR The SI unit of resistance is Ohm. The symbol of ohm is W. 1 Ohm = 1 Volt/1 Ampere 1 W = 1V/A · Can you guess the reason why the ratio of V and I in case of LED is not constant? · Do all materials obey Ohm’s law? · Can we classify the materials based on Ohm’s law? Based on Ohm’s law materials are classified into two categories. Those which obey Ohm’s law are called ohmic materials. For example, metals are ohmic materials. Those which do not obey Ohm’s law are called non ohmic materials. For example, LEDs are non ohmic materials. 9.4.1 Limitations of Ohm’s Law Ohm’s law is valid for metal conductors provided the temperature and other physical conditions remain constant. The resistance of the material changes with temperature. Hence for changing temperature the V-I graph for a conductor will be non-linear. Ohm’s law is not applicable to gaseous conductors. It is also not applicable to semiconductors such as germanium and silicon. 194 Electric Current I )erepma ni( · What is resistance? · Is the value of resistance the same for all materials? When a conductor is connected to a battery the free electrons start moving with a drift speed in a specified direction. During the motion, the electrons collide with positive ions (fixed) of the lattice and come to halt. This means that they lose mechanical energy in the form of heat. Due to the electric field that was set up by the battery throughout the conductor, these electrons A regain the energy from the field and proceed to move. The motion of electrons is obstructed by the lattice ions. The obstruction offered tNo the flow of electrons in a conductor by lattice ions depends upon the nature of the material. A Therefore, the resistance of a conductor is defined as the obstruction to G the motion of the electrons in a conductor. The material which offers resistance to the motion of electrons is called resistor. · Is there any application of Ohm’s law in daily Nlife? · What causes electric shock in the human body – current or voltage? A Let us see. 9.5 Electric shock L Let us assume that human body is a resistor. The resistance of the human body generally varies from 100 EW (if body is wet with salt water) to 5,00,000 W (if the skin is very dry). Let us calculate the amount of current that flows through the humanT body. Let us assume you have touched the two electrodes of a battery of 24V with dry fingers in such a way that the circuit is complete. Let, your body resistance be 1,00,000W. Then the current flowing throTugh your body is given by I = 24/100000 = 0.00024A. This current is very small. When such small current passes through the R human body, it does not affect the functioning of various organs inside the body. E · Do you know the voltage of mains that we use in our household circuits? C · What happens to our body if we touch live wire of 240V? SThe current passing through our body when we touch a live wire of 240V is given by I = 240/100000 = 0.0024A. When this quantities of current flows through the body the functioning of organs inside the body gets disturbed. This disturbance inside the body is felt as electric shock. If the current flow continues further, it damages the tissues of the body which leads to decrease in resistance of the body. When this current flows for a longer time, damage to the tissues increases and thereby the resistance of human body decreases further. Hence, the current through the human body will further increase. If this current reaches 0.07A, it effects the functioning of the heart and if this much current passes through the heart for more than one second it could be fatal. If this current flows for a longer time, 195 Electric Current the person in electric shock is being killed. See the table 2 that describes the effects of electric current on human body. Table-2 Current in Effect on human body ampere 0.001 Can be felt 0.005 Is painful A 0.010 Causes involuntary muscle contractions (spasms) N 0.015 Causes loss of muscle control 0.070 If through the heart, causes serious disruption ; probably fatal if current A lasts for more than one second G From the above discussions, we can conclude that an electric shock can be experienced when there is a potential difference exists between one N part of the body and another part. When current flows through human body, it chooses the path which offers low resistance. The resistance of a body A is not uniform throughout it. For example, skin offers more resistance than the organs inside the body. As longL as current flow continues inside the body the current and resistance of human body goes on changing E inversely. Hence, the electric shock is a combined effect of potential difference, electric current and resistance of the human body. So measure DC quantities only. 196 Electric Current · Why doesn’t a bird get a shock when it stands on a high voltage wire? There are two parallel transmission lines on electric poles. The potential difference between these two lines is 240V throughout their lengths. If you connect any conducting device across these two wires, it causes current to flow between the wires. When the bird sits on a high voltage wire, there is no potential difference between the legs of the bird because it stands on A a single wire. So no current passes through the bird. Hence, it doesn’t feel any electric shock. We frequently hear news about overload of current and damages caused by this overload. A Electricity enters our homes through two wires called lines. These line wires have low resistance and the potential difference between the N wires is usually about 240V. These two line wires run throughout the household circuit, to which we connect various appliances suchA as fan, TV, refrigerator etc. G All the electric devices of our home are connected at different points between these two wires. This means all the eleNctric appliances are in parallel connection. Hence, potential drop across each device is 240V. If A we know the value of resistance of the electric device, we can calculate the current passing through it using the eLquation I = V/R. For example, the current passing through a bulb with resistance 240 W is 1 A. E Based on the resistance of each electric device, it draws some current T from the supply. Total current drawn from the mains is equal to the sum of the currents passing throug h each device (Junction law). , If we add more devices to the household circuit the current drawn T from the mains also increases. C Potential difference: 240 V 2A Bulb Current: 5 – 20A S This means the line wires that are entering the meter have a 8A Fridge potential difference of 240V. The minimum and maximum limit of current that can be drawn from the mains is 5 – 20A. Thus, the 6A TV maximum current that we can draw from the mains is 20A. When the current drawn from the mains is more than 20A. Overheating Fuse 20A occurs and may cause a fire. This is called over loading. See fig.- 32. If we switch on devices, such as heater shown in fig.- 32, the current drawn from the mains exceeds the max limit 20A. 240V · How can we prevent damage due to overloading? fig-32 211 Electric Current To prevent damages due to overloading we connect an electric fuse to the household circuit as shown in fig.- 32. In this arrangement, the entire current from the mains must pass through the fuse. The fuse consists of a thin wire of low melting point. When the current in the fuse exceeds 20A, the wire will heat up and melt. The circuit then becomes open and prevents the flow of A current into the household circuit. So all the electric devices are saved from N damage that could be caused by overload. Thus we can save the house holding wiring and devices by using fAuses. It is called specific resistance. r = 2m/ne2t From equation (g) we get R = rl/A ..................(h) Note: Drift velocity and Drift speed are synonoum 218 Electric Current CHAPTER A 10 N Electromagnetism A G N In the previous chapter on ‘Electricity’ you have learnt about the heating effects of electric current. We use many eleActric appliances in our daily life such as electric motor, electric generators, electric calling bells, L electric cranes etc., E · How do electric appliances work? T · How do electromagnets work? Do you know? · Is there any relation between electricity and magnetism? , · Can we producTe magnetism from electricity? In this chapter we will study electromagnetic effects. We also study electric R motors which involve magnetic effects of electric current and electric E generator which involves electric effects of moving magnets. C Hans Christian Oersted (1777 - 1851) was one of the leading S scientists of the 19th century, played a crucial role in understanding electromagnetism. He gave lectures which were quite popular among the public and also learnt a lot during the tours. During one such lecture in April 1820, Oersted carried out an experiment that was never performed before. He placed a compass needle underneath a wire and then turned on electric current. The needle of compass showed deflection. Oersted recognized the significance of what he had just done. 219 Electromagnetism Earlier, it was believed that electricity and magnetism were two different unconnected sciences. Oersted had demonstrated that they were interconnected. Through this observation he showed that electricity and magnetism were related phenomena. Some scientists, influenced by this experiment, continued to work in the modern field of “electromagnetism”. Their research resulted in several new scientific theories and A various vital inventions like the dynamo and the electric motor, with this a new technology prospered, leading to inventions such as radio, televisionN and fiber optics. The unit of magnetic field strength is named Oersted in his honour. A Oersted was made a foreign member of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in 1822. Arrange a copper wire of 24 gaugEe so that it passes through these slits and make a circuit. The circuit consists of a 3 (or 9) volt battery, key and copper wire T which are connected in series as shown in figure 1. Now, keep a magnetic compass below the wire. E Take the bar magnet far away from the circuit and switch on the circuit. Look for changes in the position of the needle. C · What do you notice? (Recall the idea of field forces in class 8, chapter “Force”). In order to understand the reasons for the deflection of the compass needle with no bar magnet near it we need to understand the idea of ‘magnetic field’ and the influence of electric field on magnetic field. pages.text: 10.2 Magnetic Field We use the term field when a force gets applied on an object by another object without there being any physical contact between them. You have observed this already in activity-1. Let us call this field which is responsible for deflection of the compass needle as ‘magnetic field’. · How was this field produced? A · Can we observe the field of a bar magnet? N Let us try. Activity 2 A Take a sheet of white paper and place it on the horizontal table. Place a G bar magnet in the middle of the sheet. Place a magnetic compass near the magnet. It settles to a certain direction. Use a pencil and put dots on the N sheet on either side of the needle. Remove the compass, draw a small line segment connecting the two dots. Draw an arArow on it from South Pole of the needle to North Pole of the needle. Repeat the same by placing the L compass needle at various positions on the paper. The compass needle settles in different directions at diEfferent positions. · Why does this happen? T Remove the bar magnet and place the magnetic compass on the paper. It comes to rest along the no rth-south direction. Now place the bar magnet , in its previous place. T · Is there any change in the direction of the needle of the magnetic R compass? Why? The needle of the magnetic compass is affected by the bar magnet E without any physical contact. A force causes the needle to deflect and makes it Cto come to rest in a certain direction. · What is the nature of force that acts on the needle? S The force which acts on the needle from a distance is due to the magnetic field of the bar magnet. In activity-2, you have already seen that the orientation of needle is different at different places on paper. This gives us an idea that the magnetic field has direction and it varies from one point to another. When you changes the place of the compass near the bar magnet you can observe that its orientation changes from point to point. Now take the needle to places far away on the sheet and observe the orientation of the compass needle in each case. 221 Electromagnetism

· What do you observe? The compass needle shows almost the same direction along north and south at places far from the magnet. · What does it mean? From these observations we conclude that the strength of the field A varies with distance from the bar magnet. Now hold the compass a little above the table and at the top of the bar magnet. You can observe that field N exists in all directions around the bar magnet. Hence we can say that the A magnetic field is three dimensional i.e., magnetic field surrounds its source such as bar magnet. From the above discussion we can generalize that. G A magnetic field exists in the region surrounding a bar magnet and is characterized by strength and direction. N 10.2.1 Lines of magnetic field A · How can we find the strength of the field and direction of the field? You know that the direction of the fielLd can be determined by using a compass. Let us find out how to determine the strength of the field. E Activity 3 T Place a white sheet of paper on a horizontal table. Place a compass in the middle of it. Put two do ts on either side of the compass needle. Take it , out. Draw a line connecting the dots which shows the North and South of T the earth. Now place the bar magnet on the line drawn in such a way that its R north pole points towards geographic north. Now place the compass at the north pole of the bar magnet. Put a dot at the north pole of the compass E needle. Now remove the compass and place it at the dot. It will point in other direction. Again put a dot at the north pole of the compass needle. C Repeat the process till you reach the south pole of the bar magnet. Connect S the dots from ‘N’ of the bar magnet to ‘S’ of the bar magnet. You will get a curved line. Now select another point from the north pole of the bar magnet. Repeat the process for many points taken near the north pole. You will get different curves fig-2: Magnetic field lines as shown in fig.-2. 222 Electromagnetism

· What are these curves? Technically these curves are called “magnetic field lines”. Field lines are imaginary lines. These lines help us to understand the nature of the field. So these curved lines represent the field lines. If you place a compass at any point on the line, the needle comes to rest along the tangent to the line. So we conclude that the tangent drawn to the field line at a point gives the direction of the field. A · Are these field lines closed or open loops? N The field lines appear to be closed loops in fig-2, but you can’t conclude that lines are closed or open loops by looking at the picture of field lines A because we do not know about the alignment of lines that are passing through the bar magnet. We will come to know about thisG point later in this chapter. Observe the spacing between lines. In some pNlaces the field lines are crowded (near the poles of a bar magnet) and in some places the field A lines are spread apart (at long distances from the bar magnet). From this picture we can conclude that the field is strong when lines are crowded L and field is weak when lines are spaced apart. E Thus, the field drawn is non uniform because the strength and direction both change from point to point. T We may define the nature of the field with its characteristics such as its strength and direction. T he field is said to be non uniform when any one , of the characterstics of field i.e., strength or direction changes from point T to point. Similarly the field is said to be uniform if both strength and direction are Rconstant throughout the field. Let us define the strength of a uniform magnetic field. E · Can we give certain values to magnitude of the field at every point in the magnetic field? C 10.2.2 Magnetic flux - Magnetic flux density SConsider a uniform magnetic field in space. Imagine a plane of certain area ‘A’ placed perpendicular B to the field at a certain point in the magnetic field as shown in figure 3(a). You notice that a few field lines Area A pass through this plane. This number gives an fig-3(a) estimation of strength of the field at that point. The number of lines passing through the plane of area ‘A’ perpendicular to the field is called magnetic flux. It is denoted by ‘F’. Magnetic flux represents the number of lines passing through the imagined plane in the field. Of course, flux depends on the orientation of 223 Electromagnetism

the plane in the field. But here we are concerned only with the perpendicular case. The S.I unit of magnetic flux is Weber. Now strength of the field is easily defined using the idea of flux. If the imagined plane is perpendicular to the field and has unit area, then the flux through this plane of unit area gives the strength of the field. This strength of the field is technically called magnetic flux density (B). So, magnetic flux density is defined as the magnetic flux passing through unit area taken perpendicular to the field. A B is also known as magnetic field induction. Let the flux through the area ‘A’ be F. N · What is the flux through unit area perpendicular to the field? F A It is equal to . The ratio of magnetic flux passing through a plane A perpendicular to the field and the area of the Gplane is called the magnetic flux density. So magnetic flux density = magnetNic flux/ area. F B = . _ F = BA A A Units of magnetic flux density is Weber/(meter)2. It is also called Tesla. Generalize the formulaL of flux for any orientation of the plane taken in the field. E Let ‘q’ be the angle between magnetic field (B) and normal to the plane with area (A) as shown in figure 3(b). The T effective area of the plane perpendicular to the field is A cosq. Then magnetic flux density is given by, , magnetic flux T B = (this formula is used when plane effective area R makes an angle with the field). F E Then B = The flux through the plane, Acosq fig-3(b) is given by F = BA cosq. C · What is the flux through the plane taken parallel to the field? · What is the use of introducing the ideas of magnetic flux and magnetic S flux density? Later in this chapter, you will see how these ideas are used. · Are there any sources of magnetic field other than magnets? · Do you know how old electric calling bells work? Let us see 10.3 Magnetic field due to currents In activity 1 we observed that the compass needle is deflected when current flows through the circuit. This observation helps us to conclude that, “Current carrying wire produces magnetic field.” Let us discuss about the magnetic fields produced by a current carrying wire. 224 Electromagnetism

10.3.1 Magnetic field due to straight wire carrying current Activity 4 Take a wooden plank and make a hole as shown in figure 4(a). Place this plank on the table. Now Stand place a retort stand on the plank as shown in figure A 4(a). Pass 24 gauge copper wire through hole of the plank and rubber knob of the retort stand in NCompass Table needle such a way that the wire be arranged in a vertical Battery A position and not touch the stand. Connect the two ends of the wire to a battery via switch. Place 6 to GSwitch Wooden plank 10 compass needles in a circular path around the hole so that its centre coincides with the hole. N Conducting Use 3 (to or a) volt battery in the circuit. Switch wire A on. Current flows through the wire. fig-4(a) · How do the directions of the compasLs needles Magnetic change? E field lines You may notice that they are directed as tangents to the circle. T · What is the shape of the magnetic field line around wire? It must be a circular line . So we conclude that magnetic field , lines are closed lines. The magnetic field lines due to straight T wire carrying the current is shown in figures 4(b) and 4(c). This Current out of the page R fig-4(b) can be verified by sprinkling iron filings around the wire when current E flows in the wire. Magnetic field · What is the direction of magnetic field (B) induction at any lines C point on the field line? If the current flow is vertically upwards (out of the page), S xCurrent into the page the field lines are in anticlockwise direction, as shown in figure fig-4(c) 4(b). If current flows into the page, in downward direction, the field lines are in clockwise direction as shown in figure 4(c). I How do we determine the direction of field lines? It can be B easily determined with right hand thumb rule. If you grab the current carrying wire with your right hand in such way that thumb is in the direction of current, then the curled fingers show the direction of the magnetic field as shown in figure 4(d). fig-4(d) 225 Electromagnetism

10.3.2 Magnetic field due to circular coil Activity 5 Take a thin wooden plank covered with white paper and make two holes on its surface as shown in figure 5(a). Pass insulated copper wire (24 gauge) through the holes and wind the wire 4 to 5 times through holes such ATo current supply that it looks like a coil (figure 5(a)). The ends of the circuit N wire are connected to terminals of the battery through a fig-5(a) switch. Now switch on the circuit. Place a compass A needle on the plank at the centre of the coil. Put dots on either side of the compass. Again place compass at one of the dots, put othGer dot further. Do the same till you reach the edge of the plank. Now repeat this for the other side of the coil from the centre. Then draw a line joNining the dots, you will get a field line of the circular coil. Do the same for the other points taken in between the holes. Draw corresponding linAes. You will get field lines of the circular coil. L · Can you tell the direction of the magnetic field of the coil? This could be answered from the oErientation of the compass needle. You can observe this when the compass needle is kept at the centre of the coil. The direction in which the cTompass needle comes to rest indicates the direction of the field due to the coil. Thus the direction of the field is perpendicular to the plan,e of the coil. T · Why does the compass needle point in the direction of field? Place the compass in front of one of the faces of the coil and observe R the orientation of the compass needle. Note the pole of the needle that faces the coil. We know that south pole B B E is attracted to the north pole. The needle is oriented in I I suCch a way that its south pole points towards the north I N pole of the coil. So we can say that the direction of Smagnetic field, due to coil, points towards you when S the current in the coil is in anticlockwise direction. fig-5(b) Verify this in your experiment (do not touch the wires of the coil). When the current in the coil is in clock-wise direction, the direction of magnetic field due to the coil points away from you. The direction of the field due to coil is determined by using right hand rule, which states that, “When you curl your right hand fingers in the direction of current, thumb gives the direction of magnetic field.” Observe the direction of magnetic field in figure 5(b). 226 Electromagnetism

10.3.3 Magnetic field due to solenoid Activity 6 Take a wooden plank covered with white paper. Make equidistant holes on its surface as shown in figure 6(a). Pass copper wire through the holes as shown in A figure 6(a). This forms a coil. Join the ends of the To current coil to a battery through a switch. Switch on the supply circuit N circuit. Current passes through the coil. Now sprinkle fig-6(a) iron filings on the surface of the plank around the A coil. Give a small jerk to it. An orderly pattern of G iron filings is seen on the paper. · How do they adjust in such an orderly pattern? I I N This long coil is called solenoid. A solenoid is a long N S A wire wound in a close packed helix. The field of solenoid is shown in the figure 6(b). The magnetic L field lines set up by solenoid resemble those of a fig-6(b) E bar magnet indicating that a solenoid behaves like a bar magnet. The direction of the field due to solenoid is also determined T by using right hand rule. One end of the solenoid behaves like a north pole and other behaves like a south pole. The field lines outside the solenoid , are continuous withT those inside. Outside the solenoid the direction of the field lines is from north to south while inside the direction is from south R to north. Thus the magnetic field lines are closed loops. This is so for the bar magEnet too! We have seen that current carrying wires produce magnetic field. So, C electric charges in motion produce magnetic fields. S· What happens when a current carrying wire is kept in a magnetic field? Let us see. 10.4 Magnetic Force On Moving Charge And Current Carrying Wire Activity 7 Take a bar magnet and bring it near the TV screen (The old CRT type TV). What do you observe? You can observe that the picture on the screen is distorted. · Why does the picture get distorted? 227 Electromagnetism

· Is the motion of electrons reaching the screen affected by the magnetic field of the bar magnet? Move the bar magnet away from the screen. Now you will get a clear picture. Repeat this to confirm that the motion of electrons is affected by the field produced by the bar magnet. This must be due to the fact that the magnetic field exerts a force on the moving charges. This force is called magnetic A force. X indicates the direction of B · Can we calculate the force experienced by a charge moving N and it is into the page in a magnetic field? Let a charge ‘q’ move with a velocityA ‘v’ perpendicular to the magnetic field ‘B’ as shown in figure 7. The value of magnetic q v G force on the moving charge can be found experimentally and it is given by, N F = q v B fig-7 Magnetic force on the charge is the product of three quantities A charge (q), speed (v)and magnetic flux density (B). The equation for L magnetic force acting on a charge ‘q’ is F = q v B and holds well only when the direction of veloEcity of charged particle ‘v’ is perpendicular to the direction of the magnetic field ‘B’. T Generalize the equation for magnetic force on charge when there is an ang le ‘q’ between the directions of field B and velocity v. , It is experimentally proved that when there is an angle between direction T of field and velocity, the magnetic force experienced by the charge is given by, R F = q v B sinq. l What is the magnetic force on moving charge, which is parallel to the E magnetic field. C When charge moves parallel to the magnetic field (along the magnetic field or against the field) the value of q becomes zero. In the above S equations q is 00 so that sinq = 0. F Thus the charge experiences no force when it is moving parallel to the magnetic field (along field direction or against field direction). We have an easy method to find out the direction of B magnetic force acting on a charge moving in a magnetic field. Keep your right hand fingers along the direction of velocity V of moving charge and next curl your fingers towards the direction of magnetic field then the thumb gives the direction fig-8(a) of magnetic force as shown in figure 8(a). This 228 Electromagnetism

rule is applied for any case of angle between directions of velocity and field. The direction of magnetic force is always perpendicular to the direction of both velocity and magnetic field. Generally right hand rule is used when velocity and field are perpendicular to each other. This law states that, “If the fore- F finger points towards the direction of velocity of charge or A current, middle finger points to the direction of field (B) then v or I N thumb gives direction of force when the three fingers are stretched in such a way that they are perpendicular to each other A as shown in figure 8(b).” B out of paper This rule is applicable to positive charge. G fig-8(b):Right hand · What is the direction of force acting on a negative charge rule for positive charge N moving in a field? First find the direction of force acting on a positive charge. Next A reverse its direction. This new direction is the direction of force acting on the negative charge. L Let us see an example of force acting on a charged particle. E Example 1 T A charged particle ‘q’ is moving with a speed ‘v’ perpendicular to the magnetic field of induct ion B. , Find the radius of the path and time period of the particle. T Solution: Let us assume that the field is directed into the page as shown R in figure E-1. Then the force experienced by the particle is F = q v B. We know that this force is always directed perpendicular to velocity. Hence E the particle moves along a circular path and the magnetic force on a charged particle acts like a centripetal force. C v Let r be the radius of the circular path. v v B S mv2 We know that centripetal force = F F R r mv2 v v q v B = F F r mv F F v Solving this equation, we get; r = v Bq v 2pr Time period of the particle; T = fig-E-1 v 2pm Substituting r in above equation, we get T = Bq · What happens when a current carrying wire is placed in a magnetic field? 229 Electromagnetism

Electric current is charges in motion. We know that each charge experiences a magnetic force. Thus the current carrying wire (constituting collection of charges in motion) experiences magnetic force when it is kept in a magnetic field. · Can you determine the magnetic force on a current carrying wire which is placed along a magnetic field? A We know that each charge experiences no magnetic force because N they are moving parallel to the direction of field along the field. So the A force acting on wire is zero when it is kept along a magnetic field. It is represented by ‘x’ as shown in thNe figure 9. Let the field be confined to the length L. So only the part of the wire of the length ‘L’ is A inside the magnetic field. Remaining wire is outside the magnetic field. We know that the electric current meaLns charges in motion hence they move with a certain velocity called drift velocity ‘v’. Note: This equation holds well only when direction of electric current is perpendicular to magnetic field. In fig.-9, you can observe the bending in the wire due to the force applied on it. · What is the force on the wire if its length makes an angle ‘q’ with the A magnetic field? Let ‘q’ be the angle between direction of current and magnetic fNield, then the force acting on the current carrying wire is given by A F = ILB sinq (at any angle) ...................(5) G · How could you find its direction? You can use right hand rule to find out the dirNection of force on the current carrying wire. A Let us see the result of force applied on a current carrying wire by an experiment. L E Activity 8 Take a wooden plank. Fix Ttwo long wooden sticks on it. These wooden sticks are split at their top ends. A copper wire is pass,ed through these splits and the ends of the wire T are connected to battery of 9 volt, through a switch. Close the switch to make the circuRit. Current passes through the wire. Now bring a horseshoe magnet near the copper wire as shown in figure 10E. S N · What happens to the wire? C I · In which way does it deflect? F S Use the right thumb rule to find the direction of force. · Is the direction of deflection observed fig-10 experimentally same as that of the theoretically expected one? Change polarities of the horse shoe magnet. Again observe the deflection. Repeat this by changing the direction of current in the circuit. · Does the right hand rule give the explanation for the direction of magnetic force exerted by magnetic field on the wire? 231 Electromagnetism

Right hand rule helps you to find the direction of magnetic force exerted by the magnetic field on current carrying wire. It does not help you explain the reason for deflection of wire. · Can you give a reason for it? Imagine a situation where there is no current in the wire. Then there exists only magnetic field due to external source (horse shoe magnet). A When there is a current in the wire, it also produces a magnetic field. These fields overlap and give non- uniform field. Let us see this clNearly with diagrams. A G B N A fig-11(a): Field lines due to fLig-11(b): Current fig-11(c) horseshoe magnet between its poles into the page E The field in between north and south pole of horse shoe magnet is T shown in the figure 11 (a). Let us imagine a wire passing perpendicular to the paper. Let the current pass through it (into the page). It produces a , magnetic field as shoTwn in figure 11(b). Now let us try to sketch the resultant field by observing the field lines. We can see that the direction of the field R lines due to the wire in upper part (of circular lines) coincides with the directioEn of the field lines of horse shoe magnet. The direction of field lines by wire in lower part (of circular lines) is opposite to the direction C of the field lines of horse shoe magnet. So that the net field in upper part is strong and in lower part it is weak. Hence a non-uniform field is created S around the wire. This non uniform field is shown in figure 11 (c). Therefore the wire tries to move to the weaker field region. · Does this deflection fit with the direction of magnetic force found by right hand rule? · What happens when a current carrying coil is placed in a uniform magnetic field? · Can we use this knowledge to construct an electric motor? Let us try to answer. 232 Electromagnetism

10.4.1 Electric Motor To understand the working of an electric motor we need to understand the behaviour of a current carrying B C coil kept in a uniform magnetic field. Consider a rectangular coil kept in a uniform F F A magnetic field as shown in figure 12(a). Switch on the circuit so that the current flows through the rectangular A N D coil. The direction of current in the coil is shown in A figure 12(a). · What is the angle made by AB and CD with magnetic GMagnetic field (B) fig-12(a) field? N You will notice that they are always at right angles to the magnetic field. A · Can you draw the direction of magnetic force on sides AB and CD? L Apply right hand rule to get the direction of magnetic force. At AB, the E magnetic force acts inward perpendicular (F ) to field of the magnet and T on CD, it acts outward (F ). The force on the sides BC and DA varies because they make different , angles at different pTositions of the coil in the field. · What are the directions of forces on BC and DA? R If the direction of currents in BC and DA are parallel to the magnetic E field, magnetic force does’t act on them. If the direction of currents in BC anCd DA are perpendicular to the field, at BC magnetic force pulls the coil up and at DA magnetic force pulls it down. S · What is the net force on the rectangular coil? The force on AB is equal and opposite to the force on CD due to external magnetic field because they carry equal currents in the opposite direction. Sum of these forces is zero; similarly the sum of the forces on sides BC and DA is also zero for the same reason. So, net force on the coil is zero. But there is rotation of the coil. How is it possible? · Why does the coil rotate? 233 Electromagnetism

Let us consider opening a cap of the bottle as an example where F two equal and opposite forces act on the cap. Two forces equal in magnitude but opposite in direction must act on the either side of cap of the bottle as shown in figure 12 (b). These forces bring the cap into rotation. Similarly the rectangular coil comes into rotation in clockwise direction because of equal and opposite pair of forces F acting on the two sides of the coil. A fig-12(b) · What happens to the rotation of the coil if the direction of Couple action on current in the coil remains unchanged? N bottle cap If the direction of current in the coil is unchanged, it rotates up to a vertical position then due to its inertia it rotates further in Aclockwise direction. But now the sides of the coil experience forces which are in the G opposite direction to the previous case. Hence these forces try to rotate it in anti clockwise direction. As a result, this coil comes to halt and rotates N in anti clock wise direction, this will go on if the direction of current remains unchanged. A · How could you make the coil rotate continuously? If the direction of current in the coil, after the first half rotation, is L reversed, the coil will continue to rotate in the same direction. Thus if the direction of current through the cEoil is reversed every half rotation, the coil will rotate continuously in one and the same direction. T · How can we achieve this? To achieve this, brush es B and B are used, as shown in figure 1 2 12 (c). These brushes ar,e connected to the battery. The ends of the coil T are connected to slip rings C and C which 1 2, rotate along with the coil. Initially C is in R 1 Anticlockwise contact with B and C is in contact with B . rotation 1 2 2 After hEalf rotation, the brushes come into N contact with the other slip rings in such a way B C S thCat the direction of current through the coil is reversed. This happens every half rotation. Thus S the direction of rotation of the coil remains A the same. This is the principle used in “electric D C motor.” Slip-ring 1 C Communicator 2 In electric motors, electrical energy is converted into mechanical energy. We have Current B (reverses at learned that a current carrying coil rotates 1 B half turn) Brushes 2 when it is kept in a uniform magnetic field. · What happens when a coil without current + - fig-12(c) is made to rotate in magnetic field? · How is current produced? 234 Electromagnetism

Do you know? · The relation between direction of induced current, magnetic field and force can also be explained by Flemings left hand rule. Stretch the left hand thumb, middle finger and forefinger in such a way that they are mutually perpendicular to each other. The forefinger indicates the direction of magnetic field, the middle finger indicates the direction of current and thumb indicates direction of forceA. By using the Flemings left hand rule we can explain the working of electric motor. N 10.5 Electromagnetic induction A Ativity 9 G The discovery and understanding of electromagnetic S induction are based on a long series of experiments N N carried out by Faraday and Henry. Let us try to do one of those experiements. A N Connect the terminals of a coil to a sensitive L ammeter or a galvanometer as shown in the fig.-13. fig-13 Normally, we would not expect anyE deflections of needle in the galvanometer because there is no electromotive G T force in this circuit. Now if we push a bar magnet towards the coil, with its north pole facing the coil, a remarkable thing happens. While the magnet is mov,ing towards the coil, the needle in galvanometer T deflects, showing that a current has been set up in the coil, the galvanometer does not defleRct if the magnet is at rest. If the magnet is moved away from the coil, the needle in the galvanometer again deflects, but in the opposite directioEn, which means that a current is set up in the coil in the opposite direction. C If we use the end of south pole of a magnet instead of north pole in the above activity, the experiment works just as described but the deflections S are exactly reversed. Further experimentation enables us to understand that the relative motion of the magnet and coil set up a current in the coil. It makes no difference whether the magnet is moved towards the coil or the coil towards the magnet. 10.5.1 Faraday’s Law “Whenever there is a continuous change of magnetic flux linked with a closed coil, a current is generated in the coil.” This is one form of Faraday’s law. 235 Electromagnetism

The current generated is called induced current and is set up by an induced electromotive force (induced EMF). This phenomenon of getting induced current is called electromagnetic induction. Faraday observed that the changes in the magnetic flux through the coil are responsible for the generation of current in the coil. He also observed that the rapid changes in flux through coil generate greater induced A current or induced EMF. After observing this important factor, he proposed a law of electromagnetic induction, which is as follow, N “The induced EMF generated in a closed loop is equal to the rate of A change of magnetic flux passing through it.” In mathematical form, we can write this as G change in flux Induced EMF = time N DF e = .....................(6)A Dt The equation is called Faraday’s law of induction where F (phi) is the L flux linked with coil. Let F be the flux linked with single turn. chapters.fullText: 10.2 Magnetic Field We use the term field when a force gets applied on an object by another object without there being any physical contact between them. You have observed this already in activity-1. Let us call this field which is responsible for deflection of the compass needle as ‘magnetic field’. · How was this field produced? A · Can we observe the field of a bar magnet? N Let us try. Activity 2 A Take a sheet of white paper and place it on the horizontal table. Place a G bar magnet in the middle of the sheet. Place a magnetic compass near the magnet. It settles to a certain direction. Use a pencil and put dots on the N sheet on either side of the needle. Remove the compass, draw a small line segment connecting the two dots. Draw an arArow on it from South Pole of the needle to North Pole of the needle. Repeat the same by placing the L compass needle at various positions on the paper. The compass needle settles in different directions at diEfferent positions. · Why does this happen? T Remove the bar magnet and place the magnetic compass on the paper. It comes to rest along the no rth-south direction. Now place the bar magnet , in its previous place. T · Is there any change in the direction of the needle of the magnetic R compass? Why? The needle of the magnetic compass is affected by the bar magnet E without any physical contact. A force causes the needle to deflect and makes it Cto come to rest in a certain direction. · What is the nature of force that acts on the needle? S The force which acts on the needle from a distance is due to the magnetic field of the bar magnet. In activity-2, you have already seen that the orientation of needle is different at different places on paper. This gives us an idea that the magnetic field has direction and it varies from one point to another. When you changes the place of the compass near the bar magnet you can observe that its orientation changes from point to point. Now take the needle to places far away on the sheet and observe the orientation of the compass needle in each case. 221 Electromagnetism · What do you observe? The compass needle shows almost the same direction along north and south at places far from the magnet. · What does it mean? From these observations we conclude that the strength of the field A varies with distance from the bar magnet. Now hold the compass a little above the table and at the top of the bar magnet. You can observe that field N exists in all directions around the bar magnet. Hence we can say that the A magnetic field is three dimensional i.e., magnetic field surrounds its source such as bar magnet. From the above discussion we can generalize that. G A magnetic field exists in the region surrounding a bar magnet and is characterized by strength and direction. N 10.2.1 Lines of magnetic field A · How can we find the strength of the field and direction of the field? You know that the direction of the fielLd can be determined by using a compass. Let us find out how to determine the strength of the field. E Activity 3 T Place a white sheet of paper on a horizontal table. Place a compass in the middle of it. Put two do ts on either side of the compass needle. Take it , out. Draw a line connecting the dots which shows the North and South of T the earth. Now place the bar magnet on the line drawn in such a way that its R north pole points towards geographic north. Now place the compass at the north pole of the bar magnet. Put a dot at the north pole of the compass E needle. Now remove the compass and place it at the dot. It will point in other direction. Again put a dot at the north pole of the compass needle. C Repeat the process till you reach the south pole of the bar magnet. Connect S the dots from ‘N’ of the bar magnet to ‘S’ of the bar magnet. You will get a curved line. Now select another point from the north pole of the bar magnet. Repeat the process for many points taken near the north pole. You will get different curves fig-2: Magnetic field lines as shown in fig.-2. 222 Electromagnetism · What are these curves? Technically these curves are called “magnetic field lines”. Field lines are imaginary lines. These lines help us to understand the nature of the field. So these curved lines represent the field lines. If you place a compass at any point on the line, the needle comes to rest along the tangent to the line. So we conclude that the tangent drawn to the field line at a point gives the direction of the field. A · Are these field lines closed or open loops? N The field lines appear to be closed loops in fig-2, but you can’t conclude that lines are closed or open loops by looking at the picture of field lines A because we do not know about the alignment of lines that are passing through the bar magnet. We will come to know about thisG point later in this chapter. Observe the spacing between lines. In some pNlaces the field lines are crowded (near the poles of a bar magnet) and in some places the field A lines are spread apart (at long distances from the bar magnet). From this picture we can conclude that the field is strong when lines are crowded L and field is weak when lines are spaced apart. E Thus, the field drawn is non uniform because the strength and direction both change from point to point. T We may define the nature of the field with its characteristics such as its strength and direction. T he field is said to be non uniform when any one , of the characterstics of field i.e., strength or direction changes from point T to point. Similarly the field is said to be uniform if both strength and direction are Rconstant throughout the field. Let us define the strength of a uniform magnetic field. E · Can we give certain values to magnitude of the field at every point in the magnetic field? C 10.2.2 Magnetic flux - Magnetic flux density SConsider a uniform magnetic field in space. Imagine a plane of certain area ‘A’ placed perpendicular B to the field at a certain point in the magnetic field as shown in figure 3(a). You notice that a few field lines Area A pass through this plane. This number gives an fig-3(a) estimation of strength of the field at that point. The number of lines passing through the plane of area ‘A’ perpendicular to the field is called magnetic flux. It is denoted by ‘F’. Magnetic flux represents the number of lines passing through the imagined plane in the field. Of course, flux depends on the orientation of 223 Electromagnetism the plane in the field. But here we are concerned only with the perpendicular case. The S.I unit of magnetic flux is Weber. Now strength of the field is easily defined using the idea of flux. If the imagined plane is perpendicular to the field and has unit area, then the flux through this plane of unit area gives the strength of the field. This strength of the field is technically called magnetic flux density (B). So, magnetic flux density is defined as the magnetic flux passing through unit area taken perpendicular to the field. A B is also known as magnetic field induction. Let the flux through the area ‘A’ be F. N · What is the flux through unit area perpendicular to the field? F A It is equal to . N 10.5 Electromagnetic induction A Ativity 9 G The discovery and understanding of electromagnetic S induction are based on a long series of experiments N N carried out by Faraday and Henry. Further experimentation enables us to understand that the relative motion of the magnet and coil set up a current in the coil. It makes no difference whether the magnet is moved towards the coil or the coil towards the magnet. 10.5.1 Faraday’s Law “Whenever there is a continuous change of magnetic flux linked with a closed coil, a current is generated in the coil.” This is one form of Faraday’s law. 235 Electromagnetism The current generated is called induced current and is set up by an induced electromotive force (induced EMF). This phenomenon of getting induced current is called electromagnetic induction. Faraday observed that the changes in the magnetic flux through the coil are responsible for the generation of current in the coil. He also observed that the rapid changes in flux through coil generate greater induced A current or induced EMF. After observing this important factor, he proposed a law of electromagnetic induction, which is as follow, N “The induced EMF generated in a closed loop is equal to the rate of A change of magnetic flux passing through it.” In mathematical form, we can write this as G change in flux Induced EMF = time N DF e = .....................(6)A Dt The equation is called Faraday’s law of induction where F (phi) is the L flux linked with coil. R · Can you apply conservation of energy for electromagnetic induEction? 10.5.2 Lenz Law C When we push the bar magnet towards the coils, current is generated, Sin other word electromagnetic induction takes place and mechanical energy is converted into electrical energy. Let us discuss it in detail. We know that when a bar magnet is pushed S N towards a coil with its north pole facing the coil an S N induced current is set up in the coil. Let the S N N S direction of current in the coil be in clockwise S N direction with respect to north pole of the bar S N fig - 14 magnet. Then this current carrying loop behaves 236 Electromagnetism like a magnet, with its south pole facing the north pole of bar magnet. In such a case, the bar magnet attracts the coil. Then it gains kinetic energy. This is contradictory to conservation of energy. So our assumed clockwise direction of induced current is wrong. Hence the correct direction of induced current has to be in anticlockwise direction with respect to north pole of the bar magnet. In such a case, the north pole of the coil faces the north pole of the bar magnet as shown in figure 14. Then north pole of bar magnet Ais repelled by the north pole of the coil. Hence we need to do work to overcome N this force. This work done on the magnet is converted into electrical energy A in the coil. In this way conservation of energy takes place in electromagnetic induction. G Let us see a case where the bar magnet is pulled away from the coil, with N north pole facing the coil. In such case, the coil opposes the motion of bar A magnet to balance the conversion of mechanical energy into electric energy. This happens only when the north pole of tLhe magnet faces the south pole of the coil. E · Can you guess what could be the direction of induced current in the coil T in such case? , Invariably the direction of induced current in the coil must be in clock T wise direction. In simple terms, when flux increases through coil, the coil R opposes the increase in the flux and when flux decreases through coil, it opposes the dEecrease in the flux. This is discovered by a Russian Physicist HeinricCh Lenz. Lenz’s law states that “the induced current will appear in such a direction S that it opposes the changes in the flux in the coil.” · Could we get Faraday’s law of induction from conservation of energy? 10.5.3 Derivation of Faraday’s Law Let us arrange an apparatus as shown in figure 15. CHAPTER A Principles of 11 N Metallurgy A G In class 8 you have studied about certain properties of metals like, N malleability, ductility, sonarity etc. Metals play an important role in our daily life. We use various metals for various pAurposes like gold and silver as jewellery, copper, iron, aluminium for making conducting wires and L for making utensils etc. We use many house hold articles made up of metals E and their alloys at our home. · Can you mention some articles that are made up of metals? T · Do metals exist in nature in the same form as that we use in our daily life? , T · Have you ever heard the words like ore, mineral and metallurgy? · Do you knRow how these metals are obtained? To understand these questions you need to know about metallurgy. In E this chapter we discuss various concepts related to metallurgy and the process by which we are able to obtain the pure form of metal that we use C in our daily life. S“Metallurgy is the process of extraction of metals from their ores”. Human history in terms of materials had the Bronze Age and Iron Age. The bronze is an alloy of copper and tin. Now we have more than 75% metals among the elements available. 11.1 Occurrence of the metals in nature · How are the metals present in nature? The earth’s crust is the major source of metals. Sea water also contains some soluble salts such as sodium chloride and magnesium chloride etc. 249 Principles of Metallurgy

Some metals like gold (Au), silver (Ag) and copper (Cu) are available in nature in free state (native) as they are least reactive. Other metals mostly are found in nature in the combined form due to their more reactivity. The elements or compounds of the metals which occur in nature in the earth crust are called minerals. At some places, minerals contain a very high percentage of a particular metal and the metal can be profitably extracted from it. The minerals from A which the metals are extracted without economical loss are called ores. N Aluminium, for example, is the most common metal in the Earth’s crust, occurring in most of minerals. However, it isn’t economically A feasible to extract it from most of these minerals. Instead, the usual ore from which it is profitable to extract it is bauxite – which contains G 50 – 70 % of aluminium oxide . N Think and discuss A · Do you agree with the statement “All ores are minerals but all L minerals need not be ores?” Why? E T Activity 1 Look at the followin,g ores. Identify the metal present in each ore. A · Can you arrange these metals in the order of their reactivity? · What do you notice in Table – 2? G You will notice that the ores of many metals are oxides and sulphides. This is why oxygen - sulphur (16th group) group is cNalled chalcogen family (chalco = ore; genus = produce) A The metals like K, Na, Ca, Mg and Al are so reactive that they are never found in nature in free state. L The metals like Zn, Fe, Pb etc., are moderately reactive. They are found E in the earth crust mainly as oxides, sulphides and carbonates. Metals like Au, Ag are least reactive and they are found even in free T state in nature. Based on reactivity we can arrange metal in descending order of their , reactivity as shownT below: K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al Zn, Fe, Pb, Cu Hg, Ag, Pt, Au ––––––––R––––––– ––––––––––––––– ––––––––––––– High reactivity Moderate reactivity Low reactivity · Can you think how do we get these metals from their ores? E · Does the reactivity of a metal and form of its ore (oxides, sulphides, Cchlorides, carbonates sulphates) has any relation with process of extraction? S · How are metals extracted from mineral ores? · What methods are to be used? Let us find. 11.2 Extraction of metals from the ores: The extraction of a metal from its ore involves mainly three stages. They are: I) Concentration or Dressing II) Extraction of crude metal III)Refining or purification of the metal. 251 Principles of Metallurgy

Ore Hand picking Washing by Concentration of ore Froth flotation Magnetic Separation Extraction of crude metal from the ore A Metals of high Metals of medium Metals of low N reactivity reactivity reactivity ASulphide ore Halides Oxides Carbonate Sulphide Roasting G ore ore Oxides N Electrolysis of Calcination Roasting molten ore Reduction Calcination A Metal Metal Metal oxide (eg: Na, Mg, Al, etc.,) L Chemical Reduction R E eduction of metal Refining (eg:Ag) Auto Reduction T Displacement method Refining of metal Distillation (eg. Cu, Zn, etc.,) Electrolytic reduction , Poling T Liquation R Electrolytic refining 11.2.1 E Concentration or Dressing of the ore Ores that are mined from the earth are usually contaminated with large C amount of impurities such as soil and sand etc. S Concentration or Dressing means, simply getting rid of as much of the unwanted rocky material as possible from the ore. The impurities are called gangue. Here, we should get as for as possible pure or more concentrated ore. The physical methods adopted in dressing of the ore (or) enriching of the ore depends upon difference between physical properties of ore and gangue. 252 Principles of Metallurgy

Table-3 Name of the Process method Hand picking If the ore particles and the impurities are different in one of the properties like colour, size etc., Using that A property the ore particles are handpicked separating them from other impurities. Less G densive impurities are carried away by water flow, leaving the more densive ore particles behind. N Froth flotation This method is mainly useful for sulphide ores which have no wettinAg property whereas the impurities get wetted. The ore with impurities is finely powdered and L kept in water taken in a flotation cell. Air under pressure is bloEwn to produce froth in water. Froth so produced, takes the ore particles to the surface whereas impurities T settle at the bottom.
