11.2.2 Extraction of crude metal from the ore After concentrating the ore obtained from the earth we get refined ore. To extract the metal from refined ore convert ore to oxide by reduction process. The metal containing some impurities obtained by re-reducing the metal oxides. A Extraction of the metal from its ores depends on the reactivity of the N metal. To understand the order of reactivity of metals that are very familiar, we study their chemical reactions with cold water, steam, dilute, strong A acids and Cl and based on their vigorous activity order in these reactions 2 G we frame out activity series. Arrangement of the metals in decreasing order of their reactivity is known as activity series. (See table - 4) N Reduction of purified ore to the metal A The method used for a particular metal for the reduction of its ore to L the metal depends mainly on the position of the metal in the activity series. E A) Extraction of Metals at the top of the activity series (K, Na, Ca, Mg and Al)T. Simple chemical reduction methods like heating with C, CO etc to re duce the ores of these metals are not feasible. , The temperature required for the reduction is too high and more expensive. T To make the process economical, electrolysis methods are to be adopted. R Again the electrolysis of their aqueous solutions also is not feasible becauseE water in the solution would be discharged at the cathode in preference to the metal ions. C The only method available is to extract these metals by electrolysis of S their fused compounds. For example to extract Na from NaCl, fused NaCl is electrolysed with steel cathode (-) and graphite anode (+). The metal (Na) will be deposited at cathode and chloride liberated at the anode. At Cathode : 2Na+ + 2e– g 2Na At Anode : 2Cl – g Cl + 2e– 2 For the above electrolysis, a large quantity of electricity is required to keep the ore in molten state. Suitable impurities are added to the ore to decrease its melting point. 255 Principles of Metallurgy

B) Extraction of metals in the middle of the activity series (Zinc, iron, tin, lead and copper): The ores of these metals are generally present as sulphides or carbonates in nature. Therefore prior to reduction of ores of these metals, they must be converted into metal oxides. Sulphide ores are converted into oxides by heating them strongly in A excess of air. This process is known as roasting. Generally the sulphide N ores are roasted to convert them into oxides before reducing them to metal. A Example: 2PbS + 3O g 2PbO + 2SO 2 2 G The metal oxides are then reduced to the corresponding metal by using suitable reducing agent such as carbon N i) Reduction of metal oxides with carbon: The oxides are reduced by coke in a closed furnace which gives the metal and carbon monoxide A (CO). L Example: at 1400 oC PbO + C ––––––––––> Pb + CO E ii)Reduction of oxide ores with CO. Example: T in blast furnace Fe O + 3CO ––––––––––––> 2Fe + 3CO 2 3 2 iii) Auto (self) reduction of sulphide ores: In the extraction of Cu from its sulphide ore, the, ore is subjected partial roasting in air to give its T oxide. 2Cu SR + 3O g 2Cu O + 2SO 2 2 2 2 When the supply of air is stopped and the temperature is raised. The rest of thEe sulphide reacts with oxide and forms the metal and SO . 2 2Cu O + Cu S g 6Cu + SO C2 2 2 iv)Reduction of ores (compounds) by more reactive metals. Thermite Reactions:- Thermite process involves the reaction of S metal oxides with aluminium. When highly reactive metals such as sodium, calcium, aluminium etc., are used as reducing agents, they displace metals of lower reactivity from the compound. These displacement reactions are highly exothermic. The amount of heat evolved is so large that the metals produced are in molten state. The reaction of Iron oxide (Fe O ), with aluminium produces molten 2 3 iron which is used to join railings of railway tracks or cracked machine parts. This reaction is known as the thermite reaction. Fe O + 2Al g Al O + 2Fe + Heat 2 3 2 3 Cr O + 2Al g Al O + 2Cr + Heat 2 3 2 3 A N A G fig-3(a) fig-3(b) fig-3(c) N C) Extraction of metals at the bottom of the activity series (Ag, Hg etc) A Metals at the bottom of the activity series are often found in free L state. Their reactivity with other atoms is very low. The oxides of these E metals can be reduced to metals by heat alone and sometimes by displacement from their aqueTous solutions. i) When cinnabar (HgS) which is an ore of mercury, heated in air, it , is first converted into (HgO) then reduced to mercury on further heating. T Example: 2HRgS+ 3 O –H–ea–t–> 2HgO + 2 S O –H–e–at–> 2HgO H–e–a–t > 2Hg + O 2 2 2 (s) (g) (s) (g) (s) (g) DispElacement from aqueous solutions: Example: Ag S + 4CN - g 2[Ag(CN) ] - + S2 - C 2 (s) (aq) ( 2 (aq) (aq) 2[Ag(CN) ]- + Zn g [Zn(CN) ]2- + 2Ag S 2 (aq) (s) 4 (aq) (s) Here Ag S is dissolved in say KCN solution to get dicyanoargentate 2 (I) ions. From these ions Ag is precipitated by treating with Zn dust powder. 11.2.3 Purification of the crude metal The metal obtained by the reduction of the ore is usually contaminated with impurities like unchanged ore, other metals present in the ore and non metals from the anions in the ore. For example, the (blister) copper obtained from its sulphide ore, a compound of copper iron pyrites (CuFeS ), contains some copper sulphide, 2 257 Principles of Metallurgy

iron and sulphur. It is purified by suitable methods including electrolysis. The process of obtaining the pure metal from the impure metal is called refining of the metal. Refining of the metal involves several types of processes. Some refining methods are given below: a) Distillation (b) Poling (c) Liquation (d) Electrolysis etc. A The process that has to be adopted for purification of a given metal depends on the nature of the metal and its impurities. N a) Distillation: This method is very useful for purification of low A boiling metals like zinc and mercury containing high boiling metals as impurities. The extracted metal in the molten state is dGistilled to obtain the pure metal as distillate. b) Poling: The molten metal is stirred with logsN (poles) of green wood. The impurities are removed either as gases or they get oxidized and form A scum (slag) over the surface of the molten metal. Blister copper is purified by this method. The reducing gases, evoLlved from the wood, prevent the oxidation of copper. E c) Liquation: In this method a low melting metal like tin can be made to flow on a slopy surface to Tseparate it from high melting impurities. d) Electrolytic refining: In this method, the impure metal is made to act as anode. A strip o,f the same metal in pure form is used as cathode. T They are put in a suitable electrolytic bath containing soluble salt of the same metal. TRhe required metal gets deposited on the cathode in the pure form. The metal, constituting the impurity, goes as the anode mud. The E reactions are: Anode: M g Mn+ + ne- C Cathode: Mn+ + ne- g M (M = pure metal ) S Where n = 1,2,3, ... We use this electrolytic method to refine copper. For this an impure copper is taken as anode and pure copper strips are taken as cathode. The electrolyte is an acidified solution of copper sulphate. As a result of electrolysis copper in pure form is transferred fig-4: Experimental setup for the electrolytic from the anode to the cathode. refining of copper 258 Principles of Metallurgy

Anode: Cu g Cu2+ + 2e- Cathode: Cu2+ + 2e- g Cu The soluble impurities go into the solution, where as insoluble impurities from the blister copper get deposited at the bottom of anode as anode mud which contains metals like antimony selenium, tellurium, silver, gold and platinum; recovery of these metals may meet the cost of refining. A Zinc may also be refined this way. N 11.3 Corrosion The rusting of iron (iron oxide), tarnishing of silver (silver sulphide), A development of green coating on copper (copper carbonate) and bronze are some of the examples of corrosion. G · Do you know why corrosion occurs? · In which coses corrosion occurs? N Let us find A Activity 2 L · Take three test tubes and place clean iron nails in each of them. E · Label these test tubes A,B and C. Pour some water in test tube A and cork it. T · Pour boiled distilled water in test tube B, add about 1 ml of oil and cork it. The oil will floa t on water and prevent the air from dissolving , in the water. T · Put some anhydrous calcium chloride in test tube C and cork it. AnhydrouRs calcium chloride will absorb the moisture, if any, from the air. Leave these test tubes for a few days and then observe (see figure). E · You will observe that iron nails rust in test tube A, but they do not rust in test tubes B and C. In C the test tube A, the nails are exposed to both air and water. In the test tube B, the nails are exposed S Air Air Dry to only water, and the nails in test tube C are air exposed to dry air. Layer of oil · What does this tell us about the conditions under Rusty which iron articles rust? iron nails In metallic corrosion, a metal is oxidised by loss of electrons generally to oxygen and results in the Water formation of oxides. Corrosion of iron (commonly Boiled Anhydrous known as rusting) occurs in presence of water and distilled water calcium chloride air. fig-5: Investigating the conditions under which iron rusts 259 Principles of Metallurgy

The chemistry of corrosion is quite complex but it may be considered essentially as an electrochemical phenomenon. During corrosion at a particular spot on the surface of an object made of iron, oxidation takes place and that spot behaves as anode. We can write the reaction as. Anode: 2Fe g 2Fe2+ + 4e– (s) Electrons released at this anodic spot move through the metal and go A to another spot on the metal and reduce oxygen at that spot in presence of N H+ which is believed to be available from H CO formed due to dissolution 2 3 of carbon dioxide from air into water in moist air condition of atmosphere. A Hydrogen ion in water may also be available due to dissolution of other acidic oxides from the atmosphere. This spot behaves asG cathode with the reaction is. Cathode: O + 4H+ + 4e- g 2H ON 2(g) (aq) 2 (l) The overall reaction is: 2Fe +O +4H+ g 2Fe2+ +2H O (s) 2(g) (Aaq) (aq) 2 (l) The Ferrous ions (Fe2+) are further oxidised by atmospheric oxygen to Ferric ions (Fe3+) which come out as ruLst in the form of hydrated ferric oxide (Fe O .XH O) and with further production of hydrogen ions. 2 3 2 E 11.3.1 Prevention of corrosion T Prevention of corrosion is of prime importance. It not only saves money but also helps in preventing accidents such as a bridge collapse or failure , of a key component due to corrosion. T One of the simplest methods of preventing corrosion is to prevent the R surface of the metallic object to come in contact with atmosphere. This can be done by covering the surface with paint or by some chemicals E (eg: bisphenol). C Do you know? S Alloying is a method of improving the properties of a metal. We can get desired properties by this method. For example, iron is the most widely used metal. But it is never used in its pure state. This is because pure iron is very soft and stretches easily when hot. But, if it is mixed with a small amount of carbon, it becomes hard and strong. When iron is mixed with nickel and chromium we get stainless steel which will not rust. Pure gold, known as 24 carat gold, is very soft. It is, therefore, not suitable for making jewellery. It is alloyed with either silver or copper to make it hard. Generally in India 22carat gold is used for making ornaments. It means that 22 parts of pure gold is alloyed with 2 parts of either silver or copper. 260 Principles of Metallurgy

Another simple method is to cover the surface by other metals like Sn, Zn etc that are inert or react themselves with atmosphere to save the object. This is generally done by electroplating. An electrochemical method is to provide a sacrificial electrode of another metal like Mg, Zn etc which corrodes itself but saves the object. A 11.4 A few important processes used in metallurgy N 11.4.1 Smelting: Smelting is a pyrochemical (pyre = heat) process, in which A the ore is mixed with flux and fuel and strongly G heated. The heat is so strong that the ore is Skip reduced, and the metal is obtained in molten cNar state. Charge A hoppers During smelting the impurities (gangue) in L the ore react with flux to form slag which is E ~200 oC removed. For haematite (Fe O )ore, coke is 2 3 used as fuel and lime stone (CTaCO ) is used as Waste ~700 oC 3 gases flux. The smelting is carried out in a specially Reduction Alternating , built furnace known as blast furnace. layers of iron T ore and coke Heat The reactions inside the furnace are: ~1200 oC absorption R zone 2C + O ––––> 2CO Fuel (s) E2 (g) (g) Fusion Hot air zone Fe C O + 3CO ––––> 2Fe + 3CO ~2000 oC Com zo bu n s e tion 2 3(s) (g) (l) 2(g) Molten haematite Molten iron slag S CaCO ––––> CaO + CO 3(s) (s) 2 (g) fig-6: Blast furance Limestone(flux) lime CaO + SiO ––––> CaSiO (s) 2(s) 3(l) Lime silica(gangue) calcium silicate(slag) 261 Principles of Metallurgy

11.4.2 Roasting: Roasting is a pyrochemical process in which the ore is heated in the presence of oxygen or air below its melting point. The products (like metal oxide from sulphide ore) obtained in the process also are in solid state. Generally reverberatory furnace is used for roasting. 2ZnS + 3O ––––> 2ZnO + 2SO (s) 2(g) (s) 2(g) zinc blende A 11.4.3 Calcination: Calcination is a pyrochemical process in which the ore is heated in the absence of air. Sea water also contains some soluble salts such as sodium chloride and magnesium chloride etc. 249 Principles of Metallurgy Some metals like gold (Au), silver (Ag) and copper (Cu) are available in nature in free state (native) as they are least reactive. Other metals mostly are found in nature in the combined form due to their more reactivity. The elements or compounds of the metals which occur in nature in the earth crust are called minerals. At some places, minerals contain a very high percentage of a particular metal and the metal can be profitably extracted from it. The minerals from A which the metals are extracted without economical loss are called ores. N Aluminium, for example, is the most common metal in the Earth’s crust, occurring in most of minerals. However, it isn’t economically A feasible to extract it from most of these minerals. Instead, the usual ore from which it is profitable to extract it is bauxite – which contains G 50 – 70 % of aluminium oxide . For example, the (blister) copper obtained from its sulphide ore, a compound of copper iron pyrites (CuFeS ), contains some copper sulphide, 2 257 Principles of Metallurgy iron and sulphur. It is purified by suitable methods including electrolysis. The process of obtaining the pure metal from the impure metal is called refining of the metal. Refining of the metal involves several types of processes. Some refining methods are given below: a) Distillation (b) Poling (c) Liquation (d) Electrolysis etc. A The process that has to be adopted for purification of a given metal depends on the nature of the metal and its impurities. It not only saves money but also helps in preventing accidents such as a bridge collapse or failure , of a key component due to corrosion. T One of the simplest methods of preventing corrosion is to prevent the R surface of the metallic object to come in contact with atmosphere. This can be done by covering the surface with paint or by some chemicals E (eg: bisphenol). C Do you know? S Alloying is a method of improving the properties of a metal. We can get desired properties by this method. For example, iron is the most widely used metal. But it is never used in its pure state. This is because pure iron is very soft and stretches easily when hot. But, if it is mixed with a small amount of carbon, it becomes hard and strong. When iron is mixed with nickel and chromium we get stainless steel which will not rust. Pure gold, known as 24 carat gold, is very soft. It is, therefore, not suitable for making jewellery. It is alloyed with either silver or copper to make it hard. Generally in India 22carat gold is used for making ornaments. (AS ) 4 265 Principles of Metallurgy CHAPTER A 12 Carbon and its N Compounds A G N The food you eat, the clothes you wear, the cosmetics you use, the fuels you use to run automobiles are all the compounds of carbon. A Carbon was discovered in prehistory and it was known to the ancients. L They used to manufacture charcoal by burning organic material. E Carbon is a non-metal. It belongs to the fourteenth group or IV A group in the modern periodicT table. The elements of this group have four electrons in the valence shell. , Let us write the electronic configuration of Carbon ( C). T 6 Atomic number of carbon is 6. R Electronic configuration of carbon (ground state) C: 1s2 2s2 2p2. To 6 get the oEctet in its outer shell it has to gain four more electrons to form C4-. The electronegativity of carbon is only 2.5 and its nucleus has only C six protons. Therefore it would be difficult for a nucleus with six protons S to hold ten electrons. Hence, carbon cannot form C4- ions so easily. · Can carbon get helium configuration by losing four electrons from the outer shell? If carbon loses four electrons from the outer shell, it has to form C4+ ions. This requires huge amount of energy which is not available normally. Therefore C4+ formation also is a remote possibility. Carbon has to satisfy its tetravalency by sharing electrons with other atoms. It has to form four covalent bonds either with its own atoms or atoms of other elements. 266 Carbon and its Compounds The possibility of bonds formation by a carbon atom is as follows: a) i. We can explain it by the phenomenon called hybridisation. 12.2 Hybridisation The concept of hybridisation was introduced by Linus Pauling (1931). The redistribution of orbitals of almost equal energy in individual atoms to give equal number of new orbitals with identical properties like energy and shape is called “hybridisation”. The newly formed orbitals are called as ‘hybrid orbitals.’ In the excited carbon atom its one s-orbital (2s) and three p-orbitals (2p , 2p , 2p ) intermix and reshuffle into four identical orbitals known as x y z sp3 orbitals. The first discovered organic compounds became known by their common names. Ex: Ethyne (C H ) is 2 2 known as Acetylene. 284 Carbon and its Compounds

As carbon compound is very big it is difficult to remember their names individually. To overcome this problem they have to be properly named. For this, the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) had been formed, and one of its responsibilities is to name the organic and inorganic compounds in a systematic order. The basic idea behind the systematic nomenclature is that there should be only one name for the A given structure throughout the world and also there should be only one structure for the given name. N The IUPAC name of an organic compound consists of three parts : 1) Word A root 2) Prefix 3) Suffix. 12.10.1 The number of carbon atoms present in the molecGules or principle chain is called word root. N C - Meth; C - eth; C - prop; C - but ; C -pent; C - hex; 1 2 3 4 5 6 C - hept; C -oct; C -non; C - dec and so on. A 7 8 9 10 12.10.2 Prefix: The substituents in the molecule are shown as the prefix. L Prefix again has several parts known as primary prefix secondary prefix, numerical prefix and nEumber prefix. (i) Primary prefix : It is useful only for cyclic compounds (Cyclo). If T the compounds are not cyclic, this part of the name is absent. (ii)Secondary prefix : Thi s tells about the second grade functional groups , known as substiTtuents. For example halogens, alkyl groups(R), alkoxy groups(-OR) etc. which are written as halo, alkyl, alkoxy. R (iii) Numerical prefix : When the same substituent, multiple bond or functional group is repeated twice, thrice etc., are denoted by di, tri, E tetra... respectively. These are written before secondary prefix, primary C secondary suffix. (iv)Number prefix : This tells about to which carbon atoms of the S compound the substituent(s), multiple bond(s) or functional group(s) are attached. 12.10.3 Suffix : The functional groups in the molecule are shown as the suffix. It also contains several parts known as primary suffix, secondary suffix, numerical suffix and number suffix etc. (i) Primary suffix : This tells about the saturation of the compound. For saturated (C-C) single bonded compounds it is ‘ane’. For unsaturated (C=C) double bonded compounds it is ‘ene’. For unsaturated triple bonded (C C ) compounds it is ‘yne’. 285 Carbon and its Compounds

(ii)Secondary suffix : This tells about the functional groups with the particular term. While writing the names of the derivatives of hydrocarbons the last letter ‘e’ of ane, ene, yne is dropped if the suffix starts with a vowel. ‘e’ should be maintained if the suffix including numerical preffix with a consonent. For example: For hydrocarbons it is ‘e’ for Alcohols it is ‘ –ol ’ Aldehydes it is ‘ –al ‘ A Ketones it is ‘ –one ‘ and Carboxylic acid it is ‘ –oic acid’ N You can see some more secondary suffixes and primary suffixes in table 4. They are: A 1) Combustion 2) Oxidation reactions 3) Addition reactions 4) Substitution reactions N 12.13.1 Combustion reactions A Carbon, and its compounds burn in presence of oxygen or air to give CO , heat and light.

G 2 The process of burning of carbon or carbon compound in excess of N oxygen to give heat and light is called the combustion reaction.
